Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) are powerful deep learning models for noise-resistant analysis of noisy time-series, with their core time-dilated convolution mechanism being key to their temporal modeling capabilities. While TCNs have shown promising results in machine maintenance, prior studies indicate that their core parameterization is suboptimal. Although recent approaches have sought to learn dilation factors alongside weights, they are limited to constant dilations over sliding windows and rely on heuristics for initial dilation values. We propose a novel scheme that learns both the dilation factor and network weights jointly and end-to-end. By formulating the search for an optimal constant dilation for dense convolution layers as a weighted combination of model accuracy and sparsity, we utilize the LIME algorithm to derive a compact network with an optimally learned dilation factor. Our methodology significantly enhances the model space exploration for TCNs, yielding up to a 7.4x reduction in memory usage and a 3.1x decrease in inference time on CPU platforms without sacrificing accuracy. Furthermore, our approach delivers tighter training error bounds on test data for power load, electricity heating/cooling, and industrial sensor noising tasks compared to state-of-the-art manually tuned TCNs. The effectiveness of our proposed optimization for TCNs is validated through numerical and theoretical analyses. Consequently, our work establishes a carefully optimized baseline of compact and accurate time-dilated convolutional networks, creating a robust foundation for improving model resistance to noisy temporal data. containing missing values (nulls) alongside functional dependencies. While the conventional stance holds that table instances must adhere to all imposed functional dependencies, it is equally significant to formulate theories for handling instances that violate certain dependencies. Concerning missing values, we do not presuppose their existence; rather, a missing value is considered to exist only if it can be inferred from the table's functional dependencies.

We present a formal framework where each table tuple is assigned one of four truth values: true, false, inconsistent, or unknown. We demonstrate that this framework facilitates the study of critical issues such as consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality metrics, among others. However, this work primarily concentrates on consistent query answering, a problem that has garnered significant attention over recent decades.

The paper's main contributions are as follows: (a) we introduce a novel approach for addressing inconsistencies in tables with nulls and functional dependencies, (b) we offer a new definition for table merging that accommodates missing values, and (c) we propose a comprehensive data quality measure to assess the inconsistency level of such tables. Regarding consistent query answering, we examine the problem of determining the certain truth value of an atom relative to a table instance and its functional dependencies, and we investigate the complexity of computing this certain truth value.

The paper is structured into ten sections. Section 2 provides the necessary background, followed by Section 3, which outlines the formal language and notations used to represent tables with nulls and functional dependencies. Section 4 defines the four truth values (true, false, inconsistent, and unknown) for table tuples, and Section 5 details the concept of table merging and its relationship with consistent query answering. Furthermore, Section 6 explores the complexity of consistent query answering, along with the complexities of merging tables that contain missing values. Sections 7 through 10 are dedicated to data quality, beginning with an analysis of inconsistency measures, followed by the formulation of consistent query answering, merging tables with missing values, and determining the highest complexity for such merging operations, respectively. Finally, Section 11 concludes the paper with a summary of the results and suggestions for future research.

In Section 2, we review the foundational elements of our work, including first-order logic, relational databases, missing value representation, functional dependencies, data inconsistency, table merging, consistent query answering, and data quality measures.

Consequently, the TV-PARX-MLE model is created to capture the time series properties of these distributions. The representation of these distributions as special cases also enables the modeling of negative dependence structures among variables with strictly positive values using multivariate extensions of these distributions. for the future International Linear Collider (ILC), a configuration validated in 2012. It employs a compact, cost-effective architecture tailored for precise Higgs boson measurements and sensitivity to diverse new physics phenomena. By integrating a robust silicon vertex and tracking system with a five Tesla central solenoidal magnet, the design achieves superior momentum resolution. Additionally, its highly granular calorimeter is optimized for Particle Flow techniques, ensuring excellent jet energy resolution across a broad energy spectrum. As the ILC's potential construction date approaches, it is crucial to review the design and technology decisions finalized during the Design-Building (DBD) phase, updating them based on recent technological advancements. The discussion will cover R&D topics and opportunities for involvement across all areas of SiD development. The SiD Detector plays a pivotal role in searching for dark matter through various indirect methods, such as reconstructing final states with missing energy or identifying recoil phenomena; this process is enhanced by precise vertexing, tau lepton reconstruction, low-threshold electron measurement, and the accurate determination of hadronic energies even at minimal energy levels. This presentation encompasses a wide array of R&D areas, including upgrades to the outer support structure to accommodate new magnet designs, the integration of superconducting materials in the calorimeter for improved hadronic resolution, innovations in silicon vertex detectors and hadronic pre-sholders, and the deployment of advanced timing layers for photon reconstruction and suppression of out-of-beam backgrounds. Furthermore, the ILC will facilitate direct dark matter production through s-channel interactions, potentially offering higher luminosity than current LHC capabilities. The SiD Detector is also essential for resolving ambiguities in global electroweak parameters and searching for heavy, long-lived particles with decay lengths up to a meter; its full reconstruction capability extends to significantly lower mass thresholds for specific particle types. Finally, the discussion will address the application of Machine Learning and other cutting-edge technologies to ensure the optimal utilization of the ILC's vast data output. This session will also showcase the extensive global collaboration required for the successful operation of the SiD Detector.

Our study examines chemical abundances across various elemental groups—including light, odd-Z, $\alpha$, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements—based on high signal-to-noise spectra of seven giant members. The resulting mean cluster metallicity is determined to be [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$, showing no signs of intrinsic metallicity dispersion. Ton~2 displays a standard $\alpha$-enrichment pattern consistent with other high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters, mirroring trends observed in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. However, we detect a significant spread in nitrogen abundance ($>0.87$ dex) and a substantial population of nitrogen-enriched stars. Considering Ton~2's relatively high metallicity, these nitrogen levels far exceed typical Galactic averages, confirming the prevalence of the multiple-population phenomenon; the cluster also hosts stars with low, first-generation nitrogen abundances. Additionally, we identify a [Ce/Fe] abundance spread in Ton~2 that correlates with nitrogen enhancement, suggesting that \textit{s}-process enrichment was likely driven by an intermediate-mass star from an external population during the cluster's evolution. Finally, the analysis of nitrogen, carbon, and oxygen abundances offers novel constraints on theoretical models of early cluster evolution. Ton~2 is confirmed as a dynamically relaxed system that formed with a classic two-component mass spectrum, exhibiting no significant expansion during its evolution. These findings provide crucial observational benchmarks for constraining the mass-loss laws of red giants and evaluating evolutionary scenarios for globular clusters. As the second chemical analysis of a high-metallicity, nitrogen-rich, multiple-population globular cluster utilizing APOGEE-2 data, this work should be viewed in the context of the concurrent study by {\"O}zdemir et al. (2024). The derived abundances will also serve as essential benchmarks for interpreting nucleosynthetic predictions from stellar structure codes in upcoming machine learning investigations.

Defined as intricate electromagnetic structures, they are characterized by extreme thinness relative to the wavelength, extensive transverse dimensions, and composition of subwavelength scatterers with minute features. These structures often exhibit properties such as bianisotropy, spatial and temporal variability, nonlinearity, curvature, and multiphysics interactions. Given this complexity, effective metasurface design demands a comprehensive strategy that integrates synergistic synthesis and analysis grounded in a robust theoretical model. The Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions (GSTCs), when paired with bianisotropic surface susceptibility functions, offer such a framework. We validate this framework through two case studies: time-reversal modulation and polarization conversion. Ultimately, this research provides an essential foundation for the effective design of advanced metasurfaces.

### 1 Introduction

Metasurfaces represent a specific class of metastructures typically several wavelengths thick, consisting of subwavelength meta-atoms arranged in one, two, or three dimensions. Their unique attributes—including extreme thinness, curvature, temporal variability, nonlinear behavior, and complexity—enable the manipulation of wavefronts to achieve functionalities that are unattainable with conventional structures. For instance, metasurfaces can effect spatial and temporal changes in transmissivity, impedances, and boundary conditions across both magnetoelectric and magnetoelectric regimes. These capabilities make them ideal for applications such as beam steering, super-lensing, polarization conversion, and sensing. However, the complex geometry and material构成 of metasurfaces make their analysis and synthesis particularly challenging. While various parameterization techniques exist, susceptibility functions provide a potent method for modifying wavefronts. Specifically, susceptibility functions allow for the transformation of standard metallic or dielectric structures into ultra-thin layers without altering their external scattering characteristics. This paper investigates various types of susceptibility functions usable with GSTCs for designing thin metasurfaces.

Introduction: Accurate determination of the total energy for the ground state of few- and few-electron atomic systems is critical for advancing both fundamental physics and practical applications. The most accurate technique for calculating atomic energies is the Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) method [1, 2]. FCI provides the exact non-relativistic solution to the Schrödinger equation for atomic systems without relying on model Hamiltonians or approximations. Although FCI yields highly precise total energies, it demands excessive computational resources, making it infeasible for larger systems. To overcome this barrier, various approximation and acceleration approaches have been proposed. These include quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods [3, 4], which offer a different accuracy-precision balance; density functional theory (DFT) [5, 6]; and the self-consistent field (SCF) method [7, 8]. However, each comes with specific limitations and challenges. For instance, while DFT offers greater accuracy than SCF by employing an exchange-correlation functional, its reliance on approximate functionals still results in lower precision than FCI. Similarly, QMC achieves higher accuracy than DFT but remains computationally intensive for larger systems. Although the stochastic fixed-point algorithm can converge to the exact FCI ground state [9, 10], it requires significant computational resources. Consequently, there is a pressing need for cost-effective and precise algorithms to compute atomic energies.

Acrylic plastic (PMMA) acoustic lenses have long been used to widen the acceptance angle of sensitive detectors and improve lateral resolution, but they frequently introduce image artifacts due to internal ultrasound reflections. This work examines a new lens material, Stycast 1090SI, by comparing its acoustic properties with those of PMMA. The performance of detectors fitted with these lenses was assessed through both theoretical acceptance angle analysis and experimental lateral resolution tests. Our findings reveal that Stycast 1090SI possesses superior acoustic properties to PMMA, resulting in image artifacts at least five times smaller. Additionally, its smooth surface allows direct placement against biological tissue, a capability PMMA lacks. These theoretical conclusions were confirmed using experimental detection efficiency and lateral resolution data. Consequently, Stycast 1090SI lenses are poised to enable high-resolution imaging in scenarios where PMMA limitations currently exist. Finally, this new material paves the way for diverse acoustic sensor applications. Keywords: lateral resolution; acceptance angle; sonar; hydroacoustics; transducer; Stycast 1090SI. This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. However, we show that generalized $\theta$-terms induce a generalized Witten effect, implying that the charged state spectrum forms an infinite tower. Although these states are heavy, they become light in the non-perturbative regime of the effective theory, adhering to the expectations derived from the Swampland Distance Conjecture. Additionally, we demonstrate that generalizing global symmetries in this manner aligns with the principles of the Tower of States Conjecture. Finally, we note that our analysis does not account for generalizing global symmetries via charged hypermultiples. This work serves as a crucial step toward formulating the Generalized Swampland Conjecture. I thank Zhaozhu Zhi for valuable discussions. Our objective is to reduce both the quantity and intricacy of hardware and software elements that users must trust to resist adversarial attacks. We propose a multi-domain hardware architecture featuring statically partitioned, physically isolated trust domains. For security-critical applications, our machine significantly lowers the required trust compared to standard Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) while maintaining satisfactory performance. For standard applications, performance remains comparable to that of legacy systems. To validate the security guarantees of our machine, we conducted a series of hardware attacks, including glider attacks and simultaneous instruction dumping, specifically targeting the FPGA. Additionally, we evaluated the security of our hardware attacks by implementing them on a TEE prototype, ensuring that our multi-domain machine provides at least as much security as standard TEEs. To assess the security of our hardware attacks, we implemented them on a TEE prototype, guaranteeing that our multi-domain machine offers at least as much security as conventional TEEs. This work aims to aid users in allocating applications to trust levels by automatically migrating security-critical apps to strongly isolated domains (such as our multi-domain machine's strongest domains) from weaker ones (like single-core CPUs), utilizing a static application analyzer that relies on hardware hints to efficiently and accurately identify migration requirements. Our evaluation shows that for migrated applications, our machine provides security comparable to fully trusted hardware while maintaining high performance. To validate that our machine does not unnecessarily restrict application functionality, we tested over 100 apps from Google Play, observing no significant source-code changes were required for compatibility. We propose an attack model featuring an \textit{adaptive} adversary capable of arbitrarily corrupting rewards and transitions based on the policy being optimized. Our model, grounded in maximum entropy game theory, establishes a novel min-max formulation that seeks to maximize the entropy of the optimal policy's state-value distribution while minimizing the adversary's corruption cost. We demonstrate that the attack complexity defined within this framework is tight. Building on this, we introduce an attack complexity-aware policy gradient algorithm, proving its robustness against bounded corruption of both rewards and transitions. Finally, we extend our approach to handle corrupted observational data, introducing a novel algorithm for robust off-policy evaluation. Experimental results across various environments validate our theoretical findings. This work initiates a program aimed at developing efficient algorithms for reinforcement learning systems exposed to arbitrary levels of sensor corruption.

We introduce a unified framework for online learning with expert advice that simultaneously addresses two challenging aspects: an adaptive time horizon and an adversary controlling the availability of experts. The model's competitive cost captures the interplay between the algorithm's adaptivity to an uncorrupted world and its robustness against an adversary attempting to degrade reward access. This framework yields several novel online learning algorithms with optimal competitive costs. Specifically, it resolves two research questions posed in \cite{JN20}. Our findings imply that any algorithm robust to corrupted rewards cannot tolerate more than an sublinear number of arbitrarily corrupt transitions without incurring superoptimal sample complexity. Furthermore, for decision problems with corrupted transitions, we achieve an algorithm with competitive cost matching the lower bound (up to logarithmic factors) recently established in \cite{JKKLSLKS}. These results encompass robust MDPs with transition corruption, algorithms for absolute-sense robust MDPs, methods for identifying maximally reliable experts, and high-dimensional robust bandits with margin. The proof technique relies on a new mixtures-of-experts algorithm with optimal competitive cost \cite{JKKS}. While not the primary focus, we exhibit extensions to monotone MDPs and extendivity, offering insights into simultaneously achieving robustness to corrupted transitions and sample efficiency. Finally, we present extensions for handling corrupted transition density estimates in off-policy evaluation.

Quantum acoustic cavities and resonators are instrumental in investigating these multi-phonon phenomena through both theoretical and experimental lenses. Specifically, this work examines a system comprising a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser and coupled to an acoustic cavity. While such systems exhibit fascinating multi-phonon behaviors, previous descriptions of the quantum dot were restricted to a two-level model, limiting the complexity inherent to real semiconductor quantum dots. In contrast, our proposed model incorporates both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot; the latter are especially valuable due to their reduced decoherence rates, as they do not undergo spontaneous phonon emission. Within this framework, we demonstrate that by precisely adjusting the driving laser frequency, one can induce giant Rabi oscillations between the vacuum state and a dark exciton state involving $N$-phonon components. This approach highlights two significant achievements: first, it enables the creation of dark state excitations with defined $N$-phonon components through external control, a goal unattainable in conventional quantum dot-acoustic cavity systems, and second, it offers a novel pathway to prepare dark state excitons surrounded by a specific number $N$ of phonons. Consequently, this method provides a route to generate phonon cat states within the quantum dot-acoustic cavity system. Furthermore, implementing this proposal requires a quantum dot with both electron and hole confinement along the acoustic wave propagation direction. While current quantum dot technology largely achieves perfect confinement in one dimension (typically the hole), electron confinement remains imperfect. Therefore, the required quantum dot can be constructed using an alloy device design, such as InGaAs embedded in a GaAs matrix. Additionally, necessary support structures, including a quantum well and a semi-infinite semiconductor, are required to ensure the quantum dot is isolated from the cavity. Since this configuration is standard in cavity quantum electrodynamics, the proposed setup is technically feasible. Finally, the resource cost, measured by purity, required to generate $N$-phonon states within the dark exciton state is significantly lower than in conventional quantum dot-acoustic cavity systems. This research not only clarifies the implementation of multi-phonon effects in these systems but also paves the way for future investigations into higher-order correlation functions and related phenomena in quantum dot-acoustic cavity systems. Additionally, this system offers a viable platform for implementing a phonon laser. The threshold condition for this device is realizable with current quantum dot technology

Consequently, physicians often rely on supplementary data, such as endoscopic reports, clinical histories, and PET scans; however, gathering this information is time-consuming, prone to errors, and can yield non-deterministic outcomes. bons are frequently found in complex reservoirs, making real-time optimized well placement (geosteering) essential for effective production and cost reduction. This process typically relies on updated formation evaluations derived from real-time well-log interpretation. Therefore, a workflow that is reliable, computationally efficient, and robust for interpreting logs while capturing uncertainties is critical. This study integrates an iterative ensemble-based approach, specifically the approximate Levenberg-Marquardt form of Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (LM-EnRML), into such a workflow. By minimizing the statistical misfit between actual well-logging measurements and theoretical outputs from forward simulators, the method estimates model parameters—including resistivity, density, and boundary locations—along with their associated uncertainties. Analysis of various synthetic cases with different log types confirmed the method's ability to accurately estimate these parameters. Comparative CPU time analysis reveals that the proposed approach is approximately 10 to 125 times faster than common statistical methods like Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, and it supports parallel processing across multiple CPUs. Furthermore, testing on a case inspired by a real field demonstrated accurate formation evaluation. Consequently, the proposed ensemble-based method has proven to be both robust and computationally efficient for simultaneously calculating multiple parameters and their uncertainties, satisfying the demands of geosteering applications.

Nested NER, a specific subset of NER, involves named entities that are contained within one another. However, many prior studies on nested NER utilize linear structures to model entities that inherently possess a hierarchical organization. To resolve this discrepancy, this work treats all nested entities within a sentence as a unified structure and introduces a holistic structure parsing algorithm to identify the complete set of entities simultaneously. Furthermore, addressing the current lack of research on incorporating corpus-level information into NER, we integrate Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI) and other frequency-based features derived from corpus-aware statistics. We hypothesized that this phenomenon significantly influences online misinformation dissemination because, despite their global potential, digital interactions are inherently localized, with interaction likelihood dropping sharply as distance increases. Analyzing over 8 million Reddit comments containing news links from January 2016 to December 2019, we discovered that Reddit does not function as a "hype machine" for misinformation as other platforms do; instead, it operates as a supply-and-demand system. Specifically, the volume of misinformation news scaled linearly with the population of each state (scaling exponent $\beta=1$, $R^2 = 0.95$). Moreover, variations from this universal trend were best predicted by state-level personality and cultural attributes ($R^2 = \{0.12, 0.39\}$), rather than socioeconomic factors ($R^2 = \{0.15, 0.29\}$) or political characteristics ($R^2 = \{0.06, 0.21\}$). We observed that states with residents exhibiting lower conscientiousness and cultures characterized by loose norms (low cultural tightness) experienced higher-than-expected circulation of all news and specifically misinformation news. Additionally, states where residents score highest in openness to experience showed lower-than-expected misinformation news spread. Finally, we examined whether the "Big Sort" exacerbates misinformation impact by restricting exposure to only a fraction of the national population. However, despite each state containing just a small percentage of America's total population, a disproportionate amount of misinformation news traffic—up to 70%—originated from within each individual state. This evidence suggests that the Big Sort does not create demand for misinformation across state lines; instead, it amplifies impact by confining exposure to nearby residents. In summary, our findings indicate that the offline Big Sort is a primary driver of online misinformation spread, as digital news consumption is a highly localized behavior that enhances impact by limiting exposure to proximate communities. Consequently, both the individual and cultural properties of these segregated offline environments must be integrated into future models of misinformation diffusion.

Maximal coprimality graphs, recently popularized by Gebauer and Knill, represent points by the prime factorization patterns of their coordinates. This study investigates 3-maximality within the Cartesian product of two finite abelian groups, $\mathbb{Z}_{n_1} \times \mathbb{Z}_{n_2}$, where $n_1 > n_1 > 1$. We derive precise bounds for the maximal coprimality number of this set, with our lower bound constructed via a coloring algorithm inspired by Brooks' Theorem. Special cases including $\mathbb{Z}_n^3$ and $\mathbb{Z}_p^d$ (for any prime $n$ and positive integer $d$) are also addressed. Finally, we propose several open questions regarding the inherent maximality of $\mathbb{Z}_n$-modules.

This work examines the robustness of over-parametrized ResNets under label noise. Our theoretical analysis reveals that ResNet architectures naturally induce a regularization effect under noisy labels, effectively preventing model collapse. Specifically, we establish that the test risk is bounded by a term inversely proportional to the network width, indicating that wider networks offer greater resilience to label noise. Numerical experiments confirm these findings and offer further insights into the influence of network depth and initialization scale.

Electric vehicles offer promising potential for both increasing grid resilience and supporting transportation system robustness. We construct a multi-agent optimization problem featuring equilibrium conditions (N-MOPEC) to represent the decentralized decisions of decision-makers (DMs) in both transportation and energy sectors. Specifically, private EV owners act as DMs in the transportation network, seeking to minimize travel costs (such as time and money), whereas power dispatchers act as DMs in the energy network, aiming to optimize power allocation. We design a computational algorithm capable of efficiently solving the N-MOPEC problem. Through extensive numerical experiments, we evaluate the impact of charging dynamics on the resilience of both coupled networks and derive practical policy implications for charging private EVs. Our results indicate that while decentralized charging can improve the resilience of the transportation network, it may significantly degrade the resilience of the power network or the coupled systems. Consequently, allowing unrestricted charging for all private EVs can severely compromise the resilience of the power network or the coupled networks after a disruption. These findings suggest that utilizing private EVs for resilience purposes is only feasible if charging is limited to a subset of these vehicles. To satisfy the requirements for triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom, the model necessitates exactly three families. Additionally, $X$ and $Y$ bosons are posited to facilitate the conversion of two protons into two electrons, offering a potential resolution to the "missing satellite" problem by inducing a cutoff in the dark matter density profile near galactic centers. To account for the absence of decay observations between protons and electrons, $X$ and $Y$ bosons acquire their masses through mixing with Higgs doublets and triplets, respectively; however, to suppress the decay rate below current experimental limits, the Higgs triplet's mass must exceed 1 TeV. Consequently, this work analyzes the constraints imposed by direct search experiments on the masses of bileptons, $X$, and $Y$ within this framework. Furthermore, to address the "gamma excess" observed in satellite galaxies by the Fermi satellite, a specific decay mode for dark matter is proposed in this model. Although this mode has not yet been detected, it can account for the excess if the associated cross-section is approximately $10^{-27}$ cm$^2$. This analysis also clarifies why certain solutions to the missing satellite problem remain incompatible with the gamma excess. Finally, to explain both the "110 GeV dip" reported by ATLAS and the "110 GeV excess" found by Fermi, we propose that dark matter decays via $X$ bosons into two muons. Although this scenario has been constrained by LHC data, it remains viable for future investigations. The proposed bilepton model provides a unified framework for dark matter, neutrino masses, and various anomalies identified by the Fermi satellite and particle accelerators. Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context. We release the contextual evaluation dataset, ContextEval, at https://conide.github.io/ContextEval/. We also provide additional insights, including a discussion on receptive fields, an analysis of instance segmentation metrics, and details on the sequential removal of objects and background. Finally, we outline limitations regarding the dataset, such as constraints on difficult contexts, the exclusion of text-based contexts, and issues with the context evaluation methodology. We hope these insights will guide future research into context-aware deep detectors. We hope our comprehensive analysis of context in object detection will inspire the development of context-aware deep detectors.

Wikipedia functions as a massive, collaboratively built, and dynamically updated repository of structured knowledge. While it offers comprehensive information on over five million entities and millions of inter-entity relationships, this richness is inherently discrete and structured. Traditional entity recommendation methods generally fall into two categories: content-based and link-based (or graph-based) approaches.

Content-based methods rely on natural language processing to extract features from entity titles and their corresponding pages, often utilizing a learning-to-rank technique to suggest related entities. For instance, Google's Freebase system uses a neural network to compute 64-dimensional vectors for entities based on their page content, subsequently ranking similar entities using cosine similarity. Our framework shares this content-based philosophy but differs by deriving embeddings from the article text of an entity's direct neighbors within a specific graph layer rather than the entity's own text.

Graph-based methods leverage the hyperlink structure of Wikipedia or the edge structure of knowledge graphs to generate entity embeddings and suggest connections. These approaches are often evaluated through entity similarity tasks in embedding generation. Notably, the author's framework integrates both content-based and graph-based methodologies. However, incompatible transplants carry higher risks of rejection, infection, cancer, and graft loss compared to compatible ones. This study investigates the optimal acceptance strategies for potentially incompatible kidneys tailored to individual patients with end-stage kidney disease. By employing a mathematical formulation, we reveal the implicit structural assumptions inherent in adopting this model. Specifically, we demonstrate that Markovian assumptions provide a clear theoretical framework for understanding embedding formation, particularly regarding the capture of frequentist synonyms. These assumptions facilitate the creation of generative models and enable an explicit examination of the loss function standard in NLP. Furthermore, we generate synthetic corpora with varying structural levels to empirically evaluate the algorithm's success or failure in learning them. This leads to an empirical assessment of the model's ability to capture structures in a Twitter corpus, utilizing the Wikipedia grammar dataset from W2V.78. Empirical results indicate that the model effectively learns frequentist synonym classes and certain transitive verb structures, while struggling with intransitive verbs and hierarchies. Ultimately, we propose a methodology for generating test cases designed to target specific structural types, thereby enabling the rigorous and explicit evaluation of embeddings for structural induction. We release our code and synthetic corpora as open source to support this initiative. As a practical application, we utilize this methodology in the "Guess the Structure" challenge at W2V.80. This work extends upon the limitations identified in the prior paper "Introducing a Generative Perspective on Embeddings" by demonstrating how to construct and learn artificial corpora.

In this paper, we utilize an existing generative model to infer a graph's structural equation from linearized vertex sequences. We introduce the concept of structural priors and their parameterization through context-free grammars. Building on this, we develop algorithms for learning these grammars from data, which enables the inference of graphs given their linearizations. We test these methods on three tasks: inferring Guibas graph languages, completing partially observed matrices, and resolving entity coreferences. Our findings indicate that learning a graph's structural equation is at least as accurate as using embeddings alone and, crucially, allows for the completion of partial inputs—a capability that purely vector-based methods lack. Our code is available at github.com/dfryar/Generative_Structures_for_Embeddings.

These controlled operations generate derivational ambiguities that the original Lambek Calculus and its pregroup variant fail to capture. Although proposals exist for interpreting extended Lambek Calculus compositionally within the compact closed category of FVect and linear maps, these approaches treat syntax-semantics mappings as ignoring the control modalities, thereby limiting their influence to syntax alone. Our objective is to elevate these modalities to first-class status within the vectorial interpretation. Leveraging directional density matrix semantics, we expand the type system's interpretation by incorporating an additional spin density matrix space. Consequently, proof interpretations tensor ambiguous derivations with orthogonal spin states. This methodology offers a mechanism for concurrently representing multiple interpretations of ambiguous utterances and establishes a unified framework for integrating both lexical and derivational ambiguity. Furthermore, it enables the expression of constraints that regulate either level. Our experimental results indicate that enriched representations of ambiguity enhance the accuracy of syntactic constraint predictions. To achieve this, we have released a library on PyPI for constructing λ calculus interpretations of ambiguous natural language derivations using our extended Lambek Calculus.
Ambiguity inherent in natural language arises from two primary sources: the coexistence of multiple meanings for single words (lexical ambiguity) and the potential for several interpretations of word sequences (derivational ambiguity). While prior work has addressed each independently, this paper focuses on unifying derivational ambiguity with lexical ambiguity through appropriate extensions of type theories and their semantic interpretations. Although natural language phenomena are fundamentally local, meaning is attributed to entire utterances; thus, we must represent ambiguity at both the lexical and grammatical levels. To manage this, we introduce a framework utilizing extended versions of the Lambek Calculus and its associated interpretations in the compact closed categories of FVect and linear maps. Specifically, we enhance the type system with two sets of control modalities that regulate ambiguity in derived judgments. These modalities are interpreted as orthogonal phases in an interpretation space and are designed to remain consistent across tensor products, mirroring their role in governing natural language derivations. To validate our approach, we implemented a prototype system that resolves ambiguous utterances into sequences of lexically ambiguous judgments. These sequences are then resolved sequentially, similar to standard parsing, to produce sequences of ambiguous semantic representations. Our experimental findings demonstrate that explicitly modeling lexical ambiguity during grammatical analysis improves the prediction of syntactic constraints governing semantic interpretations. Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current algorithms necessitate an exponential number of samples relative to the player count to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper introduces the first family of efficient algorithms capable of learning rationalizable Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) with sample complexities that are polynomial in every problem parameter, including the number of players. To accomplish this, we also propose a new, efficient method for identifying a single rationalizable action profile (which need not be an equilibrium), significantly improving upon the sample complexity achieved by Wu et al. (2021). Our approach integrates several innovative techniques to ensure both rationalizability and no (swap-)regret, such as a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which may hold independent value. We further validate our findings with a sample complexity lower bound that demonstrates the tightness of our guarantees. Beyond these theoretical assurances, we also present a numerical study illustrating the advantages of our algorithm over existing methods.

Recently, Huang et al. (2022) investigated multiagent reinforcement learning for reaching correlated equilibria, yet their approach suffers from a sample complexity that is exponential regarding the number of agents. This work proposes a straightforward and efficient algorithm to reach any correlated equilibrium within a finite Markov Decision Process (MDP) by leveraging public randomization, also determining its sample complexity requirements. Building on this, we extend the method to enable the learning of correlated equilibria without public randomization, although the associated sample complexity remains exponential in the number of agents. Unlike previous approaches, this methodology does not rely on iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies to achieve rationalizability. To facilitate these advancements, we develop several tools of potential broader application, such as replay buffers for off-policy multiagent learning, relative frequency estimators, and meta-algorithms for correlated equilibrium learning in both simultaneous-move and sequential games. Our findings guarantee a polynomial dependence of sample complexity on the state and action spaces, a contrast to the complexity bounds found in Huang et al. (2022) or Luu et al. (2022).

The network structure follows an Erdős–Rényi random graph, but susceptible individuals adjacent to infectious nodes may sever or rewire these links during the epidemic. We derive large-population limits that establish convergence for the initial branching process phase and, under the assumption of a major outbreak, for the subsequent epidemic phase, which approaches a deterministic model equivalent to a specific pair approximation. Additionally, we obtain law of large numbers results for the final size of a major outbreak. Two key findings emerge across various parameter configurations: (i) the limiting proportion of infected individuals can exhibit a discontinuity at the critical infection rate $\lambda_c$, resulting in an abrupt jump from zero to a positive value, and (ii) when rewiring is restricted to uninfected individuals, this discontinuity causes the final infected fraction to leap from $0$ to $1$ as $\lambda$ crosses $\lambda_c$. These observations indicate that the macroscopic epidemic behavior is influenced not only by the average degree but also significantly by the network's degree distribution and the rewiring rules. Notably, if rewiring depends on the number of infected neighbors, the limiting infected fraction remains $0$ regardless of the infection rate $\lambda$. This research extends prior work~\cite{LSZ06} on homogeneous networks and aligns with recent studies~\cite{DHJ18,DHJL19,DHJL20a,DHJL20b} focusing on networks with growing sizes. Finaly, the findings regarding a discontinuous transition in a model with limited rewiring contrast with models allowing extensive rewiring, such as those generating scale-free networks~\cite{BH98,BA99}.

While classical experience replay enables agents to retain knowledge by reusing past observations, its uniform sampling strategy treats all data points equally, neglecting their varying significance. To address this, we introduce a general Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER) framework that selectively prioritizes the most relevant samples to refine policy gradient estimates. libcommute offers features for defining and manipulating polynomial operators via {Additive, Multiplicative, Canonical, and Dense} expressions, as well as methods for operator simplification, commutation relation calculation, and exact diagonalization. Furthermore, the accompanying pycommute library enables the diagonalization of systems comprising up to ~20 spin-1/2 particles (corresponding to ~4 million basis states) directly from Python 3.

The main features of libcommute include:
- A modern, robust design built on generic programming for high performance.
- Support for basic algebraic operations and properties, allowing for the definition of systems in an intuitive manner.
- Efficient memory usage achieved through a non-copying approach.
- A modern API for defining Hamiltonians and state basis states using generic templates.
- A modern API for constructing linear combinations of states, offering a user-friendly interface for loading Hamiltonians.
- Robust tools for simplifying polynomial operator expressions by applying commutation relations, grounded in a decision procedure for polynomial equivalence under a given set of commutation rules.

- Capabilities for calculating expectation values and off-diagonal matrix elements, supported by pycommute.
- Methods for finding exact eigenvalues and eigenvectors using external libraries like ARPACK, accessible via pycommute.

We address these discrepancies by performing high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) on the material using both Helium lamps and laser sources. Although multiple approaches now exist for evaluating integrals over positive-definite Hermitian matrices weighted by analytic functions, we focus here on matrices with positive-definite symmetric or antisymmetric components. This paper serves as a pedagogical introduction to these powerful tools, which are essential for analyzing models with matrix order parameters, a common feature in the theory of disordered systems.

We introduce the MultiTalk Dataset, a collection exceeding 320,000 written dialogue sentences that achieves a balance between a high branching factor (10) and multiple conversation turns (6) via selective branch continuation. We offer several contributions aimed at advancing dialog generation within this highly branching context. To assess a diverse range of generated outputs, we propose a straightforward scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, designed to optimally integrate a set of varied references. Furthermore, we examine multiple language generation tasks across varying depths of predictive conversation, utilizing textual attributes derived automatically from pretrained classifiers. Our final task addresses a challenging theory of mind problem, a controllable generation challenge that necessitates reasoning about the anticipated reactions of a listener. Our outcomes indicate only marginal improvements in performance as prediction depth increases, suggesting an ability to generate coherent text across shallow to medium conversation histories; these findings are validated both quantitatively and qualitatively. Unlike many existing studies, we explicitly consider the impact of correlated Rayleigh fading and the coupling between the amplitude and phase shifts of each IRS element's reflection coefficient, factors often overlooked despite their practical relevance. Leveraging random matrix theory, we derive a closed-form probability density function (PDF) for the cascaded channel, from which the EC is calculated based solely on large-scale statistics and phase shifts. We further optimize the EC with respect to phase shifts using a low-overhead approach, updating the parameters only every few coherence intervals rather than relying on computationally intensive frequent optimizations based on instantaneous channel data. Monte-Carlo simulations confirm our analytical findings and reveal the critical interactions among key parameters and their influence on the system's EC. The results highlight that while large-scale fading significantly determines the EC, there exists an critical number of transmit and receive antennas ($N_t=N_r$) beyond which increasing the antenna count yields diminishing returns. Additionally, we demonstrate that accounting for the mutual coupling among IRS elements is essential for effective passive beamforming design. Finally, we establish that the achieved EC markedly surpasses the theoretical EC of active IRS systems under high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. This research offers crucial insights into designing practical wideband wide-area MIMO communications utilizing reflective surfaces. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic perturbations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating superior accuracy in predicting reacting flow fluctuations compared to DNS, other EBU variations, and RANS models with more complex closure terms. Subsequently, the linearized model was applied to a jet flame to examine the effects of acoustic actuation and modifications to the combustion process on instability thresholds. These actuations varied in intensity and location, including changes to inlet boundary conditions, which altered global dynamics. The findings indicate that RANS-EBU can successfully predict reacting flow fluctuations and the effects of acoustic actuation, although it fails to capture instability growth. This discrepancy arises because the simulations are situated near a bifurcation point in parameter space, causing the linear model to underestimate the impact of acoustic actuation on global dynamics. Ultimately, this study confirms that a linearized RANS-EBU model can effectively investigate the effects of acoustic actuation on jet flames, specifically regarding heat release fluctuations and acoustic pressure, independent of upstream turbulence intensity. These insights aid in constructing reduced-order models for such systems. Ultimately, the success of these models relies on the validity of the underlying assumptions, so further research should address their limitations. This includes refining the EBU model to account for turbulence-scoustic interactions and incorporating DNS or LES models to accurately represent turbulence-heat release interactions.

We introduce a topological framework for certain time-periodic, multi-layered, rotating fluids, deriving topological fluid modes (TFMs). These modes may explain energy transfer in atmospheric and oceanic circulation and offer insights into topological mechanisms behind topographic eddies. Depending on fluid properties, TFMs can exist as standing or traveling modes across various latitudes, resembling atmospheric planetary waves, Rossby waves, Kelvin waves, inertial waves, and gyres. In many instances, TFM asymmetrical gaps arise from the coupling of Coriolis and centrifugal forces. We illustrate that topological hole gaps emerge when Coriolis and centrifugal accelerations are unequal, whereas topological surface states appear where these accelerations balance.

These energy estimates may facilitate future investigations into wave turbulence, weakly nonlinear resonant interactions, cascades, and weakly dissipative inertial cascades within the topological regime.

We introduce a general framework for analyzing measurement-driven entanglement distillation in quantum Markov chains. This approach facilitates the examination of various quantum information protocols, notably including erasure-code pumping. We investigate the influence of classical noise on these protocols and derive an upper bound for the entropy of measurement-generated streams. This bound relies on a dynamic correlation length that characterizes the convergence rate of the quantum channel's repeated iterations. We apply these findings to specific cases, deriving analytical expressions for entanglement generation rates and their fluctuations for qubit stabilizer codes under single-qubit erasure noise. These results imply that, to achieve near-unit fidelity, the lattice size must scale exponentially with the inverse of the entanglement entropy of the distilled state. Additionally, we propose that measuring entanglement entropy directly provides a lower bound for these length scales. (Created using LaTeXSourceFile).

performance. To ensure low-latency access, replicas typically accept updates independently without coordination, relying on asynchronous propagation to synchronize changes. This approach introduces the significant challenge of resolving conflicts among concurrent updates. Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) offer a principled solution to this problem. However, current CRDT designs are often complex and difficult to generalize across different data types, creating a need for a framework to guide the systematic creation of new CRDTs. To address this, we introduce RWF, the Remove-Win design Framework for CRDTs. RWF employs the straightforward yet potent remove-win strategy to handle conflicting updates and provides a generic design applicable to various data container types. We present two implementations of RWF based on Redis data types, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness. Furthermore, performance evaluations of these implementations confirm the efficiency of CRDT designs built upon RWF. The implementations and tests are accessible at https://github.com/CY-CA/RWF. In conclusion, our contributions include: (1) proposing the novel RWF, which bridges a gap in existing CRDT design methodologies; (2) developing practical and efficient implementations of CRDTs using the vector-clock-remove pattern within RWF; and (3) proving the reliability and performance of our implementations through comprehensive experiments. These findings underscore the potential of our work for creating performance-efficient distributed storage systems.

Distributed storage systems rely on replica-based approaches to improve reliability and throughput. Unlike traditional methods that resolve update conflicts through user-defined strategies and application-layer coordination, CRDTs provide a unified framework for managing concurrent updates across all data types, thereby increasing system availability and performance. However, existing CRDT designs remain largely ad hoc. To facilitate the creation of robust and efficient CRDTs, we propose the Remove-Win Framework (RWF). RWF offers both theoretical foundations and practical implementations for constructing CRDTs. Based on experimental evaluations of multiple implementations, we concluded that: (1) CRDT designs built on RWF achieve significantly lower space and update overheads than existing approaches; (2) leveraging common data types in system-specific implementations reduces the overhead of space optimization; and (3) ensuring reliability and performance, our implementations of CRDTs via RWF outperform those based on prior designs. Our code is available at https://github.com/CY-CA/RWF. In summary, our research advances the principle of unified conflict resolution in CRDTs and establishes a practical framework for their implementation.

We present a statistical framework that leverages genome-wide association statistics to pinpoint classes of genomic elements that are either enriched for or depleted regarding loci influencing a specific trait, with the model inherently accommodating multiple annotation types. Applying this approach to GWAS data for 18 human traits—including red and platelet cell metrics, glucose and lipid levels, height, BMI, and Crohn's disease—we assessed the relevance of 450 genomic annotations across over a hundred tissues and cell lines, covering protein-coding genes, enhancers, and DNase-I hypersensitive sites. Our results indicate that the proportion of phenotype-associated SNPs affecting protein sequences varies by trait, ranging from approximately 2% for platelet volume to roughly 20% for LDL cholesterol. Additionally, we observed significant depletion of repressed chromatin for SNPs linked to several traits and enrichment of cell type-specific DNase-I hypersensitive sites for others (e.g., spleen-specific sites for platelet volume). Finally, re-weighting GWAS results using functional genomics data increased the count of high-confidence associated loci by approximately 5%. We have made the code for our model accessible at https://github.com/max-wainewright/Association-FunctRev. These findings demonstrate that integrating genome data on potentially regulatory elements can help interpret complex traits and prioritize variants for molecular validation. Introduction: Although prior studies have linked specific functional annotations to SNPs associated with individual complex traits or subsets of missense variants, it remains unclear how these depletions and enrichments vary across different phenotypes. Methods: We developed a model to identify genomic element classes relevant to specific traits, based on the hypothesis that genomes are not neutral. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. While this does not disprove the existence of black hole LMXBs in the Galactic Centre, it underscores the necessity of more sensitive observations with greater sensitivity to robustly establish the proposed significant neutron star LMXB population there. In this context, we advocate for the term 'magnetic LMXB' to describe these systems, replacing terms like 'transient' or 'outbursting' which refer to their time-variable emission resulting from globular cluster dynamics. Galactic Nuclei (AGN) has garnered significant interest due to the critical role of magnetic fields in their physics, their utility as tracers of intergalactic plasma, and their potential impact on cosmic microwave background polarization measurements. Understanding the statistical relationship between polarization and source characteristics is essential for all these applications. In this work, we calculate the median fractional polarization ($\Pi_{0, \rm med}$) for extensive samples of radio sources from three evolutionary stages of the Simba hydrodynamic simulation. Our results indicate that $\Pi_{0, \rm med}$ for linearly polarized emission rises as a function of the observed flux density. Furthermore, we find that $\Pi_{0, \rm med}$ for elliptically polarized emission is roughly 2-3 times larger than that for linearly polarized emission. These findings align with predictions derived from numerical models of small systems featuring complex, dynamical magnetic field configurations. We also examine the median statistics of other emmission properties, such as total magnetic field strength and order parameter, across different radio source types and their surrounding environments. Finally, we address the implications of our discoveries for upcoming CMB polarization experiments. Index keywords: cosmology: theoretical - radio-line radiation.

We investigate the connection between the median fractional polarization ($\Pi_{0,\rm med}$) of decimetric radio emission from AGN and their intrinsic physical parameters using hydrodynamic simulations. While $\Pi_{0,\rm med}$ for linearly polarized radiation is observed to increase with radio flux density for AGN in both real skies and simulations, our analysis reveals that this correlation is actually inverse when expressed in terms of power injected into the intergalactic medium. Additionally, we document distinct trends in $\Pi_{0,\rm med}$ relative to other radio source properties, including host galaxy mass, spin parameter, jet power, and proximity to large-scale structures. These findings offer crucial design constraints for future cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization experiments. We also derive an expression for the bias of polarized radio emission, demonstrating that it is not simply proportional to the square of the mean radio surface brightness. The study concludes with suggestions for improving the accuracy of $\Pi_{0,\rm med}$ estimates from simulations and enhances future research into the statistical moments of radio source polarization. vibrational modes within molecules and crystals. We demonstrate that the circular motion of ions generates inertial influences on electrons. Mirroring Coriolis and centrifugal forces experienced by rotating bodies, rotating lattices impose additional forces on electrons. Near equilibrium, these inertial terms establish strong couplings between electrons and phonons resulting from angular displacement. Similarly, angular acceleration triggers electron-hole flow driven by irrotational vortex phonons. Terahertz-induced displacements may stimulate macroscopic lattice vibrations deep within the branch regions of both dispersive and flat-band phonons. In materials hosting flat-band phonons, these modes can exhibit bulk coherent phonon activity. Silicon epitaxial diamond exhibits terahertz-driven ultrashort flat-band phonons capable of carrying electric current. Similarly, flat-band phonons are anticipated in substances possessing two interlinked sublattices, such as organic crystals, certain oxides, and graphite. Premixed hydrogen-air flames utilize a standing longitudinal acoustic wave to generate large-scale vortices through acoustic radiation pressure. Flow visualization using OH* chemiluminescence reveals that these vortices induce an elliptical distortion in the chemiluminescence zone, whose orientation oscillates in sync with the driving acoustic wave. # Contents

## 1 Introduction

$\tau$-tilting theory, which finds its roots in the work of Auslander-Reiten, represents a captivating and dynamic area of representation theory. This area, born approximately fifteen years ago, has garnered significant attention and remains highly active. Consequently, comprehensive surveys are difficult to produce. The following notes aim to introduce $\tau$-tilting theory for those new to the subject and, more importantly, to function as a survey by unifying many of the area's most crucial results.

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Representation-Finite Algebras

We adopt the conventions and notation of [ARS86] throughout. Let $\kappa$ denote a fixed algebraically closed field. A representation-finite algebra is an Artinian algebra with only a finite number of isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional modules. A primary example comes from tilting theory; specifically, if $\kappa Q$ is the path algebra of a finite acyclic quiver $Q$ and $S$ is a quiver representation that is both skew-symmetric and connected, then the tilting module $T(S)$ associated with $S$ (as defined in [Fra73]) over $\kappa Q$ yields the endomorphism algebra $\operatorname{End}_{\kappa Q}(T(S))$ as a representation-finite algebra (see [Fra73, Theorem 3.3]).

A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. For humanoid robots to navigate unstructured terrains and recover from unexpected disturbances, they must leverage their multi-body dynamics to exploit passively stable gaits, like walking, during task execution. While control laws based on nonlinear optimization have shown promise in generating robust periodic gaits, they often rely on computationally intensive algorithms. We introduce a bi-module control scheme that utilizes two distinct controllers: a fast nonlinear feedback linearizing controller and a slower nonlinear model predictive controller. This setup enables the generation of disturbance-rejected periodic gaits at frequencies unattainable by existing methods, all while maintaining computational loads suitable for embedded systems. We illustrate the efficacy of this two-module system by creating a periodic walking gait on a 12-DOF upper-body-free biped. Our results highlight the ability to reject disturbances as large as 2.5 times those required for stability using only thrusters, while also achieving periodic gaits on platforms where such adjustment is currently impossible.

to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Our findings establish that the diagonal move serves as a fundamental unknotting operation for both classical and welded knots, capable of transforming any such knot into a trivial knot. The study of these moves may also aid in determining recombination events during DNA relaxation and self-knotting. Ultimately, the diagonal move offers a more efficient method for altering knot diagrams compared to crossing changes. In classical knot theory, diagonal moves facilitate the transformation of a knot with few crossings into a trivial knot using fewer operations than crossing changes. Consequently, they are essential for understanding 3-manifolds, link field theories, chemistry, and the relaxation and self-knotting of DNA. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 covers classical knot diagrams, while Section 3 addresses welded knot diagrams. Section 4 defines the band move and classifies its types. Section 5 details the diagonal move and its properties. Sections 6 through 13 explore specific variants of these moves, including the Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, 4-move, and the general classification of diagonal moves on classical and welded knots. Finally, Section 14 presents our conclusions. In classical knot theory, diagonal moves are more efficient for transforming knots into trivial configurations than crossing changes. These moves are also relevant to the study of link field theories, molecular chemistry, and DNA self-knotting. Future research could extend this work to virtual knots, -links, or other specialized knot types. Additionally, understanding how diagonal moves influence 3-manifolds, link field theories, molecules, and DNA would be a valuable direction for subsequent study.

Consequently, parallel computing has emerged as a necessary solution to mitigate this performance bottleneck. This report presents a comparative analysis of sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, implemented using CUDA and OpenMP. The findings demonstrate that parallelization is particularly critical for achieving optimal performance with large-scale matrices. In this study, matrix multiplication is modeled as a parallel sorting problem. The proposed methods have been tested on standard and large matrices, evaluating various parallelization techniques for both sequential execution and deployment on graphics processing units (GPUs). The results clearly illustrate the superior efficiency of the parallelized method compared to the sequential version. Finally, the work concludes with suggestions for future enhancements. The reported findings align with existing research on accelerating matrix multiplication through graph parallelization. Various strategies for optimizing this operation are explored, including graph partitioning, memory hierarchy utilization, and GPU-specific implementations. The results confirm that parallelization is essential for efficient and scalable execution. This report introduces multiple parallelization methods for graph-based matrix multiplication on GPUs, comparing their performance based on graph size and partitioning schemes. The comparative study demonstrates the advantages and limitations of these approaches, highlighting the significance of graph partitioning for maximizing performance. Additionally, the findings illustrate how parallelization enables the multiplication of very large matrices that exceed the capacity of a single processor's main memory. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently calculating a data-driven Nash equilibrium restricted to the class of affine policies. Multiagent systems are increasingly deployed to address difficult tasks across diverse fields such as robotics, drone swarms, sensor networks, and edge computing. A fundamental step in designing these systems is defining the set of achievable tasks; however, many systems can perform only a restricted range of functions. For instance, individual agents often lack the capacity to execute complex tasks independently, whereas the collective team can succeed. Although tasks are not always decomposable, multiagent systems typically possess the ability to choose between multiple tasks of comparable complexity. We investigate how a team of agents with comparable capabilities allocates itself to two such tasks characterized by uncertain difficulties. We model an allocation policy as a function mapping observations to the probability of assigning a task to an agent. Assuming a constant total number of arriving tasks, we seek to minimize the expected number of high-difficulty tasks uncompleted by the team. While this problem is NP-hard in its most general form, we analyze specific cases where each task's difficulty is revealed individually and where all tasks of one type are identical. In these scenarios, we show that any optimal policy can be represented as a vector indicating the number of agents assigned to each task type. We derive bounds on the number of agents required to approximate the optimum using a polynomial amount of information relative to the problem size. Additionally, we formulate a game-theoretic model where an fixed number of agents compete to allocate themselves to two competing task types with shared characteristics. We prove that for any given prior distribution over task difficulty, the resulting game always admits a Nash equilibrium.

This discussion examines how amplitude-based resummation can address this need, illustrated through examples drawn from the LHC, upcoming collider proposals, and quantum gravity. Resummation is particularly valuable in processes involving massive or highly energetic particles, where certain logarithmic terms reach magnitudes comparable to standard perturbation theory terms. We highlight specific scenarios where resummation enhances theoretical precision, ranging from several percent down to $10^{-5}$, though the underlying motivations apply even more fundamentally to processes at the TeV scale and beyond. After illustrating these points with both established and novel resummation techniques, we conclude by noting that analogous methods are likely relevant for extracting precision physics from existing and future experimental data.

We examine the unitarization of vector boson scattering (VBS) in quantum gravity within four dimensions, focusing on tree-level amplitudes. Utilizing the CHY formalism, we derive explicit expressions for VBS amplitudes in quantum Einstein gravity (QEG). These amplitudes exhibit local unitarity factorization consistent with unitary theory expectations. Furthermore, they display correct high-energy behavior, allowing for unitarization via standard effective field theory approaches, specifically through unitary Einstein-Higgs amplitudes. This result offers fresh insight into how unitarity and symmetry operate in QEG, suggesting that the unitary limit of QEG may involve nontrivial resonant structures, as seen in BSM VBS, alongside the standard unitary resonances characteristic of quantum gravity. We also discuss implications for constructing a complete set of four-dimensional quantum gravity theories capable of describing all observed particle interactions and their local quantum unitarity behavior, with potential relevance for both current and future high-energy experiments.

This report assesses the feasibility of searching for nonstandard interactions (NSIs) using deep submillimeter quantum gravity probes, specifically planetary and satellite missions. Unlike previous studies, we incorporate finite size effects of celestial bodies, which are significant for NSI searches but negligible in tests of modified gravity. Our analysis covers three potential signatures of NSIs in quantum gravity: changes in orbital periods, variations in orbital semi-major axes, and deviations in tidal Love numbers. We provide order-of-magnitude estimates for constraining NSIs using existing data and forecast sensitivity improvements from future missions. Under plausible assumptions, current planetary and satellite observations could constrain two of three NSI parameters

Based on collaboration structures, FL is categorized into Horizontal Federated Learning (HFL) and Vertical Federated Learning (VFL). In HFL, entities share identical feature spaces and data samples, whereas in VFL, they share common sample identifiers and collaborate on features. VFL offers a wider application scope and is particularly well-suited for joint model training among large enterprises.

This paper concentrates on VFL, examining potential privacy vulnerabilities within real-world frameworks. We developed and executed two practical privacy attacks: a reverse multiplication attack targeting the logistic regression VFL protocol and a reverse sum attack targeting the XGBoost VFL protocol. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that these attacks are (1) effective, allowing adversaries to extract private training data even when intermediate outputs are encrypted; (2) evasive, as they adhere strictly to protocol specifications and do not degrade the target model's accuracy; and (3) low-effort, requiring minimal prior knowledge of the target participant's data distribution. Furthermore, we show that the information leaked is as potent as the original training data for training alternative classifiers. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and their associated challenges, aiming to inspire future research directions. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/MyronZ/Real_VFL_Attacks.

In today's data-driven era, deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely adopted for solving complex machine learning problems. To build high-performance models, practitioners typically aggregate massive datasets from multiple sources. However, factors such as privacy regulations, customer trust, and competitive advantages often prevent the centralization of this data. Consequently, DNN training on decentralized data has emerged as a promising solution. Recently, transfer learning (TL) has gained significant attention in decentralized settings because it allows models trained on one task to be fine-tuned on related tasks using new data.

This work introduces a unified theoretical framework for decentralized transfer learning (DTL), establishing performance bounds and identifying key elements for TL in decentralized environments. Our findings indicate that the performance limit of DTL is determined by both the generalization capacity of the initial DNN and the statistical divergence between training and test datasets. Notably, when training and testing data originate from the same source, a TL algorithm specifically designed for horizontally decentralized learning (where data is split across machines but each sample has all features) outperforms not only TL protocols in vertically decentralized settings (where data features are partitioned) but also standard deep learning

To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. Consequently, reducing feature dimensions is essential for effective scaling. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. Experimental results indicate that PRFF outperforms both the original kernel method and RFF across various datasets. Furthermore, PRFF supports online learning, allowing it to scale effectively to large-scale, streaming datasets. The code for PRFF is available at https://github.com/MahdiNarmani/PRFF. In summary, PRFF provides: (1) reduced feature dimensions for training data, improving prediction accuracy for both classification and regression tasks; and (2) scalability to large-scale streaming datasets through an online learning approach. These findings demonstrate that PRFF is well-suited for practical implementation in real-world scenarios.
