Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients currently relies on ventricular volume and function as per established guidelines. These metrics are most accurately quantified through the segmentation of 3D cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. While U-Net architectures have demonstrated remarkable performance in recent grand challenges, clinical environments present greater variability due to diverse patient pathologies and scanner-specific image characteristics. Furthermore, training data for complex, rare conditions like TOF remains limited. This study addresses two objectives: 1) evaluating the performance gap when training on a public dataset (ACDC) and testing it on TOF data, and vice versa, and 2) determining if consistent results can be achieved on a more heterogeneous database. We trained multiple deep learning models using four-fold cross-validation and evaluated them on unseen CMR images from the alternative dataset. Our findings indicate that while current models yield excellent segmentation accuracy (left ventricle Dice of $0.951\pm{0.003}$/$0.941\pm{0.009}$ for train/validation within a single collection), cardiac function measurements derived from the public data suffer significant errors when applied to TOF ($0.166\pm{0.048}$/$0.128\pm{0.068}$ $L{/}min$ for val/id within a single collection). Consequently, we conclude that leveraging large, diverse datasets is essential for robust automatic analysis of clinical CMR in TOF. Finally, we introduced and assessed a new model capable of segmenting both the left and right ventricles as well as the septum across two different populations. The code is accessible at https://github.com/majid-rezaei77/TOF_Segmentation.

ultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT), designed to enhance communication efficiency in next-generation mobile networks while reducing overall power consumption through green energy sourcing. First, a distinct architecture is proposed where receivers harvest energy from an Access Point (AP) without requiring a signal splitter; in this model, the transmitted signal correlates with the energy signal at the transmitter, whereas a non-linear function generates a new frequency component for energy harvesting at the receiver. Second, a joint optimization problem is formulated to determine the optimal source codebook, precoder, decoder, and time allocation. This optimization aims to maximize harvested energy at all users while ensuring QoS constraints—specifically, that the information transmission rate meets each user's demand—and to verify feasible information transmission across the network. The resulting non-convex problem is addressed using an iterative two-step algorithm. The first step involves information-theoretic time allocation followed by joint optimization of the source codebook, precoder, and decoder to satisfy user rate requirements. The second step applies evolutionary computation to simultaneously optimize the time allocation, source codebook, precoder, and decoder. Simulation results demonstrate the advantages of the proposed scheme compared to conventional SWIPT time-division approaches. Notably, the time allocation solutions derived from this scheme are applicable to receiver architectures that do utilize splitters. The core innovation of this research lies in the joint optimization of time allocation, source codebook, precoder, and decoder within a SWIPT network designed for minimum energy harvesting under strict rate constraints within a single-cochannel environment. The paper concludes with suggestions for future research directions. fundamental component in object detection systems, yet it has long been observed that its integration often degrades the detection performance of large-scale objects. This paper re-examines FPN within the detection framework to uncover the underlying reasons for its success from an optimization standpoint. We identify that the decline in large-object performance stems from improper back-propagation paths created when FPN is incorporated, which restricts each backbone level to processing objects only within specific scale ranges. Based on this analysis, we propose two viable strategies to ensure every backbone level can perceive objects across all scales in FPN-based architectures. The first strategy involves introducing auxiliary objective functions so that each backbone level directly receives back-propagation signals from objects of various scales during training. The second approach entails constructing the feature pyramid more rationally to eliminate illogical back-propagation routes. Extensive experiments on the COCO benchmark confirm the validity of our analysis and the efficacy of our proposed methods. Without relying on complex additions, we demonstrate that our approach yields substantial improvements (exceeding 2%) across diverse detection frameworks, including one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Our open-source implementation surpasses the current state-of-the-art anchor-based detector, RetNet, by 2.6% on the COCO dataset. Additionally, we introduce a new anchor-free detector utilizing the direct feature pyramid, which achieves an improved AP by over 3% against existing large-object detectors. The source code is available at https://github.com/ghyghy/Feature-Pyramid-Network-Reason.

Currently, no methodology exists to compute extremal characteristics for these models because their copulas and marginals lack closed-form expressions. This study focuses on bivariate conditional models that define the distribution of $X$ and the distribution of $Y$ given $X$. We develop tools to quantify the implicit assumptions concerning the joint tails and provide a case study to demonstrate these concepts. Specifically, we examine a conditional model where $X$ follows a Student distribution and $Y$ given $X$ is normally distributed, which is widely used to analyze financial asset returns (e.g., DCC models). We demonstrate that the probability of joint extremes cannot be calculated within this framework. Furthermore, we assess the accuracy of implicit joint tail probabilities by applying an unconditional conditional model to Australian rainfall data. Finally, we propose a modification to the model that preserves most of its advantages while explicitly allowing for the calculation of joint tail probabilities. The proposed method is validated using both the conditional rainfall data and a dataset of extreme sea surface temperatures from the Australian region. The parameter estimation techniques employed can be extended to a broader class of conditional models. We introduce a method to optimize ensemble learning algorithms by incorporating data adjustability, addressing the issue that data from diverse domains varies in quality and informativeness. Unlike previous approaches that focused solely on model parameter tuning, our method employs a maximum likelihood approach to learn adjustability factors, which are then applied to combine ensemble predictions. Evaluated on text classification tasks, our experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly improves ensemble performance with minimal computational cost. Consequently, this technique can be integrated into any ensemble framework, including those using domain-specific datasets, as confirmed by the findings of Liu et al. (Liu et al., 2020).

Although BERT has revolutionized Natural Language Processing (NLP), it remains unclear how the model acquires world knowledge, a crucial component for human-like language comprehension. Using a theory-driven approach, this study investigates world knowledge within BERT by formulating three research questions: (1) Does BERT acquire world knowledge?; (2) How does BERT acquire world knowledge?; and (3) Can World Knowledge Evaluation (WKE) be applied to enhance NLP model evaluation? To answer these, we first define World Knowledge in NLP and construct a new evaluation dataset, the World Knowledge Evaluation (WKE) dataset. Subsequently, we conduct an analysis of BERT's world knowledge

understanding and reasoning about real-world task procedures, which typically demand a deep grasp of temporal common sense and multimodal data, as these instructions are frequently conveyed through a blend of text and visuals. This capability is critical for applications like sequential task planning and multi-source instruction summarization. Although humans excel at sequencing unordered multimodal procedural instructions, it remains an open question whether current machine learning models possess this essential ability. In this study, we evaluate models' capacity to reason about and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by curating datasets from popular online manuals and gathering extensive human annotations. Our findings reveal that models not only perform significantly worse than humans but also appear unable to efficiently leverage multimodal information. To enhance machines' performance in multimodal event sequencing, we introduce sequentiality-aware pretraining techniques that harness the sequential alignment properties of both text and images, yielding over 5% significant improvements. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these models can be adapted with minimal additional data for specific tasks, such as sequencing event lists or completing visual instructions, achieving over 7% significant gains. Our code and data are accessible via this link.

Traditional methods for assessing attack effectiveness typically rely on macro-level metrics, like the critical percolation probability ($p_c$) and the size of the giant component, often overlooking the micro-level dynamics of node removals, their specific traits, and immediate outcomes. This paper introduces and applies a micro-scale approach to attack analysis. Grounded in network percolation theory, we examine the "watermelon" network as a case study. Our methodology dissects attack processes into distinct micro-stages, elucidating the underlying mechanisms of each step and how they contribute to network fragmentation. Specifically, we focus on the "drop" probability—the likelihood that a targeted node is immediately disconnected from the giant component upon removal. We analyze the network's topology to reveal the distribution laws of this probability across various attack strategies and the network's evolution. Furthermore, we establish that the distribution of the "drop" probability directly influences attack efficiency and can characterize the distinct micro-stages of network disintegration. Consequently, this study offers a detailed micro-scale perspective for understanding attack efficiencies and mechanisms, potentially offering new insights for evaluating and designing network attacks and immunization strategies, especially within complex information networks. The source code for all simulations is available at https://github.com/1227853/Attack-drop-probability.

Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). While most theoretical efforts to interpret these findings assume that such structures arise from disk-planet interactions, confirmed exoplanet detections in these systems remain scarce. Moreover, certain substructures are anticipated to emerge prior to planet formation, as they play a crucial role in concentrating small solids to facilitate planetesimal accretion. This study presents observational predictions derived from high-resolution 3D radiative hydrodynamical models that simulate the evolution of gas and solids in protoplanetary disks. Specifically, we examine substructures in the distribution of millimeter-sized and smaller particles generated by the vertical shear instability. Our results demonstrate that these features are consistent with some shallow gaps observed recently at sub-mm/mm wavelengths, and we offer predictions for future observations utilizing the enhanced sensitivity and angular resolution of ALMA and the Next Generation Very Large Array. These findings suggest that analyzing substructures in solid particle distributions can provide insights into the physical conditions during the early stages of protoplanetary disk evolution. However, it is expected that predicting features linked to specific planet-forming processes will necessitate future 3D simulations incorporating more comprehensive physics.

Although recent studies have identified ALMA-millimeter observable structures in 3D shearing-box simulations driven by the magnetorotational instability (MRI), they lack the angular resolution to capture smaller-scale substructures. This letter introduces a hybrid approach combining high-resolution nested grids with global resolution to identify such detailed substructures within otherwise realistic disk configurations. We find that, unlike the global MRI instability, these substructures persist throughout the disk's evolution. Although this phenomenon is often blamed on forecasting inaccuracies or operational breakdowns, we argue it stems from risk-averse scheduling strategies. By applying a stochastic self-scheduling model to real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, we show that risk-averse storage units adopt a short-sighted operational approach. Specifically, they focus primarily on near-term price arbitrage, targeting only a limited number of extreme price peaks and valleys, which leaves them inactive during many periods characterized by significantly high or low prices. These findings carry significant policy weight, particularly given the lack of transparency surrounding unit-level risk aversion and the visible risks involved in intervention decisions. Our results validate the necessity of incorporating unit-specific risk aversion into models assessing storage adequacy and underscore the value of such approaches for determining when interventions are truly warranted. Additionally, we confirm the potential for risk-averse storage to artificially exacerbate the impact of load shedding on price volatility. The evidence presented here can facilitate the development of standardization or regulation for risk-averse operational schemes, either by proving their harmlessness or by informing more efficient risk aversion levels. This effect is more pronounced than in a pure spot market environment due to the presence of price caps and shedding mechanisms. Ultimately, the 2-step optimization strategy employed in this study can be adapted for various applications, including the recent analysis by Deane and Kehrberg (2023) regarding hidden risks in risk-neutral long-term scheduling. Our approach offers the advantage of accounting for risk aversion, scaling, and load shedding effects within low-carbon markets, whereas the method used by Deane and Kehrberg (2023) is restricted to spot market environments without these factors.

Our primary objective is to examine how key physical parameters—including cooling rate, surface roughness, the presence of mountains, Coriolis force, and radiative convective equilibrium—influence these circulation systems. Our findings indicate that both the Coriolis force and mountainous terrain significantly contribute to establishing global Hadley and Ferrel cells. Hamiltonian neural networks are employed to identify and classify these states. We derive symbolic expressions from learned symbolic formulas to explicitly define the variables defining each state in phase space. Additionally, we investigate a simplified barotropic beta-plane model to elucidate how these networks learn to represent symbolic functions. Symbolization enables the explicit representation of non-linear dynamical system learning as a sequence of operations, offering a pathway to interpret "black box" machine learning models through sequence-based human learning mechanisms. By explicitly encoding operability into the learning process, we enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of understanding how these systems function. Network-based symbolization allows for the inference of phase transition conditions and the assignment of learned functions to dynamical processes, thereby enabling the classification of non-linear attractors such as limit cycles and chaotic attractors. In essence, this approach infers the human capability to comprehend the world through a series of operations. Network-based symbolization enables the explicit representation of sequence-based operations as a method for humans to understand and explain the world symbolically. Human learning, like machine learning, utilizes operations to learn; however, unlike black box machine learning, human learning explicitly employs these operations to understand and explain our symbolized world. We elucidate how these insights advance both interpretability and causal learning. Understanding causal learning through the lens of state space representation provides a framework for defining state space attractors and their associated information content, which we apply to application-oriented causal learning tasks. Furthermore, this research clarifies the application of universal approximation theorems to sequential functions, highlighting the necessity of multi-state space representations for modeling the world. We examine how the state space embedding theorem applies to dynamical systems, providing applications for analyzing chaotic attractors, particularly the symbolization of sequential dynamics such as weather patterns.

The paper addresses transmission in cognitive radio networks utilizing Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) when a primary user (PU) is active. It derives the bit error rate (BER) for both orthogonal and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) protocols, accounting for Rayleigh and Nakagami-m fading channels. These protocols are evaluated across three scenarios: single-user, multi-user, and cooperative multi-user communication. The obtained expressions facilitate performance comparison and data visualization for the described protocols and environments. Monte-Carlo simulations verify the theoretical findings, and the simulations confirm the network's potential for real-world deployment. This research opens avenues for optimizing parameters in multi-user and cooperative multi-user non-orthogonal TDMA cognitive radio networks. While the derived expressions apply to any number of secondary users, the simulations specifically examine networks with two and three secondary users. All outcomes are discussed in the context of practical implementation. Although the expressions are generated for a multi-user setting, the findings are applicable to single-user communication as a special case. Monte-Carlo simulations validate the expressions for multi-user and cooperative multi-user protocols, and the network expressions can be extended to multi-hop communication systems. All simulations were conducted using MATLAB.

The model posits that the Hall anomaly arises from the movement of vacancies within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. Initial validation explores vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition within the vortex crystal. Subsequently, the measured activation energies are compared against the calculated creation energies for vortex-anti-vortex pairs and vacancies on the flux-line lattice without employing any adjustable parameters. This analysis clarifies the theoretical foundations and prerequisites of the vacancy model, notably revealing that vacancy activation energies are approximately one order of magnitude lower than those of an isolated vortex line. Ultimately, this proposed mechanism may offer a macro-theoretical framework applicable to other investigations. Additionally, the successful comparison of activation energies strengthens the case for the vacancy model over the competing vortex-branching theory. The document concludes with a brief overview of other potential mechanisms. Finally, a detailed examination of the lower-field region of the mixed-state Hall resistivity is addressed, focusing on the "type-II" Hall anomaly, which may be attributed to the motion of vortex cores or current-induced spin polarization near the superconductor-vacuum interface.

Keywords: superconductors; type-II; vortex lattice; vacancy; activation energy; Hall anomaly; vortex core; spin polarization.

At higher magnetic fields in the mixed state, the vortex lattice is believed to be the source of the Hall anomaly. Various mechanisms have been proposed to explain this phenomenon. The figure compares the measured activation energies with those of an isolated vortex line and a vacancy on the vortex lattice, providing support for the vacancy model.

In earlier work [Low Temp. Phys. 22, 281 (1996)], it was suggested that the vortex lattice is not perfectly Bravais in the intermediate field range. This figure compares the measured activation energies again, providing support for this approach.

At lower fields, different mechanisms are thought to cause the Hall anomaly. One such mechanism involves the motion of vortex cores; the corresponding activation energy is shown in the figure for comparison.

This study examines the temperature dependence of second- to fourth-order (factorial) cumulants of the order parameter by employing the parametric representation of the three-dimensional Ising model, which shares the same universality class as Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). Results indicate that at the critical temperature, normalized cumulants remain independent of the external magnetic field, establishing a fixed point in their temperature evolution. Monte Carlo simulations of finite-size systems confirm that this fixed point behavior persists at temperatures close to the critical value. Furthermore, this phenomenon is observed in the temperature dependence of normalized factorial cumulants starting from the fourth order. Through a mapping from the Ising model to QCD, a similar fixed point behavior is identified in the energy dependence of normalized cumulants (including fourth-order factorial cumulants) along various freeze-out curves. Although the behavior at the phase transition does not directly reflect that at the freeze-out, the existence of such a fixed point in energy dependence offers potential as an experimental signature, provided that thermal transport of the order parameter occurs before the system freezes out. Additionally, this behavior distinguishes critical dynamics from other dynamical scenarios. The findings for factorial cumulants up to the sixth order suggest that they could aid in determining the dimension of the critical universe. Finally, this behavior may serve to test theories regarding the nature of the QCD phase transition.

To date, most reinforcement learning (RL) research has operated as a black box, lacking transparency into agent decisions. While recent studies have assigned trust scores to RL agents, they typically rely on white-box techniques to analyze internal model structures—a method often impractical for complex RL systems. We propose a novel, generalizable approach to assess RL agent trustworthiness by analyzing state action attention maps without requiring insight into the agent's internal architecture. Our method compares the attention map of an input state against those of similar states by measuring feature space distances between one-hot encoded actions, followed by applying a clustering algorithm to determine trust scores. We validate the efficacy of this approach across various RL tasks, including grid worlds, Atari games, and MuJoCo motor control problems.

To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of volume conjecture behavior observed in a virtual (non-classical) link. Additionally, we provide new proofs of the equivalence between the two construction methods. Finally, we examine the specialization of $J_n^T$ at $q=1$, interpreting the resulting invariants at $q=1$ geometrically through the lens of Fox quotients of the torus fundamental group.

Typically, PTMs, which are ELM-postcursors, are explained by magnetic field ergodization caused by edge localized modes and the subsequent development of a seed magnetic island into a PTM. In software testing, mutation analysis stands as the gold standard for assessing test quality; it evaluates a test's capacity to identify synthetic bugs, operating on the principle that tests failing to catch these artificial faults will also miss real ones. numerous continual learning approaches that leverage pretrained models. Many of these methods rely on mechanisms applied to pre-trained representations, restricting or entirely avoiding updates to the backbone during continual training. In this paper, we challenge the necessity of such model complexity for achieving high performance by introducing a simple baseline for comparison. We contend that a pretrained feature extractor alone can deliver competitive or superior continual learning results on the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we developed a straightforward baseline that: 1) utilizes a frozen pretrained model to extract features for each class encountered, computing their mean on training data, and 2) classifies inputs using nearest neighbor distance to these class means, termed the Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This single-headed, exemplar-free, and potentially task-free baseline (via continual mean updates) achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 dataset, outperforming most state-of-the-art methods initialized with the same pretrained transformer. We hope this work encourages future research into learning systems that can continuously enhance representation quality, even when starting from pretrained weights. Furthermore, we investigate leveraging these stable estimates to enhance performance, demonstrating that J-K-fold CV can yield substantially improved performance for medium-sized datasets (approximately 10k examples), as measured by both stability and computational cost. Our findings suggest that adopting J-K-fold CV for performance estimation can result in significant gains for medium-scale dataset evaluations. We release our code alongside predictions on various NLP benchmarks to support future research.

Our repository is available at https://github.com/zhuoh99/J_KfoldCV_ParameterTuning.

In an effort to enhance the stability of performance estimates from K-fold cross-validation (CV) when used for learning parameter tuning, we conduct theoretical and empirical investigations into determining appropriate values for J and K in extended J-K-fold CV frameworks. We apply this approach to named entity recognition (NER) and evaluate its efficacy across datasets of varying sizes. Our results indicate that for small datasets (around 2k examples), an configuration of J=K=10 yields stability comparable to standard K-fold CV with K=5, while simultaneously achieving better performance. Conversely, for larger datasets (approximately 17k examples), setting J=30 with a single fold (K=1) delivers both higher stability and performance than the typical best-performing 10-fold CV setup. These conclusions assist practitioners in selecting suitable parameters for real-world applications involving cross-validation and parameter tuning.

Introduction: Dense suspensions, which encompass a vast array of materials, suddenly surge in viscosity under high stress, causing sudden stops in sudden movements. We introduce a generalized Heisenberg algebra $\mathcal{H}_q(\mathfrak{g})$ for any finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$. A notable characteristic of $\mathcal{H}_q(\mathfrak{g})$ is that its center comprises only scalars, contrasting sharply with the standard Heisenberg algebra, whose center consists of a infinite abelian Lie subalgebra. Additionally, we examine the relationship between $\mathcal{H}_q(\mathfrak{g})$ and the quantum affine algebra $U_q(\hat{\mathfrak{g}})$, establishing several connections with quantum affine algebra invariants. In light of these insights, $\mathcal{H}_q(\mathfrak{g})$ emerges as a promising candidate for generalizing the 6j-symbols of $ADE$ type.

This study examines how public sector officials evaluate their reliance on Google, their awareness of algorithmic biases affecting information retrieval, and the extent of relevant data potentially lost due to personalization. Our experimental results reveal that most participants are unaware of these risks and lack strategies to mitigate the possibility of missing crucial information. Most notably, we present empirical evidence suggesting that personalization can cause the omission of up to 20% of relevant information. Consequently, this research underscores the need for public sector professionals to receive training on algorithmic biases that influence decision-making and to follow clear guidelines for minimizing the risk of overlooking pertinent data during online searches. Such preparations are critical, especially given the potential for search algorithm personalization to contribute to both intentional and unconscious discrimination. We propose incorporating these perspectives into public administration curricula and policy discussions. Furthermore, we suggest establishing "hybrid" professional standards for officials' digital competencies, merging traditional key indicators with metrics for algorithm literacy. Finally, we offer recommendations for fostering an organizational digital literacy that acknowledges the risks of personalization and creates protocols to prevent the loss of relevant information in decision-making processes. These insights into public employees' relationships with AI and algorithms are essential for developing policies that ensure AI systems serve the public interest. Additionally, future inquiries should examine how personalization affects risk assessment, evidence-based policy development, historical record-keeping, and administrative accountability. **Approach:** Continuous k-space data were collected using a rewound Cartesian acquisition with spiral profile ordering (rCASPR). This method was designed to match the contrast of conventional linear phase encoding while organizing data into multiple respiratory phases. Low-resolution, respiratory-correlated 4D images were reconstructed via compressed sensing to estimate non-rigid deformation vector fields, which facilitated motion-compensated image reconstruction. The rCASPR sampling technique was compared against linear and CASPR sampling methods at various in-plane resolutions. Additionally, the proposed rCASPR approach was tested in phantom studies and a human subject.

**Findings:** rCASPR demonstrated equivalent magnetic resonance image (MRI) contrast to linear sampling across all resolutions. At the highest resolution, rCASPR yielded superior reconstruction quality at both inhale and exhale phases compared to linear sampling. In the human scan, rCASPR produced highly detailed lung parenchyma throughout the entire resolution range. However, when rCASPR was applied at lower resolutions, it exhibited excessive noise in the mediastinum during both respiratory phases.

**Conclusion:** rCASPR is an efficient sampling strategy that maintains the same contrast as linear sampling without introducing additional artifacts. It enables the reconstruction of multi-respiration 4D images from continuous k-space data, offering significant potential for clinical image reconstruction.

This paper examines domain representations through CF-approximation spaces, introducing the concepts of CF-approximation spaces and CF-closed sets. It is demonstrated that the collection of CF-closed sets within a CF-approximation space, when ordered by set inclusion, forms a continuous domain, and conversely, every continuous domain is isomorphic to the family of CF-closed sets of some such space. Furthermore, CF-approximable relations are defined via a categorical approach, which enables the proof that the category of CF-approximation spaces and CF-approximable relations is equivalent to the category of continuous domains and Scott-continuous maps. Additionally, the study investigates the connection between CF-approximable relations and Scott's partial order, revealing that the transitive closure of a CF-approximable relation is a Scott-continuous map between domains of Scott's closed sets. Finally, it is shown that the category of CF-approximation spaces and their CF-approximable relations admits small complete interpolants, a property essential for ensuring continuous relational composition. This work aims to provide an alternative, non-order-theoretic framework for continuous domains and their continuous maps. Specifically, there exists a bijective correspondence between Scott's continuous relations and CF-approximable relations on CF-approximation spaces, characterized by a map $\mathcal{R} \leftrightarrow \chi(\mathcal{R})$ that preserves small complete interpolants, Scott continuity, and composition. The paper also explores the relationships among CF-approximable relations, their Scott counterparts, Scott's partial orders, and Scott's continuous functions.

, has been essential for ensuring that performance differences between NLP systems are statistically significant rather than due to chance. However, practitioners have historically relied on Monte Carlo approximations because no suitable exact algorithm existed. This paper introduces an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test applicable to a specific family of structured test statistics. The proposed algorithm operates in $\mathcal{O}(GN (\log GN )(\log N ))$ time, where $N$ represents the dataset size and $G$ denotes the range of the test statistic. Experimental results indicate that our exact algorithm is 10 times faster than a Monte Carlo approximation using 20,000 samples on a standard dataset. Furthermore, our implementation is now accessible as a library within the widely used spaNLP framework. We anticipate that this exact algorithm will enable researchers to conduct performance significance tests on larger datasets, a current limitation for many significant test computations. Our implementation can be integrated into the HPO framework cause effect for performing significance testing, facilitating more robust evaluation of candidate models' performance improvements. Additionally, our implementation will support future research on general exact algorithms for other test statistics commonly used in NLP model evaluation. Although this work focuses on evaluating discriminative models for sequence classification and generation, the introduced algorithm is extensible to other tasks and model types, including those with wider performance significance testing requirements. In terms of implementation, the algorithm is compact at under 300 lines of code, and we provide a reference implementation that aligns with the related system for evaluating both classical NLP tasks and neural machine translation. Finally, our contributions open avenues for extending to other structured test statistics, as discussed in the related work on sequence performance testing and holistic evaluation goals for machine translation. We hope our implementations will assist the broader machine learning and computational linguistics communities in conducting more rigorous significance tests across various performance metrics and language tasks.

Although Vision Transformers (ViTs) now rival or exceed CNNs in visual recognition accuracy, they lack inductive biases inherent to convolutional operators, potentially limiting generalization on data-poor domains like medical imaging. We investigate label propagation as a means to inject such biases into Vision Transformers. Our findings show that even a single labeled image can generally improve performance when performing inference on similar target images within the same domain. Furthermore, we develop a meta-learning algorithm that trains a ViT using a mini-batch of labeled images to propagate labels to a unseen query image. We release our code at https://github.com/AhmedRashed13/Transformers_for_LaProp.

We present a method for enhancing the performance of graph neural networks (GNNs) through targeted label smoothing. This technique identifies overly confident predictions with high probability mass assigned to incorrect labels and reduces their labels toward zero, thereby encouraging the model to rely more on label information. We release the code at https://github.com/AhmedRashed13/Transformers_for_LaProp.

We propose a method to endow Vision Transformers (ViTs) with inductive biases typical of CNNs by leveraging label propagation. Our approach begins with one or a few labeled images and propagates their labels to similar query images, creating a synthetic dataset for pre-training the ViT. However, current aggregate flexibility metrics are typically slow-timescale estimations, with limited focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper addresses online optimization within a closed-loop system by proposing a real-time aggregate flexibility feedback mechanism called Maximum Entropy Feedback (MEF). The advantages of this approach include: (1) Efficient Communication, as the operator running PPC requires only the MEF rather than exact load states and constraints; (2) Fast Computation, since PPC involves significantly fewer variables than traditional MPC formulations; and (3) Lower Costs, as PPC is shown to be optimal under specific regularity assumptions. We validate the PPC's effectiveness using data from an adaptive electric vehicle charging network, demonstrating that it outperforms classical MPC. Furthermore, the paper establishes the theoretical benefits of PPC by linking it to Log Barrier Control (LBC), revealing that PPC minimizes a modified risk function derived from the operator's cost via the Aggregators' MEF. These findings on communication efficiency, computation speed, and cost performance represent the first of their kind for control systems utilizing reinforcement learning. Ultimately, this work bridges non-asymptotic learning guarantees with asymptotic control stability, offering a holistic view of their interconnections.

Rising inflation rates have driven individuals to shift funds from savings into stocks, commodities, and other investment avenues. Deep Learning models have repeatedly demonstrated their efficacy in forecasting time series data. Consequently, technical analysis utilizing various indicators remains a standard practice for traders and investors. Additionally, sentiment analysis gauges investor emotions and their propensity to invest. Globally, practitioners have employed diverse techniques ranging from basic Machine Learning to advanced Neural Networks, experimenting with methods from simple linear regression to complex architectures to predict market movements. Recent events clearly illustrate the impact of news and headlines on stock markets and cryptocurrencies. This paper introduces an ensemble of cutting-edge methods for stock price prediction. Specifically, it performs sentiment analysis on news and headlines concerning Apple Inc. (NASDAQ) using BERT, a pre-trained transformer model for Natural Language Processing. Subsequently, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) forecasts Apple Inc.'s stock price by integrating technical indicators, global stock indices, commodity prices, historical data, and sentiment scores. The proposed approach is benchmarked against baseline models, including Long Short Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), vanilla GANs, and the Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) model. During the training phase, the dataset is segmented into technical features, global indices, sentiments, and prices, with the model fine-tuned on technical features before adding global indices. The process continues sequentially with commodity prices and historical data, with the final model trained on historical data. Finally, news and headlines about Apple Inc. are incorporated. Experimental results on Apple Inc. data confirm the model's accuracy and validity. The paper concludes that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches. Finally, it addresses challenges related to data acquisition and suggests directions for future research.

However, standard maximum likelihood (ML) estimation and inference techniques are often fragile, lacking robustness against minor model misspecifications or data contamination. While non-parametric alternatives offer robustness, they frequently suffer from a significant loss in efficiency. To address this, we propose a robust parameter estimation method for discretely observed data from parametric stochastic processes, leveraging the advantageous properties of the density power divergence within a minimum distance inference framework. Specifically, we introduce minimum density power divergence estimators (MDPDE) tailored for independent increment and Markov processes. We derive asymptotic consistency and distributional properties for these MDPDEs under dependent stochastic process settings and demonstrate their superiority over conventional ML estimators through examples such as Poisson processes, drifted Brownian motion, and autoregressive models. Furthermore, the success of MDPDEs can be enhanced by integrating modern outlier detection mechanisms like robust deep learning. Consequently, extending this approach to state space models represents a promising direction for future research.
Poisson processes are fundamental building blocks in probability theory and find extensive applications across various fields. This paper introduces a robust estimation procedure for the parameters of a Poisson process, a method that is also extensible to other Markov processes. Unlike traditional approaches, this new method demonstrates resistance to both gross errors and slight deviations or contamination in the underlying data or assumptions. Specifically, for a Poisson process where the parameter of interest is $\theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for $\theta$ minimizes the empirical Kullback-Leibler divergence (or log-likelihood) between the theoretical distribution $F_\theta$ and the empirical distribution $G_n$ of the observed data. Formally, the robust estimator $\hat{\theta}$ is defined as the minimizer of the robustifying function $\rho_\gamma(F_\theta||G_n)$ for a tuning parameter $\gamma > 0$: $$\hat{\theta}=\textrm{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\rho_\gamma(F_\theta||G_n).$$ The proposed minimization algorithm is validated using simulated Poisson processes with known parameters and time-horizon data, as well as stock price data where the process is assumed to follow a parametric model. In the latter case, the estimator proves valuable when the assumed model is only an approximation. Finally, the methodology is extended to handle unit root problems associated with Poisson processes.

For Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, we identify direct evidence of shock-ionization oriented orthogonally to the ionization axis; these shocks are readily detectable because the nuclear dusty torus shields the AGN radiation field. Additionally, we report the first observation of curved shocks in an AGN, noting that both the ionization and shock fronts exhibit S-shaped structures. This study offers robust evidence that shocks contribute substantially to the ionized gas surrounding AGN nuclei, often alongside ionization by the central engine. Finally, we propose that the orientation of shocks relative to the ionization axis around AGN can serve as a diagnostic tool for characterizing outflow dynamics. Introduction Many time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) possess underlying structures in their continuous solutions that must be maintained by discrete methods, such as conservation laws, symplecticity, or more general geometric invariants. Preserving these structures is vital for achieving long-time stability, although it does not necessarily dictate the entire design of a numerical scheme. This work focuses on creating schemes that maintain a discrete version of energy—a common property for many important time-dependent PDEs. tracking the evolution of superbubbles driven by stellar winds and supernovae from young, coeval massive star clusters situated within low-metallicity ($Z = 0.02$Z$_{\odot}$), clumpy molecular clouds. The investigation focuses on the early phases of superbubble development, specifically examining pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae events. The primary objectives are to analyze dust grain growth within orbiting dusty clumps and the swept-up supershell of the superbubble, as well as to assess the survival of pre-supernova dusty clumps. The models incorporate the gravitational potential of the cluster, the thermal bath from stellar wind-driven hot gas, and a population of orbiting dusty clouds. Consistent with prior findings by previous hydrodynamical and analytical studies, we observe that supershifts and secondary supernovae cause abrupt changes in the density, temperature, and velocity profiles of both the dusty clouds and the supershell. We also determine the growth rate of dust grains using the Whitten and Hunt surface accretion model. Our results indicate that heavy element accretion dominates over collisional accretion for dust formation in this scenario. Depending on the supershell's age and the amount of metals available for dust formation, silicon grain radii range from sub-micron to a few microns. Furthermore, we derive the distribution of superbubble internal pressures, cluster gravitational potentials, and the sizes of both surviving and destroyed dusty clouds. These outcomes provide insights into the evolution of cluster-induced supershifts and emphasize the significant impact of the combined effects of dust growth and supernovae on the supershell and orbiting clouds. This work presents the first 3D simulations of supershifts arising from the interaction between an isolated, gravity-bound, coeval massive star cluster and the surrounding molecular cloud. The derived dust mass generation rates and grain size distributions from these 3D simulations can serve as boundary conditions for global chemical evolution models. Additionally, future research should examine multi-year stellar evolutionary tracks, varying cluster mass distributions, and a broader range of chemical compositions. The simulated cluster chemical enrichment is expected to aid in interpreting observational data from upcoming surveys conducted by the JWST and ALMA. This capability is critical for autonomous vehicles (AVs) traveling at highway speeds, as detecting distant obstacles is essential for maintaining adequate braking distances. However, existing AV benchmarks like nuScenes largely overlook this challenge by restricting performance evaluation to distances within 50 meters. This limitation stems partly from the difficulty of generating far-field 3D annotations, especially for LiDAR sensors, which often yield sparse point returns for distant objects; our analysis reveals that nearly 50% of objects beyond 50 meters have zero LiDAR points. Additionally, current 3D detection metrics apply uniform tolerance thresholds to both near and far objects, a "one-size-fits-all" approach that contradicts the varying tolerances inherent in human vision and stereo disparity. These factors result in an incomplete assessment of Far3Det. For instance, despite the conventional belief that high-resolution RGB sensors are crucial for detecting distant objects, LiDAR-based methods currently outperform RGB counterparts on standard benchmark leaderboards. As an initial step toward a dedicated Far3Det benchmark, we identified well-annotated scenes within the nuScenes dataset to create a robust far-field validation set. We also introduced a new evaluation protocol and tested various 3D detection methods specifically for this task. Our findings strongly validate the established wisdom that high-resolution RGB significantly enhances far-field detection performance, surpassing both LiDAR and combined sensor fusion approaches. We encourage the research community to build upon nuScenes to explicitly solve Far3Det and to adopt the proposed benchmark for future evaluations. The source code and dataset are publicly available.

This process involves aligning a preoperative CT-derived organ model with an intraoperative surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video. The task is complex due to factors such as sparse and noisy real-time data, numerous unknowns regarding tissue properties and boundary conditions, and the difficulty of establishing correspondences between pre- and intraoperative datasets. These challenges are exacerbated by the liver's lack of distinct surface features and the disparate noise characteristics of the imaging modalities used. The network was trained on physically accurate biomechanical simulations of randomly generated, deforming organ-like structures, enabling immediate generalization to new patients without retraining. By incorporating varying levels of noise into the intraoperative surfaces during training, the model achieves robustness against noisy data. During inference, the network generates a displacement field that aligns the preoperative volume with the partial intraoperative surface. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach effectively translates to real-world data while maintaining high inference speed, and the source code is publicly available. This method facilitates tracking dynamic organ surfaces in partial 3D voxel and point cloud representations, offering potential support for needle insertion and other surgical tasks requiring surface visualization on 2D displays.

Non-rigid registration is critical in medical procedures involving multiple imaging scans, as it enhances situational awareness, improves diagnostics, and increases surgical precision. Successful outcomes rely on accurately understanding both the patient's condition and the current surgical context. For instance, when placing surgical instruments, it is essential to know their position relative to the target anatomy; similarly, updating tumor locations on resection scans ensures that cancerous tissue is completely removed. While various techniques have been proposed to resolve these challenges, they often struggle to perform optimally across diverse scenarios. Although recent advances utilize machine learning to generate patient-specific solutions, many of these methods remain dependent on extensive simulation data, still failing to adequately generalize to clinical reality.

This paper addresses the problem of registering a three-dimensional organ model to a partial surface captured during surgery. Specifically, we focus on reconstructing and updating the position of a liver intraoperatively from noisy laparoscopic images. Although significant research has been dedicated to this issue, existing solutions do not fully encompass all stages of the workflow, and performance remains hindered by uncertainties and variations in both data and boundary conditions.

Originating in the 1970s through the work of Las Vergnas and Häggkvist, the investigation of graphs with the PMH-property integrates three fundamental graph concepts: matchings, Hamiltonicity, and edge-colourings. This study focuses on cubic graphs, aiming to characterize those where every perfect matching aligns with a specific colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. We demonstrate that this condition is equivalent to the graphs being even-2-factorable (E2F), meaning all their 2-factors consist exclusively of even cycles. While bipartite cubic graphs trivially satisfy the E2F property, our analysis is restricted to non-bipartite cubic graphs. Although the PMH-property provides a sufficient (though not necessary) condition for a cubic graph to be E2F, the primary objective of this work is to define an infinite family of non-bipartite, E2F cubic graphs parameterized by two variables, which we term "papillon graphs." We further determine the specific parameter values under which these papillon graphs exhibit the PMH-property or are merely E2F, and we prove that papillon graphs with distinct parameters are never isomorphic. Additionally, we establish that certain papillon graphs admit no 3-edge-colourings, indicating their strict reliance on the E2F property. Finally, we derive several significant combinatorial characteristics common to all papillon graphs. As a contribution to random graph theory, we show that almost all cubic graphs are E2F and converge in distribution to a limit distribution supported on the family of papillon graphs. Consequently, papillon graphs represent the typical structure of random cubic graphs. This research extends previous findings by L. Miermont regarding 2-factors in random cubic graphs. To support this conclusion, we also introduce and examine the distribution of even 2-factors within these graphs. A companion paper, titled "Typical 2-factors in random cubic graphs," presents the proof for the asymptotic almost sure (a.a.s.) establishment of the papillon graph family and elucidates the distribution of even 2-factors in them. In that context, a.a.s. random cubic graphs lack the E2F property, are not 3-edge-colourable, do not contain Hamiltonian cycles, and are not 1-tough.

### I. Introduction

Soccer, a sport defined by sparse rewards, sees its final outcome hinging on events that occur infrequently throughout the game. While the 22 players on the field execute numerous actions, only one goal is required to win, and many teams play entire matches without scoring. Even in cases of multiple goals, the vast array of possible player actions remains underexplored. This scarcity of feedback makes it difficult to assess which actions are truly critical and what constitutes an optimal behavior, a challenge evident for players, scouts, and the public. Although recent studies have evaluated soccer actions through various lenses—such as statistical analysis, data mining, and machine learning—the performance assessment of these actions in sparse reward environments remains an open problem. Specifically, there is a need to evaluate whether certain contexts demand specific behaviors to achieve maximum reward and to identify the distributions of these optimal behaviors. This paper addresses the challenge of assessing soccer actions and learns the resulting optimal policy distribution within this domain.

Wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) alleviates the requirement for strict adherence to the physical wave equation during iterations, whereas extended source waveform inversion (ESI) employs a non-physical source distributed across the computational domain that iteratively migrates toward the true physical source. Both WRI and ESI operate within a shared mathematical framework utilizing the Lagrangian-based adjoint-state method, with a specific emphasis on time-domain formulations using extended sources. Conceptually, WRI and ESI can be regarded as weighted variants of classical FWI. To efficiently solve the resulting normal equations in a matrix-free manner, the conjugate gradient method is applied, leveraging the symmetric positive definite Hessian; this approach supports both time and frequency domain wave equation solvers. However, the primary challenge remains the substantial storage requirements needed to retain time-domain wavefields throughout the iterative process. To address this, two strategies are proposed: extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data directly instead of wavefields. It is recommended that these approaches be further investigated to develop more tractable workflows. Additionally, both methods can be extended to incorporate multiple physical fields and irregular computational grids. Finally, replacing the Lagrangian-based adjoint-state method with operator-based techniques like the L-BFGS algorithm is suggested to significantly reduce storage demands. These advancements would make full waveform inversion more accessible to practitioners working with sparse sensor arrays, deep oceans, and offshore time-lapse monitoring systems. This study derives a semi-analytical formula for the dynamical density-density linear-response function (the "Lindhard" function) of noninteracting massless Dirac fermions at finite temperatures. This result is essential for characterizing the finite-temperature screening of interacting massless Dirac fermions within the Random Phase Approximation. Specifically, we utilize this formula to generate quantitative predictions for the specific heat and compressibility of doped graphene sheets. Our findings indicate that at low temperatures, the specific heat exhibits the standard linear-in-temperature behavior typical of a normal Fermi liquid, with the slope determined exclusively by the renormalized quasiparticle velocity. These theoretical predictions align well with recent experimental data from both graphene sheets and few-layer graphite. This paper investigates theories featuring multiple symmetries, analyzing both the conventional thin- and thick-wall limits and establishing sufficient conditions for existence in the latter. Furthermore, we propose a novel state within this theoretical framework known as the cored Q-ball. Although we demonstrate that this state can achieve energetic stability, a comprehensive phenomenological analysis is reserved for future research. In addition to the standard charges derived from individual symmetries, the cored Q-ball carries a composite charge from a combined symmetry, which is considerably more robust against perturbative corrections to the effective potential. This suggests that such objects could persist in string theory scenarios, even when fine tuning is prohibitive. We also explore potential applications to dark matter phenomenology. Although the state described here is not novel in the Standard Model, it has significant differences from the commonly studied solitonic balls. This state could offer crucial insights into the cosmological consequences of phase transitions affecting symmetries, particularly regarding the mitigation of dangerous relics from earlier transitions. While a detailed examination of phase boundary energy density is left for future work, we show in the effective theory that the state examined here provides an explicit example of suppression without requiring the energy density to drop monotonically. This study examines the complementary nature of these signatures for the Belle II experiment, specifically focusing on axion-like particles ($a$) generated from meson decays. We introduce a novel approach to detect two-body decays characterized by $B^+ \to K^+ a$ followed by $a\to E\!\!\!/$, where $E\!\!\!/$ represents missing energy. Utilizing an integrated luminosity of $50\,$ab$^{-1}$, Belle II is capable of probing light invisible resonances with branching ratios $\mathcal{B}(B^+\to K^+ a) \gtrsim 10^{-7}$ and decay lengths $c\tau_a \gtrsim 1\,$m. For axion-like particles, we anticipate that the sensitivity of the $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ channel to small couplings could improve by up to two orders of magnitude relative to prior searches at fixed-target and collider facilities. Specifically, for sub-GeV particles, the combination of $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ at Belle II and beam-dump experiments offers the greatest sensitivity, whereas for heavier particles, the smallest couplings can be probed through $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ alone, provided the B factories achieve a sensitivity of $10^{-6}$. Furthermore, we examine the feasibility of discovering axion-like particles arising from flavor-changing neutral currents in fixed-target experiments, which could extend current limits by a factor of ten. Finally, we assess the potential for discovering generic stable or long-lived neutral particles using the ATLAS detector's missing energy channel, based on existing Belle II constraints on two-body decays. We conclude that future searches should be tailored to the specific characteristics of the particles they aim to detect. Additionally, we provide public access to the analysis code on GitHub to support the TLEB2022 report.

We first introduce an ensemble method that surpasses prior contextualized approaches, which then serves as the foundation for a detailed analysis of predicted semantic shifts in English vocabulary over five decades. Our results indicate that these methods frequently assign high change scores to words that are not actually undergoing genuine diachronic semantic shifts, or where the validity of such shifts is dubious. We provide detailed discussions of these challenging instances with specific examples and propose corresponding linguistic classifications. Ultimately, we conclude that pre-trained contextualized language models tend to conflate changes in lexicographic senses with variations in contextual frequency, a bias inherent to their distributional nature that differs from issues seen in static embedding methods. Furthermore, these models often blend syntactic and semantic features of lexical items. Finally, we suggest several potential future solutions to address these problems. This work extends upon our preceding quantitative evaluation, which demonstrated that current methods for detecting diachronic semantic change perform poorly compared to established golden standards. This research clarifies the underlying causes of these failures and offers practical methods for identifying authentic changing words, boasting significantly higher precision. Since the findings are broadly applicable across different language models and periods, we anticipate these insights and recommendations will aid in developing more robust models and techniques for accurate diachronic semantic change detection. We also make all code, data, and documents available on GitHub: https://github.com/MohammadParvini/Diachronic-Embedding. Documents within this paper are accessible on Zenodo: Papers, Sections, and Tables.

We examine a subset of English words that have been confirmed as undergoing genuine diachronic semantic shifts, utilizing a manual golden standard. Our findings demonstrate that state-of-the-art methods for detecting diachronic semantic change achieve a precision and recall of only 17% and 52%, respectively, when measured against these golden standards. These results stem from the fact that existing techniques primarily rely on surface-level distributional properties, which cause them to conflate frequent context variations with authentic diachronic semantic change. Consequently, we anticipate that our identified golden standard will prove beneficial for developing novel methods capable of distinguishing true diachronic semantic shifts from frequentency-induced context changes. We employ the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear relationship linking four source-frame variables: radio luminosity, X-ray or optical luminosity (derived from the [OIII] emission line), black hole mass, and spin. By incorporating uncertainties related to luminosity measurements, conversion factors, relativistic beaming, and AGN physical properties, we establish lower limits on the spins of a sample of massive, jetted AGNs. Considering that self-interactions might inhibit axion instability and explain the lack of observed superradiance, we derive upper limits on the axion decay constant (which correspond to lower limits on self-interaction strength). Furthermore, assuming axions are defined by mass and decay constant, we determine the maximum fraction of dark matter attributable to ultra-light particles, accounting for both linear growth and superradiance effects. Our analysis also yields model-dependent upper limits on the fraction of dark matter available to be captured by stellar-mass black holes, as this process could induce a bulk spin-down that counteracts any acceleration of the [OIII] line. Our conclusions are robust against systematics arising from selection effects, bias in the mass estimate distribution, and variations in the functional form of the fundamental plane.

In this study, we utilize long-term, rapid lightsheet and two-photon imaging of zebrafish retinas *in vivo* during early development to identify the physical mechanisms driving nuclear behavior during IKNM. These imaging techniques enable the reliable tracking of nuclear movements and divisions within densely packed populations during early retinogenesis. By analyzing these tracks, we formulate and validate a theoretical model of retinal IKNM as a diffusive process influenced by a nuclear concentration gradient established by the continuous addition of new nuclei at the apical surface. Our findings elucidate how apical nuclear packing affects migration dynamics, offer a robust quantitative account of nuclear distribution across the retina, and suggest potential implications for stochastic cell division processes. Overall, this work provides a quantitative examination of how a simple physical mechanism governs nuclear migration during retinal IKNM in early vertebrate eye development. Image credit: Adamus.

Additional context is provided by citations from related literature. For instance, research on retinal neurogenesis in vertebrates highlights that while proliferation generates the vast number of cells required for eye function, subsequent differentiation into diverse photoreceptor types defines the retina's physiological characteristics. This process involves staged cell cycle pauses followed by terminal differentiation; specifically, newly formed cone precursors undergo a cell cycle pause before migrating to the outer nuclear layer (ONL) to differentiate. Furthermore, studies on cellular packing in the developing zebrafish retina explore how random nuclear addition drives a transition from a broad to a bistable distribution of nuclear positions across the tissue. Other works investigate the biophysics of these dividing tissues, noting that while cell proliferation expands tissue area, physical packing constraints eventually trigger apoptosis or delamination to maintain homeostasis. Additional references discuss the coordinated processes of neurogenesis and migration in the developing eye, detailing how cell cycle exit drives the formation of distinct neuronal layers. Finally, analyses of retinal development emphasize that understanding how the eye generates a functional array of light-sensing cells requires examining both cell proliferation and the subsequent sorting of postmitotic cells into functional layers; specifically, in the zebrafish retina, cones pause their cell cycles in intermediate layers (ICL) before migrating to the ONL to mature. These related findings underscore the complex interplay of migration, packing dynamics, and cell cycle regulation central to retinogenesis.

In these contexts, physically viable code patterns are inherently non-negative, systematically structured, and often lack coherence. This study addresses the common denoising challenge across these fields through a new perspective: separating a visible image (like a coded pattern) from one or multiple invisible images (such as RGB color data) using visible light-only measurements. We introduce a general framework where visible light captures the superposition of all target images; for instance, this enables video compressed sensing or color image reconstruction without any visible light coding. Notably, the source code requires no hyper-parameter tuning except the camera exposure time, which is determined experimentally based on the code's maximum transmission intensity. Our theory demonstrates that these fluids can maintain coherent motion, characterized by a non-zero mean velocity in the hydrodynamic limit, despite the disruptive effects of the disorder. Nevertheless, linearized hydrodynamics fails to capture the scaling behavior of these active systems in spatial dimensions ranging from 2 to 5. Despite this limitation, we derive the precise dimension-dependent scaling exponents for these ranges. This achievement stems from formulating and solving a self-consistent equation for the dimensionless correlation factor, an approach grounded in the generalized Navier-Stokes equations for incompressible flow. Our findings offer insights into the hydrodynamic ordering of dimensionally varying active systems. Active particles consume internal energy to sustain motion, generating spatially extended correlated flows that enhance mixing and support pattern formation in macroscopic ensembles. While experimental inquiries into polar active fluids have primarily targeted efficient energy consumption and sustained flow, theoretical models have often overlooked the impact of environmental disorder, such as chemical or structural variations, despite its ubiquity in nature. We construct a model for dimensionally active polar fluids with embedded disorder. Although not strictly random, this system shares characteristics with random media. By deriving a dimension-dependent scaling exponent, we illustrate how active matter can exist within these dimensions. Furthermore, we show that homogeneous polar active matter exhibits active frictionless flow, a consequence of self-propelled motion, whereas random friction generally arises in active matter with orientational disorder. In higher dimensions, disorder averages out, yet in lower dimensions, it remains relevant due to correlated flows. The resulting dimension-dependent scaling exponent indicates that disorder continues to influence the scaling of correlation functions, although its dimension-dependent nature becomes less significant as space dimensions increase. To address the challenge of deriving a dimension-dependent scaling exponent, we propose a random field Ising model (RFIM) as a conceptual framework. We establish a mapping between the RFIM and our disorder model, suggesting a method to derive the dimension-dependent scaling exponent through an exact solution of the RFIM. Although this mapping is not fully rigorous, it provides a useful analogy. Finally, we demonstrate that both systems exhibit the same dimension-dependent scaling behavior. Although random field disorder is not strictly applicable to polar active matter, this analogy offers a novel framework for investigating dimensionally active matter. We also suggest that anonymized data from these centers could support further investigation into the factors influencing network vulnerability.

This singularity marks the contact point between these two separated Fermi surface components. We demonstrate that this exceptional singularity lies close to a standard second-order van Hove singularity, reachable by adjusting a dispersion parameter. Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect, a net torque generated by the reflection and thermal re-emission of solar radiation from their surfaces. This phenomenon causes a gradual alteration in rotation periods, which is most readily observable in light curves due to the quadratic accumulation of phase shifts over time. We gathered archived light curves and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids (10115) 1992 SK, (1620) Geographos, and (1685) Toro. Using light curve inversion, we fitted the data to convex shape models, modeling the YORP effect as a linear variation in rotation frequency within an expansion similar to that used in astrometric fitting. We estimated the non-gravitational acceleration components along and perpendicular to the spin axis, along with their uncertainties, using various model configurations that varied in the number of observation epochs included and the level of smoothing applied to convex shape models derived from light curve fitting. For (10115) 1992 SK, the along-axis YORP acceleration lies within the range of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-8}$ cm/s$^2$, while for (1620) Geographos, it falls between $10^{-8}$ and $10^{-7}$ cm/s$^2$. The perpendicular acceleration for (1685) Toro is approximately $3 \times 10^{-8}$ cm/s$^2$. Although these values represent lower bounds that would be valid if light curve morphology remains constant, they serve as robust minimum estimates of the along-axis YORP acceleration when shape changes occur on timescales longer than those required for significant rotational variations. These findings align with, and aid in refining, previous determinations based solely on light curve analysis. Additionally, we offer explanations for reported discrepancies in the secular variation of the rotation periods for (1620) Geographos and (1685) Toro. This represents the initial application of direct least-squares fitting of the YORP effect to light curve inversion results. Although this method demands more precise astrometric data than that typically available from light curve studies, it may become viable with astrometry from instruments like JWST. Furthermore, this approach could prove valuable for leveraging archival data from wide-field surveys, such as LSST.

This study examines online political discussions on Instagram through a network lens, specifically focusing on the formation of "co-commenter communities"—groups of users who frequently interact by commenting on the same posts and potentially steer ongoing conversations. We specifically target "salient co-interactions," which are interactions among co-commenters that occur significantly more often than would be expected by chance or independent behavior. Unlike casual interactions that happen frequently by accident, these salient interactions are crucial drivers of online discourse and information spread. Our research analyzes ten weeks of data centered on major elections in Brazil and Italy, tracking both politicians and celebrities. We characterize these co-commenter communities by examining their topological structure, the nature of the discussions within them, and how community composition and topics evolve over time. Furthermore, political discussion communities tend to be more dynamic; however, top commenters maintain their activity and membership within these groups over time. Instagram offers extensive data on user interactions, including images, comments, and sharing activities, making it a key environment for political figure debates. This analysis employs network science methods to examine these interactions and their evolving dynamics over time, specifically looking at Instagram data from Brazil during the 2018 elections. Over ten weeks, we identified "co-commenter communities" as groups of users who actively engage with the same posts. Our research focuses on "salient co-interactions"—interactions among these co-commenters that occur significantly more frequently than by chance. These critical interactions drive online discourse; the study characterizes community topology, discusses topics, and explores their temporal dynamics. Results show that political discussion communities are more dynamic, though top contributors remain active over time. Additionally, while some topics are fleeting, those related to core political issues are consistently active. We suggest pathways for future inquiry.

Within the M-dwarf sector, significant research has focused on developing empirical relations that utilize easily obtained observables to determine physical properties. This paper presents a novel Bayesian framework designed to simultaneously and self-consistently apply multiple empirical calibrations to fully characterize the mass, luminosity, radius, and effective temperature of field-age M-dwarfs. We investigate the virus's propagation starting from a single infected person in a restaurant, deriving a formula for the infection radius that aligns with the number of infections observed in early outbreak phases. This formula depends on the room's acoustic radius and the person's breathing rate. The total number of infections is determined by the room's volume and the infected person's breathing rate. If the room is airtight, the infections follow a power law with respect to the room's acoustic radius; if not, they follow a power law with respect to the square of the acoustic radius. Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) techniques are essential for solving strongly correlated many-body problems that are otherwise inaccessible. However, time-dependent QMC methods are often limited by a sign problem that causes exponential computational cost growth with inverse temperature $\beta$. Although transforming the imaginary-time path integral into a deformed contour can eliminate this obstruction, the resulting Jacobian determinant becomes exponentially voluminous as system size $V$ increases. Traditional algorithms can only manage microscopic $V$ scales ($V \lesssim 10^3$). To perform simulations on macroscopic scales ($V \sim 10^5$), a more efficient Jacobian handling method is required. This study evaluates several such techniques, with the most promising being the stochastic series expansion. Using this combination, we cleared a signature sign problem for the bosonic Hubbard model, enabling investigations into Bose-Einstein condensation across five orders of magnitude in system size. The elimination of this obstacle paves the way for studying finite-temperature phenomena in mesoscopic and macroscopic quantum boson systems.

Previously, under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), an asymptotic formula for the count of such integers up to $x$, denoted $\Psi(x,y)$, was established only for $y \ge (\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ by Hildebrand and Saias. In this work, we provide an unconditional asymptotic formula for $\Psi(x,y)$ within the broader range $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula takes the form $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ multiplied by correction factors that account for contributions from zeta zeros and prime powers. Using this result, we address two inquiries posed by Hildebrand and Pomerance.

First, regarding Hildebrand's conjecture that $\Psi(x,y)$ is not asymptotically equivalent to $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ when $y < (\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, we confirm unconditionally that his assertion was correct.

Extending prior research, we fit median [X/Mg] versus [Mg/H] trends using a two-process model that separates abundance patterns into a "prompt" component linked to core-collapse supernovae and a "delayed" component associated with Type Ia supernovae. For individual stars, we determine the amplitudes of these two components and calculate residuals, denoted as \Delta[X/H], from the resulting two-parameter fit. The root-mean-square residuals span approximately 0.01–0.03 dex for the most precise APOGEE measurements, rising to about 0.1 dex for Na, V, and potentially Ca. Correlation analyses of these residuals expose a complex underlying structure, featuring a correlated group of Ca, Na, Al, K, Cr, and Ni, alongside a distinct group comprising Cu, Cl, Ar, and Ti. De-projecting the stellar sample reveals that the Ni, Cu, Ca, and Ca–Cu groups persist even at low metallicities (up to [Fe/H] \approx -1.5 dex), whereas the remaining groups are either newly identified or only apparent at higher metallicities. Identical residual analyses applied to two-point correlation functions highlight the importance of measuring abundances in low-mass, long-lived stars within nearby moving groups and associations for characterizing Galactic field star chemical diversity. Finally, we briefly address the "super solar" Na abundance observed in metal-poor disk stars and speculate on its connection to Ca, Na–Ca anti-correlations, and presolar nanodust. These findings are largely based on a public dataset containing stellar abundance measurements for 16 elements across 1.5 million field disk stars.
