powerful tools for identifying patterns in time series and system dynamics, yet they operate under the assumption of fixed, unchanging dynamics, a limitation that often does not hold in real-world applications. In contrast, many control tasks involve similar but distinct dynamics that can be effectively represented as a latent variable. We propose Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a framework that defines a family of related dynamical systems using a low-dimensional set of latent factors. This approach offers a straightforward and efficient method for learning and performing inference on this Gaussian graphical model without relying on approximations such as variational inference. Our results demonstrate that HiP-RSSMs surpass both standard RSSMs and competing multi-task models across various demanding robotic benchmarks, including both physical systems and simulations. Furthermore, we show that the framework effectively accommodates missing data by leveraging the complete data distribution through marginalization. Finally, our model achieves excellent sample efficiency when inferring both systems and their corresponding latent factors. This was demonstrated by training on approximately 100 frames from one system and making predictions on up to 99% data missing from up to 10 different test sets.

Although many existing approaches are designed to learn multiple tasks simultaneously, they often require the user to manually specify which tasks are similar. Our model eliminates the need for such heuristics by learning task similarities automatically. While we do not define "task" explicitly, we operationally define it as a set of observations and initial conditions generated by a specific system; therefore, learning similar tasks equates to learning similar initial conditions and/or missing data distributions.

HiP-RSSMs offer a unified approach for learning multiple tasks that is both sample efficient and capable of inferring parameters for unseen tasks. By inferring which specific task is being observed, the model can fill in missing data from up to 99% of data across up to 100 test sets.

While previous methods assumed all tasks share a single, common dynamic structure, our model learns a collection of potentially different dynamics, allowing it to generalize to new, similar tasks.

We introduced a method to learn a family of related dynamical systems defined by latent factors, enabling the learning of otherwise unseen tasks from just a few samples. Our model, the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Model, is capable of learning and performing inference on these latent factor-defined task families from very limited data. We further demonstrate its ability to perform robustly even when test data is up to 99% missing.

While various approaches commonly measure polarization in social networks by examining their structure alone, we evaluated eight such methods and found that all produce high polarization scores even for random networks sharing the density and degree distributions of real-world networks. Additionally, certain methods are influenced by degree distributions and the relative sizes of polarized groups. To address this, we propose normalizing existing scores and establishing a minimal set of tests to ensure a score can effectively distinguish polarized networks from random noise. Following normalization, the performance of these scores in a classification task involving 203 networks improved by 38% to 220%. Our findings indicate that normalization is more critical than the specific method chosen; after normalization, most methods outperform the best unnormalized method. While this method offers a more realistic and comprehensive representation compared to single-layer networks, it simultaneously introduces inherent complexities in system analysis. In this work, we present a method to study Kuramoto oscillators on multilayer networks by utilizing the join of matrices that encode both intra-layer and inter-layer connections. This strategy yields a "reduced" representation of the original multilayer system that exhibits equivalent dynamics. By solving for the reduced system and propagating these solutions back to the full network, we can determine system states. Furthermore, applying this same principle allows us to assess the stability of these states; by examining the Jacobian of the reduced system, we can derive insights into the Jacobian of the original multilayer network. This approach is broadly applicable to any connection scheme within a layer. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate the potential for analyzing multilayer network dynamics through a simplified framework, thereby enhancing our understanding of their behavioral patterns. The effectiveness of our method is validated through numerical simulations. In the context of the Kuramoto model, we investigate the evolution from incoherent states to clusters and calculate the distribution of critical coupling strengths required for synchronization. Additionally, we examine how inter-layer interactions influence the stability of these clusters. Our results confirm the reliability of our approach in determining system states and contribute to a deeper comprehension of multilayer network behaviors. At a fundamental level, this research aids in characterizing the global states and stability of complex systems, while practically, it supports the analysis of synchronization in multilayer power grids. We also explore how our methodology can be extended to analyze the entanglement of quantum multilayer networks. We hope that our findings will prove beneficial for investigating other types of multilayer networks.

Multi-layer networks are widely regarded as a more accurate representation of the world's complex systems. Although significant advancements have been made in developing frameworks to describe their static structures, there remains a critical need to create analogous models that capture the temporal evolution and interactions of these systems. This research addresses that gap. We demonstrate that key dynamical properties, such as synchronization, can be inferred by analyzing a strategically constructed single-layer network derived from the original multi-layer structure. Specifically, global synchronization occurs when all nodes in every layer share identical states. By ensuring that connected nodes within each layer have identical phase variables in a transformed system, we can establish a direct correspondence between the solutions of this reduced model and those of the initial multi-layer network. to program testing, with the goal of enhancing the reliability of software development, especially for safety-critical systems. Our approach, which has been implemented in Python, identifies and locates errors using formal specifications defined in JML and Coq. By formally defining program invariants as JML annotations, we can detect deviations that indicate bug presence. We compare program output against these formal invariants to locate errors, utilizing the Coq standard library for integer arithmetic to define precise deviation metrics. Furthermore, textual error locations are generated through a parser that analyzes formal annotations. Errors are classified into two categories: (1) exceptions, which occur when assumptions like input validity (e.g., array indices) are violated, and (2) mismatches, which occur when formal specifications are violated. Our tool can identify both types of errors and place them contextually, distinguishing between assertion violations (mismatches) and locational information (exceptions). We hope this tool will contribute to the creation of error-classification schemas, a fundamental step toward systematic quality assurance in software testing. This tool represents a specialized version of the generic testing framework "testit," which operates without an external theorem prover.

In this work, we investigate the application of HyperNetworks to create hyper-prompts, introducing HyperPrompt—a new architecture designed for task-conditioning self-attention within Transformers using prompt-based methods. These hyper-prompts are generated end-to-end through a HyperNetwork. By functioning as global memory for queries to attend to, HyperPrompt enables the model to learn task-specific feature maps while facilitating flexible information sharing across tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that HyperPrompt rivals strong multi-task learning baselines using as little as 0.14% of additional task-conditioning parameters, thereby delivering significant gains in both parameter and computational efficiency. Extensive experiments further reveal that HyperPrompt outperforms robust T5 multi-task baselines and parameter-efficient adapter variants, such as Prompt-Tuning and HyperFormer++, across numerous model sizes on Natural Language Understanding benchmarks including GLUE and SuperGLUE. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Yihoshin/HyperPrompt.

In the Rabi model, parity symmetry restricts super-Rabi oscillations to the periodic creation of even photons within the cavity; this phenomenon is achieved through laser-driven qubit flips and parity-conserving transitions driven by the Rabi interaction. When dissipation is considered, only 2$n$-photon correlated emissions are permitted, and their purity is substantially enhanced by parity symmetry due to the near-total suppression of bundle emissions involving odd correlated photons. By manipulating the system's parity symmetry via an additional magnetic field, one can switch the bundle emissions between even and odd correlated photons. This research extends the concept of multi-photon bundle emission into the ultrastrong coupling domain and opens new avenues for investigating symmetry-protected multi-quanta physics. The findings also have significant implications for improving the purity of laser-driven hypercorrelated releases and designing quantum state preparers with symmetry protections. Furthermore, the protocol demonstrates potential for generating multidimensional entanglement among macroscopic oscillators, as realized in superconducting systems. The theoretical framework presented here is highly feasible given the current capabilities of superconducting technology.
Superconducting circuits are premier platforms for realising the Rabi model, which typically maintains parity symmetry. We propose using this model to generate multi-photon bundle emissions with high purity and entanglement. By exploiting the protection of quantum correlations offered by parity symmetry, we show that the purity of traditionally periodic multi-photon (2$n$-photon) bundle emissions can be significantly improved. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this symmetry enables the deterministic preparation of bundle emissions with either even or odd correlated photon numbers, as well as $N$-qubit W states. Consequently, the superconducting Rabi model offers a practical and robust method for supercorrelated releases and quantum state engineering.
We examine the potential of the Rabi model for producing symmetry-protected multi-photon bundle emissions. Leveraging the parity symmetry of this model, we demonstrate that the purity of periodically released even-multi-photon bundle emissions can be drastically enhanced by adjusting the system's parameters. Additionally, we show that both even- and odd-multi-photon bundle emissions are permissible when a longitudinal magnetic field is applied, allowing for the control of symmetry protection over the emissions. These findings suggest that the superconducting Rabi model can serve as a platform for generating symmetry-protected supercorrelated quanta and for creating quantum states with improved purity.

This paper addresses two critical aspects of knowledge distillation for ranking: 1) how to aggregate knowledge from multiple teachers, and 2) how to leverage data label information during distillation. We introduce a unified algorithm, Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), which simultaneously resolves these challenges. Search is fundamentally an optimization problem aiming to align system output with user intent. Traditional methods often rely on simplistic metrics like Recall or MRR, which fail to capture intent accurately or scale effectively. We propose Intent Learning (iLearn), a deep learning approach that infers user intent directly from query-document pairs using an auxiliary task. During training, the system learns to distinguish relevant documents by minimizing the classification error on this task. Consequently, iLearn infers user intent online and integrates it into ranking via an attention mechanism, effectively anadromous attention. By unifying information retrieval and deep learning, iLearn reframes the field as an optimization problem centered on user intent inference. Extensive evaluations on TPC-H and eCom datasets confirm strong performance across offline, online, and A/B tests. Specifically, iLearn yields an average CMTR提升 of 2.7% in offline settings, improves Click-Through Rate (CTR) by 2.4% online, and increases Overall CTR (OCTR) by 1.9% in A/B tests. Source code can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaSearch/iLearn.

Recent advancements in automation and experimental methodologies have accelerated these measurements and enhanced their resolution, resulting in massive datasets requiring analysis. These improvements are especially notable at user facilities and synchrotron light sources. Although machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly utilized to process and interpret large data volumes in real time, significant hurdles remain: the general user community often lacks ML expertise, and deploying ML models presents technical challenges. In this work, we showcase several representative ML models designed for on-the-fly analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II). We provide an instructive overview of these examples, emphasizing the integration of models into current experimental workflows to enable readers to incorporate their own ML strategies at NSLS-II or similar facilities. The proposed framework demonstrates that with minimal effort, diverse ML models can function alongside feedback loops by leveraging the existing Bluesky Suite for experimental orchestration and data management. This integrative approach maximizes experimental efficiency and ensures transparent access to both raw and processed data for subsequent offline analyses. Ultimately, the balance between developing rapid ML algorithms and effectively utilizing experimental resources is critical for accelerating scientific discoveries. We aim to facilitate the creation of further ML models for real-time data analysis across various scientific domains. Our work amplifies the impact of earlier studies and serves as a catalyst for the research community to overcome barriers in experimental throughput and data utilization, leveraging the capabilities of modern automated experiments. We have made all sources, including primary and secondary ML models, open source to support the development of additional strategies across different experimental configurations and analysis needs. We anticipate that our framework will accelerate the adoption of ML in materials science by improving accessibility and usability.
In conclusion, we introduce a universal framework constructed with the Bluesky Suite that enables the swift incorporation of machine learning models—for both primary and secondary data analysis—into experimental throughputs utilizing current hardware infrastructure. This report highlights the flexibility of our approach, demonstrating how distinct applications can be seamlessly integrated without modifications to the underlying framework. We have made all sources, including primary and secondary ML models, open source to encourage the development of further models for the comprehensive analysis of large datasets. Our methodology streamlines the deployment of machine learning strategies across automated experiments, from simple setups like home sources and beamlines on storage rings, to sophisticated, interconnected systems at multi-user user facilities. While our specific implementation relies on the software ecosystem at NSLS-II, our principles are broadly applicable to other environments. non-autonomous obstacle problems defined by minimizing the functional $\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx$ over the admissible class $\mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)$. The integrand $f$ satisfies $p$-growth conditions with respect to the gradient, where $1<p<2$. Specifically, we demonstrate that when the obstacle $\psi$ is bounded, a Sobolev regularity condition on the gradient of $\psi$ implies the same regularity for the gradient of the solution, assuming the partial derivative map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ resides in the Sobolev space $W^{1, p+2}$. This work introduces novelty by addressing subquadratic growth conditions, characterized by $f(x, \xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ with $1<p<2$, where the coefficient function $a$ is itself a member of a Sobolev space. To achieve these findings, we employ a reflection argument, which allows us to bypass the use of difference quotient methods typically required for classical elliptic regularity proofs. Furthermore, we extend the main theorems to accommodate independent regularity conditions on the spatial variable $x$, resulting in improved regularity outcomes for the gradient. These findings signify a significant step toward demonstrating Hölder continuity for the map $x\mapsto f_x(x,\xi)$ within the context of minimal surfaces. Finally, the proofs are adapted to address bounded obstacles that satisfy an additional monotonicity condition, thereby extending previous results established in the quadratic setting ($p=2$). The entire investigation is conducted under the assumption of convexity for the integrand $f$. approach to solving combinatorial optimization problems by embedding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian. This technique utilizes two distinct Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian. By gradually transitioning from the driver to the problem Hamiltonian over a sufficiently long period, the system is expected to settle into the target ground state representing the solution. While non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian are thought to improve QA efficiency, decoherence in NISQ-era quantum devices typically restricts usage to stoquastic Hamiltonians, characterized by real, simultaneously diagonalizable interactions. Although recent theoretical proposals suggest that certain quenches combined with QA can reduce the energy barrier and lower sampling errors in stoquastic QA, the advantages of quenches remain largely unexplored for simple Hamiltonian systems. Using simple models of stoquastic QA, we demonstrate that a quench can still yield meaningful, albeit modest, improvements for these systems. To demonstrate practical utility, we apply our findings to the photon-assisted quantum annealing model, determining the optimal quench frequency and timing. These insights offer valuable guidance for refining quantum annealing protocols on current and upcoming quantum hardware.

Recent studies have revealed that sudden quenches can make adiabatic quantum computation (ADC) more robust against decoherence when dealing with specific Hamiltonian pairs. We extend these insights to quantum annealing (QA), showing that a quench can help evade local minima caused by slow Hamiltonian evolution. First, we prove that the performance gain from quenches in ADC is limited to a constant factor improvement. We then introduce a novel quenched QA model and show that, similar to ADC, a single quench is sufficient to achieve a constant-factor reduction in the energy barrier. To illustrate the significance of these constant improvements in practical terms, we examine the one-dimensional disorder Hamiltonian. Our results indicate that for a disorder magnitude where pure QA fails to find the ground state, incorporating a quench enables the ground state to be identified with significantly higher fidelity. To achieve this optimal improvement, the sign of one interaction within the Hamiltonian must be non-stoquastic; however, we emphasize that this requirement is strictly weaker than the conditions needed for quantum speedup. Finally, we apply these theoretical results to the NiO-assisted quantum annealing model to demonstrate the benefits of the proposed quenched protocol.

Laboratory during the directorate of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, which spanned from 1921 to 1957. Founded by Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn, the institution grew into one of the world's premier astronomical research centers. Upon assuming leadership following Kapteyn's retirement, van Rhijn oversaw the coordination of Kapteyn's Plan of Selected Areas. While van Rhijn's research was robust and professional, his publications consistently failed to connect his findings to the broader astronomical context. Although perhaps lacking in imagination, his approach notably missed the connection to the evolving understanding of the Galaxy's structure. Throughout nearly his entire tenure, van Rhijn faced significant obstacles that severely restricted his ability to secure additional funding, despite local university support. These challenges included the Great Depression of the 1930s, the Second World War and its aftermath, and a prolonged battle with tuberculosis during the 1940s. Furthermore, the remote location of Groningen relative to Leiden played a crucial role; Leiden hosted a major infrastructure supported by three of Kapteyn's key proteges, while government funding was disproportionately biased toward Leiden over Groningen. Finally, this work explores the developments of the 1950s that ultimately led to the relocation of the laboratory's operations to Leiden. The paper concludes with several reflections on historical figures and events that van Rhijn overlooked, specifically the Foundations of Stellar Population Studies established by Bertil Lundmark in Leiden during the 1930s, the integrated Galaxy model created by Bertil and Jan Hendrik Oort around the same period, and Leiden's strategic advantages highlighted by Burt Garret during Kapteyn's final years. These locations were proximate to Leiden Observatory, which provided essential facilities, and to Leiden University's Astronomy Section, which offered world-class expertise. In the accompanying video, the author discusses the choice of title and addresses the delicate balance between focusing on J.C. van Rhijn's scientific work versus his administrative roles, as well as the decision-making process regarding the work's tone. Additionally, a supplementary file containing numerous images of van Rhijn and the laboratory is available. This study also clarifies distinctions between the images used here and those presented by S.F. We address the challenge of multi-armed bandits featuring contextual rewards, demonstrating that algorithms from linear and logarithmic settings can be directly extended to contextual multi-armed bandits (CMABs). Furthermore, we establish minimax rates for both stochastic and Markovian CMAB frameworks. Experimental results validate the efficiency of our proposed methods.

In this work, we examine whether the maximum entropy reinforcement learning algorithm can be reformulated using optimal control theory. Our analysis reveals a KKT system that characterizes the stationary distribution of behaviors in Maximum Entropy Path Integral Control (MEPIC). Additionally, we derive a novel loss function capable of estimating the first-order gradient of the value function, thereby unifying existing maxent methods such as SAC, MPO, and BEAR. This research is implemented and validated through experiments.

Although various learning-to-rank algorithms exist, their theoretical ranking capabilities often remain unproven. To address this gap, we propose a new algorithm called GTR (Generalized Twin Network for Learning-to-Rank). Theoretically, we establish that any pairwise comparison method yielding a stochastic order can be equivalently represented as a sigmoid function of an underlying score function, enabling score-based evaluation. Practically, our experiments demonstrate superior performance across multiple benchmarks, and we provide a detailed analysis of the network's structure and parameter distribution. The findings confirm that GTR effectively learns high-quality ranking capabilities, successfully overcoming limitations found in current state-of-the-art approaches.

These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, dimensions, or underlying mechanism. This limitation is especially problematic for laminated composites, which are prone to complex failure modes such as delaminations that are challenging to identify. To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage geometry from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, focusing on two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.19 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable the precise identification of both damage mechanisms and sizes in composite laminates. Such capabilities are essential for developing advanced health monitoring systems capable of detecting all relevant damage in critical structures. Furthermore, this technology offers significant potential for assessing the remaining service life of these components. Finally, the techniques presented here are broadly applicable to any material system that exhibits self-sensing properties.

Carbon fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRP) are increasingly used in wind turbine blades due to their superior strength-to-weight and cost-to-weight ratios. Although these materials are highly effective at withstanding in-service loads, they are susceptible to progressive damage from low-energy impacts, such as those caused by falling objects. Although changes in electrical conductivity can signal the presence of damage, accurately determining its shape and size remains difficult. To overcome this challenge, we developed a method to precisely reconstruct delamination shapes using a genetic algorithm paired with realistic 3D delamination models. These models account for how blade curvature, stacking sequences, boundary conditions, and impact locations influence delamination growth. , investigating whether individual intelligence is a prerequisite for collective wisdom and, crucially, what specific types foster it. Drawing from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reinterpret these insights through the evolving structure of a system's Lyapunov function. Ultimately, we apply this framework to the intelligence levels of citizens and their institutions, concluding that while individual contribution is necessary for collective outcome, individual wisdom can sometimes hinder it. Consequently, we suggest that cultivating individual wisdom should not be the primary goal of education. Instead, we argue that both brain neurons and individuals can productively coexist with conflicting local activity. Therefore, education should aim to align individual local activity with collective global activity, even when the former is uncorrelated with or inversely related to the latter. We term this approach "making brains work" and "making individuals work." This work aligns with recent findings in physics regarding non-cooperative self-organized criticality in granular materials. Consequently, we reiterate that education must avoid making individuals "too smart."

We propose that music offers a model for understanding how a collection of uncoordinated, diverse, and seemingly unintelligent agents can generate a state of "collective intelligence." Just as individual neurons firing in sync produce brainwaves, individual people listening to and internalizing music can achieve a unified global state. While this phenomenon is often romanticized, it relies on strict conditions: the global state must be simple, and the resulting collective intelligence is limited. This limited state is actually less intelligent than the average individual.

Listening to music imposes structure on the brain. To model this, we construct a system of linear maps representing music's effect on individual listeners, which we use to derive a system of nonlinear equations describing a collection of these listeners. In this framework, the coefficients represent the intelligence of the listeners, and the map's Jacobian matrix mirrors a brain's connectome. BCIs offer substantial promise for addressing disabilities caused by nerve damage, particularly in enabling walking for those who have lost the ability to do so. Introduction Phylogenetic networks represent evolutionary histories involving reticulate events, such as those occurring during viral co-evolution, hybridization, and horizontal gene transfer. These events allow distantly related lineages to exchange genetic material, creating a web-like structure of descent that contrasts with the strictly branching patterns of phylogenetic trees. While phylogenetic trees remain widely supported, evidence of reticulation in nature is mounting, inspiring the development of methods to detect these events and their integration into network models. Although various techniques exist for inferring reticulate evolution, they often yield differing outcomes even when applied to identical data. Research is now needed to create methods for generating random evolutionary networks to help interpret the output of inference techniques. Although recent methods for generating random phylogenetic networks have been proposed to support Bayesian analysis and uniformity checks, a comparative discussion of their properties is lacking. Such a comparison is essential to assess which methods produce the most unbiased samples relative to specific applications. In this paper, topological profile clustering is employed to compare a range of phylogenetic network generators.

This report defines the movement of general biological species as biolocomotion and introduces a computational method to identify it within raw video footage. In this study, we investigate the topological and localization characteristics of a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model featuring spatially correlated random binary disorder. Our findings reveal that such binary disorder can trigger a transition from a trivial insulator to a topological Anderson insulator across multiple parameter regimes. These topological Anderson insulators are identified by a disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states, observable via the inverse participation ratio in both real and momentum spaces. Furthermore, the boundaries of the topological phases align with analytical predictions derived from the self-consistent Born approach and the localization length of zero-energy modes. We also examine the influence of bimodal probability distributions on these disorder-induced topological phases and demonstrate that topological signatures can be detected through mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic setups. Ultimately, this work extends the concept of topological Anderson insulators to scenarios involving correlated disorders.

Despite recent focus on topological phases caused by correlated (e.g., power-law) disorders, the impact of binary correlated disorder remains unexplored. This work extends the topological Anderson insulator model to one-dimensional polymeric chains with binary correlated disorder. Additionally, it explores how statistical correlations and individual binary disorder strengths affect disorder-induced topological phases and nonreciprocal transport within these 1D polymers.

The development of scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computers remains a significant challenge. While topological quantum computation is anticipated to possess the highest error thresholds and simplest fault-tolerant gates, current surface code decoding methods lack adaptability across diverse error models. We present the surface code interaction model, a framework designed to unify the construction of error models for topological codes. This model is extended with specific modifications for characterizing error rates. We also introduce the surface code MDP, which encodes the complete set of error models into a Markov Decision Process suitable for reinforcement learning. We extend this to include modified adaptations for various topological codes. By applying this generalization, we trained agents to decode both the surface code and the XYZ plane code under diverse error models. The resulting agents consistently outperformed traditional optimal approximate decoding schemes while demonstrating greater adaptability to varying error rates. This methodology can be extended to construct agents tailored for error rates suitable in topological quantum computation. The code for the figures in this review is available at https://nielsbdevries.github.io/RL_Decoding_topological_QEC_codes/.

### I. INTRODUCTION

The multi-armed bandit framework models decision-making under uncertainty, where a learner selects an action to maximize unobserved rewards, gradually refining choices over time through trial and error. In many modern applications, contexts are integral to both performance and learning; however, due to privacy, security, or other constraints, a central learner may lack direct access to them. This paper investigates a problem where such a learner can observe contexts but cannot utilize them directly. Although the contexts are essential for both action selection and performance evaluation, their accessibility is limited. The primary challenge lies in efficiently transmitting contextual information from one or more agents to the learner. Our goal is to determine the minimum number of bits that must be transmitted to enable the learner to achieve performance comparable to a fully observable environment.

While maximal independent sets (unit network gain) offer robust simplicity, they do not guarantee fractional gains; however, managing such strictly fractional extremal gains is crucial for sublinear algorithms used in networks larger than constant size.

In contemporary communication systems, users with diverse data demands connect via software-defined networks (SDNs). Research indicates that dynamically allocating network resources based on user demand significantly enhances both network and spectral throughput. Our study experimentally evaluates the performance gains of demand-aware dynamic allocation using software-defined wireless networks as a case study. We implemented a cross-layer, demand-aware, dynamic network allocation algorithm known as MAXSUMSDoF. This algorithm jointly optimizes application-layer network flows and physical-layer wireless transmit powers (degrees of freedom) by leveraging a software-defined radio (SDR) testbed. Our experimental results show that such demand-aware, software-defined wireless allocations can increase throughput by a factor equal to the number of distinct user demands. Throughput gains using MAXSUMSDoF are independent of the total number of network users, unlike linearly scaling traditional wireless allocations. As network user density rises, MAXSUMSDoF approaches a regime where all users achieve their individual demand rates. This research provides the first empirical

Because the time step necessary to resolve collision dynamics is significantly smaller than that required for fluid flow, the computational expense of using the traditional soft-sphere model—which mandates such small steps—becomes prohibitive for simulations involving thousands of particles. While existing state-of-the-art methods artificially stretch the collision time to match several flow solver time steps, this approach introduces non-physical artifacts that compromise simulation accuracy. These findings indicate that the new algorithm is both highly efficient and precise, representing a substantial advancement for particle-resolved simulations. Furthermore, the discussion extends to potential extensions of the MTSA for coarser simulations that include additional physical phenomena. Finally, the paper examines how experimental parameters can be identified to maximize both the efficiency and accuracy of the proposed method.

Particle-laden flow simulations are essential across numerous industrial sectors, yet they present significant computational challenges due to the vast number of particles, their inherent mobility, and the complexity of resulting flow interactions. Particle-resolved methods are particularly potent because they explicitly incorporate simulations of individual particle collisions, either through soft-sphere models or by employing significantly time steps that directly model collision dynamics. Although the latter approach is approximately 1,000 times more efficient than the former, experimental validations using the soft-sphere model reveal substantial discrepancies in collision forces, particle trajectories, and clustering behaviors. Current state-of-the-art strategies artificially extend the collision duration to accommodate flow solver time steps, yet these modifications introduce non-physical effects that negatively impact simulation outcomes. This study proposes utilizing multi-step time integration algorithms to efficiently and accurately resolve particle collisions while maintaining the overall flow solver time step. The algorithm's validity was examined through simple collision scenarios, including both particle-wall and particle-particle interactions. Its effectiveness was further demonstrated in a simplified particle-laden flow case that accounts for flow recirculation, clustering, and multiple particle collisions. The findings indicate that the new method enhances computational efficiency by nearly three digits without compromising accuracy, thereby opening possibilities for simulating

terrain remains a difficult and unresolved challenge in robo-physics, as the uncertainty arising from ground deformation hinders both dynamical modeling and control strategies. Furthermore, determining efficient and stable movement mechanisms on soft ground presents a significant hurdle. This study aims to control a one-dimensional monopod hopper to achieve a target jump height. To accomplish this, I first established and validated a discrete element method (DEM) simulation environment featuring spherical granular material as the soft ground. Using this setup, I developed ground reaction force models based on resistive force theory (RFT). These RFT models were then employed to create a feedforward force control system for the robot. Within the DEM simulation, a feedback control loop was implemented to correct deviations between the actual ground reaction forces and the RFT predictions. Consequently, the robot successfully tracked desired trajectories and reached the target height within five hops, significantly reducing apex position errors compared to using feedforward control alone. Additionally, the experiment varied the robot's square foot area from 1cm² to 49cm². The results demonstrate that the feedback controller effectively manages fluctuations in ground reaction forces, even when the foot dimensions are comparable to the size of individual grains.

Our observations reveal that air circulations generated by the large-scale oscillations of a pendant water droplet subjected to a resonating electric field function similarly to micro or mini blowers within the surrounding air. This phenomenon is evidenced by the degradation of strong electrostatic capture of airborne particulates onto the droplet when it is exposed to an aerosol environment. Consequently, the pronounced local aerodynamic effects on surrounding aerosol particles, as well as the resulting heat and mass transfer within this two-phase system, inspire further fundamental and technological research. Consequently, the pendant water droplet is proposed here as a accessible platform for investigating localized three-phase interactions involving solid, liquid, and gas. Furthermore, the established scaling relationships for air flows around oscillating droplets provide a foundational understanding of self-aerodynamic three-phase systems. Indeed, our findings indicate that the three-phase interactions in these systems are dominated by inertial forces. Consequently, the system's ability to enhance mass and heat transfer is characterized by scaling laws that are identical to those found in inertial three-phase systems. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that these self-aerodynamic three-phase mechanisms enable an oil-bath-free method for rapidly and uniformly catalytically decomposing airborne volatile organic compounds. Therefore, this approach offers significant potential for various applications, including miniaturization, self-powered aerosol sensing, purification, water purification, catalytic oil separation, and air drying.

While numerous statistical and computational models exist for automatically generating these hierarchies, current methods often fail to account for the linkages inherent in information networks, which are ubiquitous in real-world contexts. Additionally, existing approaches typically represent topics as abstract probability distributions over words rather than as concrete nodes derived from the original network, and the statistical techniques employed in prior works often lack the capacity to process data at Web-scale. Information hierarchies are structural tools used to organize and navigate large bodies of data; however, manually constructing them is often labor-intensive and prone to oversight. Recent models for automatic hierarchy generation typically treat data instances in isolation, ignoring the rich contextual information provided by their surrounding information networks. Our research aims to harness the structural features of these networks to enhance the accuracy of generated hierarchies and to utilize contextual data for inferring missing connections within them. We propose a Bayesian model that infers these linkages to facilitate the construction of precise hierarchies. We have implemented this model and tested it on several news datasets. Our findings indicate that accounting for information network context significantly improves hierarchy accuracy. Specifically, our method achieves higher Human Evaluation Scores (HES) than state-of-the-art techniques while requiring approximately 100 times less data. Furthermore, our method is approximately 1000 times more memory efficient, enabling the processing of datasets too large for any current technique to handle. Annealing involves slowly varying Hamiltonian parameters to explore equilibrium phases, making it a powerful method for solving complex optimization tasks. Conversely, quenches entail sudden Hamiltonian changes that drive the system into a non-equilibrium state. This study examines the connection between these two approaches, demonstrating that the critical bottleneck of quantum annealing—the minimum of the annealing gap—can be identified through a dynamical quench parameter characterizing the post-quench quantum state. By integrating statistical methods, such as neural network training, with quench data, we can reconstruct the complete functional behavior of the annealing gap. We further show that insights gained regarding the annealing gap, either partially or fully, enable the design of optimized quantum annealing protocols, yielding practical improvements in time-to-solution. These findings are based on simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians, which model challenging instances of the exact cover problem. Our results are expected to inform the development of robust quantum annealing strategies, including the identification of critical gaps, across both static and dynamically evolving quantum Hamiltonians.

Introduction: Quantum annealing is a computational method designed to find the ground state of a Hamiltonian $H_{\rm Q}$ by slowly decreasing the influence of an initial transverse-field term within a starting Hamiltonian $H_0 = -\sum_i \sigma^x_i$. The total time evolution is governed by a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(t) = s(t)H_{\rm Q} + [1-s(t)]H_0$, where the annealing schedule $s(t)$ transitions from 0 to 1 over the annealing time $T_{\rm A}$. The efficacy of this adiabatic process in reaching the ground state is determined by the annealing gap $\Delta(t) = |E_1(t)-E_0(t)|$, the energy difference between the first excited and ground states. A larger gap reduces the minimum required annealing time, as a shorter duration increases the probability of annealing errors. Although a theoretical lower bound for $T_{\rm A}$ can be derived using the adiabatic theorem, accurately identifying the annealing gap is essential for determining a realistic annealing time on actual hardware, which is constrained by decoherence and control inaccuracies. While classical metaheuristics offer alternatives to exact cover (EC) algorithms, the computational cost of these approximations rises exponentially with problem size, necessitating potentially millions of runs to locate the optimal solution. Alignments represent a cutting-edge method for identifying, locating, and measuring deviations in process executions (traces) relative to reference process models. However, alignments typically require complete process executions that span from start to finish, or at least prefixes of such executions. This paper introduces infix/postfix alignments, outlines methods for their calculation, and assesses their performance using real-world event data. Our findings indicate that infix/postfix alignments perform as well as standard alignments and efficiently utilize currently observed event data, even when process executions are incomplete. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this approach can accommodate specific business queries, such as estimating alignment quality at any point during runtime or prioritizing immediate improvements based on early execution data. In summary, infix/postfix alignments are applicable in various practical scenarios and deliver results comparable to traditional alignments. The code for this study is available at github.com/inix-postix-alignments.

We address timing variations in process executions by adapting alignments to incorporate temporal data, resulting in time alignments. These alignments are evaluated on real-world event data. The findings reveal that time alignments perform slightly inferior to standard alignments however, they remain effective for both calculating and detecting deviations. The discussed methods are applicable to existing alignments and can be integrated into their software implementation. Additionally, we demonstrate how time alignments can address specific business questions. The findings support the conclusion that it is feasible and advantageous to compute time alignments. Time alignments account for temporal information from event logs when identifying discrepancies in process executions. We investigate the suitability of infix alignments for time alignments through empirical analysis using event logs from actual business processes. The results show that infix alignments are well-suited for capturing timing variations in process executions. As with standard alignments, infix alignments effectively identify and measure where and how significantly the actual process behavior diverges from the normative model, including regarding temporal aspects. Additionally, we illustrate how infix alignments can help answer business-specific questions. The code supporting this study is accessible at github.com/TimeInfixAlignments.

two-band model for infinite-layered nickelates, derived from $d$ and $s$-like orbitals, can be mapped onto a single-band Hubbard model, identifying the screening of the more itinerant $s$-band as a critical factor. Without screening, a strongly correlated band yields an antiferromagnetic ground state. Under weak screening, strong correlations drive electrons out of the $s$-band, resulting in an undoped Mott insulator with half-filled $d$ orbitals; this scenario contrasts with high-$T_c$ cuprate observations and suggests $s$-wave pairing for the superconducting state. Conversely, strong screening leads to partially filled $s$ and $d$ bands that couple weakly, resembling a doped Mott insulator like in cuprates, potentially fostering $d$-wave pairing. Consequently, both limiting cases favor either an undoped Mott insulator or a doped Mott insulator, with only the intermediate screening regime predicted to yield an antiferromagnetic Mott insulator. Furthermore, in the strong coupling limit, screenless hybridization opens a nodal gap in the $d$ band, offering a possible origin for $d$-wave pairing. Finally, we analyze whether screenless hybridization can stabilize charge ordering.

and Lawrence-Doniach (L-D) models, which describe cuprate superconductors via Josephson coupling between CuO planes, were regarded as the primary theoretical frameworks. However, experimental measurements of the interlayer magnetic penetration depth $\lambda_{c}$ revealed values exceeding those predicted by the ILT model. Following the identification of planar stripes and incommensurate charge ordering, it became feasible to examine Josephson coupling between these mesoscopic charge domains or blocks. We demonstrate that the average intralayer coupling exceeds the interlayer coupling and is comparable to the condensation energy, thereby facilitating a superconducting transition through long-range phase order. Furthermore, this framework implies that the ratio $[\lambda_{c}/\lambda_{ab}]^2$ is directly proportional to the resistivity ratio $\rho_c/ \rho_{ab}$ near the superconducting transition temperature, a finding consistent with multiple experimental observations. Consequently, we conclude that cuprates are predominantly governed by 2D spin ordering. Finally, this approach is contrasted with the 3D Kosterlitz-Thouless mechanism arising from collective 3D Josephson coupling. The findings support the conclusion that these materials exhibit 2D spin ordering alongside long-range phase order, which is further evidenced by the presence of an intermediate metallic state between the normal state and the 2D superconducting state. These results align with the recently proposed "stripes are glass" scenario.

Recently reported measurements on cuprates indicate an intermediate metallic state situated between the high-temperature normal state and the superconducting state. This data, alongside our earlier discovery of 2D spin ordering, led to the suggestion of an "order by disorder" mechanism driven by spatially correlated charge ordering. This mechanism was designed to resolve the apparent conflict between 2D spin ordering and the electronic transport properties observed in cuprates. We refine this proposal by integrating the concepts of "stripes are glass," a "dynamic glass" state, and the "dynamic glass" mechanism. This state is characterized by a lack of long-range charge order, finite electrical conductivity, and a local condensation energy comparable to the superexchange interaction $J$. We show that this state accounts for the experimental data, including the previously unexplained intermediate metallic phase. Additionally, the validity of this state near the superconducting transition is supported by recent findings on the electron self-energy and the nature of charge carriers. We also address how this state reconciles the stability of 2D spin ordering with the electronic transport properties

As density rises in compact stars, the sound velocity is anticipated to approach the conformal limit ($c_s/c=1/\sqrt{3}$) at high densities while adhering to the causality constraint ($c_s/c<1$), yet its precise behavior continues to be a subject of intense debate. Consequently, predicting the oscillation modes of neutron stars remains challenging. This study employs machine learning to systematically explore the parameter space regarding sound velocity profiles and their impacts on pulsar glitches, magnetic star kicks, and gravitational wave emissions from binary neutron star mergers. We specifically analyze the gravitational wave (GW) signals of post-merger binary neutron stars, focusing on the masses and decay amplitudes of excited spacetime modes. Using physically motivated sound velocity models, we anticipate that learning the relationships between sound velocity structures and these post-merger characteristics will facilitate the inference of dense matter phases from future GW data with sub-second accuracy. Furthermore, we expect that applying machine learning techniques to combine multi-messenger astronomy observations of single neutron stars with post-merger GW analysis using deep neural networks could enable more robust deductions about the phase structure of dense matter. Finally, we examine how ultralight dark matter influences the excitation masses and amplitudes of excited spacetime modes in post-merger binary neutron stars through the coupling between matter fields and spacetime curvature. Our results indicate that even a small fraction (as low as 0.1%) of ultralight dark matter can be detected through deviations in the masses and amplitudes of excited spacetime modes, provided the dimensionless coupling constant exceeds $10^{-4}$ and the dark matter mass lies between $10^{-7}$ and $10^{-5}$ eV. Consequently, future GW observations of post-merger phases could serve as a viable method for detecting ultralight dark matter. For scenarios where ultralight dark matter is present, we anticipate that an unequal mass ratio in the binary system will generate additional excited spacetime modes, opening new avenues for detecting ultralight dark matter through post-merger GW observations. However, determining a maximum-weight Tai mapping for unordered trees is an NP-complete problem. In this study, we introduce the concept of an "anti Tai mapping," denoted as $M \subseteq V_1 \times V_2$, which is a binary relation between two unordered labeled trees where no pair of elements $(x, y)$ and $(x', y')$ in $M$ satisfies the ancestor condition simultaneously. Specifically, for an ancestor order $x < x'$, the condition requires that $(x \le x' \iff y \not\le y') \vee (x' \le x \iff y' \not\le y')$. This maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem is critical for applying the cutting plane method within integer programming approaches to solve the original Tai mapping problem. We present an efficient polynomial-time algorithm to find such a mapping when one of the trees is a path. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to extend this approach to derive an approximation algorithm for the general case of two unordered trees. This advancement enables the integration of cutting planes, thereby enhancing the performance of existing algorithms for the original Tai mapping problem. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the anti Tai mapping for tree powers, showing that a "left (right) Tai mapping" constitutes a special instance of the anti Tai mapping problem. This finding offers a novel perspective on the long-standing conjecture that two left (right) Tai mappings can be combined to form a standard Tai mapping. Finally, we propose an algorithm to solve the original Tai mapping problem in polynomial time for specific practical scenarios, such as comparing two suffix trees. Our methods are applicable to various problems in theoretical computer science, including the longest common ancestor, edit distance, and subsequence distance. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system. Ultimately, the interaction between these mechanisms may drive dust processing towards larger scales. This research represents a crucial step in utilizing the VSI to model dust evolution and mass distribution in protoplanetary disks.

sum of squares has a long mathematical lineage, tracing back to Bachet and Lagrange. While established methods exist for decomposing elements into sums of squares in certain specific rings, such as the integers or polynomials over the rationals, the problem remains largely unsolved for many other significant rings and fields. This paper introduces an explicit algorithm capable of decomposing an element from any global field—whether a number field or a global function field—into a sum of squares with minimal length. When applied to global function fields, the algorithm requires $O(\log^2 q \log \log q )$ operations, where $q$ represents the field size, assuming the TAMC-LNT conjecture; this performance is expected to be achieved via the geometric approach to the Generalized Bass Conjecture, which aims to determine the real rank of certain regular noncompact adjoint algebraic groups over finite fields. For number fields, the algorithm's efficiency depends on the performance of the Bachet step, which involves identifying whether a given element is a square within the field. Although the method may generate a sum of squares of length exceeding the minimal possible sum, it has been tested on random elements from the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$, where $d$ is a square-free integer up to $10^8$. These tests demonstrate that for roughly 63% of these number field elements, the decomposition produced is indeed a minimal sum of squares. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the method processes approximately 1 million examples per second on a standard desktop system. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining several potential extensions of the algorithm.

A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and delayed convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy. Building on this, we propose an adaptive random walk learning algorithm that partitions iterations into local blocks. This approach places the model at a randomly selected neighbor for multiple updates within each block, using an upper confidence bound to determine the number of local iterations and dynamically adjust the walk path based on data quality. Experimental results confirm that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art centralized statistical learning algorithms in both performance and communication efficiency. Furthermore, our proposed federated learning algorithm achieves superior performance in a communication-constrained environment. By exploiting variations in judge-fixed effects, the analysis identifies a statistically significant 13 percentage point reduction in recidivism for defendants subjected to mandatory treatment, equivalent to more than one additional year without a new conviction. While deep learning techniques have recently advanced the field of Deep Learning-based Knowledge Tracing (DLKT), the underlying reasons for their success remain unclear, and rigorous evaluation of these methods remains difficult. For legged robots and manipulators handling uncertain environments or objects, contact force sensing is essential yet often yields inaccurate data due to delays, noise, and nonlinearities. While Sigma-Delta ($\Sigma\Delta$) modulation has been integrated into robotic force control, it inherently introduces quantization noise that contaminates contact force measurements. This study investigates the influence of sampling frequency and feedback gain on the mean, variance, and auto-covariance of quantization noise in legged robot contact force sensing. Based on a generic noise model, an optimal feedback gain formula is derived to minimize mean square error (MSE) in force measurements for robots walking on hard surfaces. Additionally, the effects of varying feedback gains and sampling frequencies on noise characteristics are experimentally investigated using a dSpace-based control system on a hexapod leg equipped with load cells modulated by second-order $\Sigma\Delta$ schemes. The findings validate the proposed noise model and the optimal feedback gain formula. Although different sampling frequencies alter auto-covariance properties, the optimal feedback gain remains unchanged to mitigate quantization noise. It is further noted that increasing sampling frequency necessitates a higher feedback gain to suppress noise, though this may risk destabilizing the control loop; thus, a trade-off is required. Although derived for load cells with proportional feedback, the findings are applicable to any $\Sigma\Delta$-based force control system featuring linear feedback. The study confirms that for a given sampling frequency, there exists an optimal feedback gain that minimizes MSE, and this value is specific to each $\Sigma\Delta$ order.

Despite recent advancements in data-efficient reinforcement learning, many state-of-the-art methods remain impractical for small underwater robots due to their high computational demands. This paper addresses this gap by presenting data and computationally efficient algorithm and implementation strategies. First, we develop a general-purpose sparse approximation for the predictive value function, enabling accurate offline and online predictions without the limitations found in previous sparse Gaussian Process Temporal Difference (S-GPTD) approaches. Second, we derive the predictive value function posterior to create a novel model-free policy evaluation algorithm, SPGP-SARSA. Third, the unified framework of the sparse approximation and SPGP-SARSA allows us to implement an efficient model-based policy evaluation method, SPGP-VIMA. Both the theoretical design and practical implementation are validated through tests on the COMBP environment and physical underwater robot trials. Our findings show that the proposed SPGP-SARSA algorithm is more data efficient than current state-of-the-art methods while delivering higher prediction accuracy in both simulation and reality. Furthermore, the system demonstrates robust performance in navigating around unknown moving obstacles, completing tasks in approximately 10 minutes with roughly 500 exploration steps on a robot possessing modest computational resources.

839 exhibits almost no star formation, except for a prominent complex of HII regions situated at the very edge of its outer disc. To investigate the origins and characteristics of this feature, researchers compared new Hα and archival broad-band imaging of UGC 8839 with similar data from four comparable spiral galaxies. The findings suggest that the off-axis star formation in UGC 8839 arises from a hyper-stable, dark matter-dominated disc throughout all radii, where the Toomre parameter reaches its lowest value only in the extreme outer disc. By employing analysis methods specifically designed for stochastic events, the study determined that the HII region cluster is a one-to-two billion-year-old, low-mass (approximately $2\times10^7~\rm{M}_\odot$) structure resulting from the rare capture of a satellite. This capture is unlikely to have significantly triggered tidal star formation. Instead, the cluster's location at the margin of the disc stability limit, combined with the absence of central concentration in the star formation, indicates that only the most precarious satellites can produce such outer-disc clusters. Furthermore, the lack of intermediate-age clusters in UGC 8839 aligns with the lack of recent satellite captures. The dynamical mass-to-light ratio derived from the disc stability condition falls within the typical range observed for spiral galaxies. UGC 8839 offers unique insights into the satellite capture process and the connection between stability conditions and the formation of these clusters. Consequently, the sample of spiral galaxies with off-axis outer-disc HII regions may be interpreted as systems that have recently captured a satellite capable of creating such a cluster, a process constrained to occur at the stability limit (roughly three disc scale lengths from the center) and to have a low mass efficiency. These objects also serve as potential, though rare, sites for satellite captures during the late stages of galaxy evolution. Additionally, the study highlights the significance of utilizing analysis techniques designed for stochastic events when investigating the formation of these off-axis clusters.

Feature importance is a fundamental aspect of any machine learning model. While numerous methods exist for calculating it, their efficacy varies by model type, making the selection of an appropriate method a critical challenge. This paper introduces a unified, model-agnostic framework designed to compute feature importance across diverse machine learning models. Our core methodology involves formulating a satisfiability problem that captures feature importance as a model property; consequently, solving this problem yields the desired importance metrics. We implemented a proof-of-concept of this approach, demonstrating its efficacy through extensive experiments on tabular datasets using popular models like Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LIME. Our method effectively calculates feature importance locally (for individual samples) and globally (for the training dataset), addressing various data types including tabular, categorical, and mixed formats. The implemented approach is accessible as an open-source library.

We define a general framework for computing feature importance both locally and globally. Traditional methods often lack a theoretical basis, relying instead on proxy metrics that compare model outputs against heuristics or proxies. In contrast, our novel method employs a model-theoretic approach to explicitly characterize feature importance as a semantic attribute of individual model instances. By encoding machine learning models into First-Order Logic (FOL), we formulate a satisfiability problem where the solution reveals local feature importance. Furthermore, we develop algorithms to derive global importance metrics from this problem formulation. Our method has been tested across various machine learning techniques and different data types.

Our analysis employs the Jefferson Lab's SIDIS event generator, JLab/SIDIS++. This tool is based on the Monte Carlo approach featuring universal fragmentation functions. We determine hadron-specific fragmentation functions from our data and test their universality by applying them to describe experimental data from the BONUS collaboration. Additionally, we investigate the usefulness of these newly derived fragmentation functions for generating hadronization in final states involving two or more hadrons, such as those measured by JLab/HallA. We also assess how well the resulting correlations align with the JeLab/SIDIS++ framework. Our findings indicate that the evolved fragmentation functions successfully describe two-hadron production in SIDIS when expressed in terms of broadened variables that account for final-state interactions. However, they fail to accurately predict two-hadron correlations in pure fragmentation processes. This discrepancy likely stems from the influence of multi-hadron interactions in hadron jets, an effect that is more pronounced in hadron-hadron collisions than in lepton-nucleon interactions. Consequently, these interactions must be properly accounted for when interpreting two-hadron correlations in hadron-hadron collisions. We offer several suggestions for future improvements to the JLab/SIDIS++ model and discuss how they can be validated using existing data from the HERA collider.

while high-order interactions in many real-world complex systems are best represented by hypergraphs, these datasets are frequently released or analyzed only as projections featuring dyadic edges. To comprehend this problem, we first develop a theoretical framework to characterize its implications and worst-case scenarios. This analysis inspires the formulation of a new task: supervised hypergraph reconstruction, which involves recovering a real-world hypergraph from its projected graph by leveraging existing application domain knowledge.

To reconstruct hypergraph data, we begin by analyzing hyperedge distributions within the projection. Based on this analysis, we establish a framework comprising two modules: (1) to manage the vast search space of potential hyperedges, we propose a sampling strategy with efficacy guarantees that drastically reduces the space to a manageable set of candidates; (2) to select hyperedges from these candidates, we design a hyperedge classifier with two effective variants that capture structural features present in the projection. Extensive experiments confirm our claims, approach, and extensions. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/MehdiBourharafah/HyperRecon.

Our primary contributions are as follows:
1.  We identify and analyze the hyperedge distribution in projections, revealing key properties that enable the significant reduction of the search space for hyperedge classification.
2.  We introduce a framework with two hypergraph classifiers, which, despite relying solely on projected data, achieve a high R-F1 score (>0.90) in reconstructing a real-world complex system with billions of possible hyperedges.
3.  We demonstrate through extensive numerical studies and theoretical analysis that our proposed methods significantly outperform strong baselines. Specifically, our approach achieves at least a 10× improvement in the objective function (minimum cost to represent the hypergraph) over state-of-the-art baselines.
4.  We examine various real-world scenarios for this task, showing how our methods aid in identifying false positives and negatives in applications like fraud detection and link prediction, with up to a 5× improvement in the Objective/K@5 metric over strong baselines.
5.  We address difficulties in optimizing the reconstruction objective via differentiable methods by proposing scalable algorithms based on tractable proxies. These algorithms achieve a marginally lower objective function value than their proxies and scale efficiently to billion-scale data.
6.  We explore extensions of the core approach, demonstrating its versatility in: inferring a hypergraph's projection, jointly reconstructing a hypergraph and its projection, and predicting missing edges in a hypergraph's projection

on deriving effective multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, a crucial step for deploying multi-agent systems in real-world scenarios. However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels; for instance, one agent might follow a random policy while others adhere to medium-quality policies. In cooperative games with global rewards, existing offline MARL approaches often allow agents to inherit these suboptimal random policies, thereby compromising the team's overall performance. This paper investigates offline MARL with explicit attention to the diversity of individual agent trajectories and introduces a novel framework termed Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to mitigate this issue. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network utilizes a differentiable key-value memory mechanism to assign credit to each agent in an offline setting. These decomposed credits facilitate the reconstruction of joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay based on individual trajectories, enabling agents to share high-quality experiences. Subsequently, agents conservatively train their policies using a graph attention network (GAT)-based critic. Evaluations across discrete control environments (StarCraft II and multi-agent particle environments) and continuous control settings (multi-agent MuJoCo) demonstrate that our method yields significantly superior results on complex, mixed offline multi-agent datasets, particularly when there are substantial disparities in the quality of individual trajectories. In this work, we utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous nonlocal nature of wave function collapse, combined with single-particle entanglement, generates the nonlocal effect known as steering. During this process, Bob's quantum state becomes contingent upon the specific observable Alice chooses to measure. To achieve this, we fully harness the spatial spreading of the single-particle's entangled wave function over large distances. . Over the last century, scientific literature—the primary conduit for sharing knowledge among researchers—has experienced exponential expansion. Although numerous tangible metrics, such as citations, impact factors, and the g-index, are frequently employed to quantify paper influence and scientific productivity from various angles, the relationship between productivity and the actual volume of knowledge remains poorly understood. Specifically, it is unclear how the knowledge value and quantity of papers evolve as a discipline develops, raising the critical question of whether high scientific productivity necessarily equates to a large knowledge base. Addressing this, we leverage extensive literature on academic journals and conferences to compile a dataset of 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines from 1970 to 2020. We construct a citation network research area to map the flow of knowledge from cited authors to citing authors within each specific domain. The resulting structure, which evolves over time, implicitly reveals how knowledge flows between nodes and how these dynamics shift as literature volume (productivity) increases. By utilizing Structural entropy in structured high-dimensional space and Shannon entropy in unstructured probability space, we introduce the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI). Defined as the difference between these two entropy types, KQI reflects the extent of disorder (knowledge amount) generated by structural order. Using KQI, our analysis indicates that while published literature has grown explosively, the actual knowledge contained within it has noticeably decelerated; however, a broader definition of knowledge suggests an exponential increase. Furthermore, we observe that high-productivity fields do not always contain more knowledge, as measured by KQI. Additionally, we identify distinct evolutionary stages in academic research: an introductory phase characterized by low both knowledge amount and density, followed by two overlapping phases of increasing density and amount. Finally, by integrating the cited paper counts of top researchers, we determine that those who contribute the most to the field's knowledge are not necessarily those with the highest publication records. These insights offer a novel perspective on how to distinguish the knowledge amount and density from academic productivity within published scientific literature.

This study tackles the challenge of generating safe CAV trajectories in such environments, with a specific focus on preventing rear-end collisions when preceding HDVs approach yellow or red signal phases. We introduce a predictive control framework that utilizes a recursive least squares algorithm to estimate the real-time driving behavior of leading HDVs, subsequently applying this estimation to compute safety-conscious trajectories over a finite horizon.
