Vehicle automation advancements are accelerating, yet achieving fully automated driving remains distant due to challenges across the entire driving loop. This work concentrates on one such hurdle: planning and controlling safe trajectories for self-driving cars navigating through streams of human drivers. We examine three critical scenarios involving lane changes and merges: changing lanes to pass a slower human driver, merging into a gap behind a human driver, and merging into a gap where the leading human driver is moving too slowly. While existing methods often rely on simplistic motion models or hand-crafted rules, we propose utilizing Machine Learning to directly synthesize safe trajectories from raw sensor data, bypassing the need for explicit model-based prediction or optimization steps. By training a neural network on millions of driving maneuvers captured by overhead cameras and side-mounted vehicle cameras, we leverage the network's internal dynamics to ensure generated trajectories are both dynamic-feasible and safe. Extensive simulations and experiments with real vehicles show that our learned controller significantly outperforms traditional optimization-based methods across various metrics. Specifically, our method decreases the frequency of all risk levels when executing these maneuvers. Furthermore, our approach outpaces model-based baselines in computational efficiency, enabling on-board implementation on a typical computing platform. These findings suggest that Machine Learning can effectively address the difficult problem of planning and controlling safe trajectories for automated vehicles driving among human drivers.

Recently, researchers have investigated data augmentation techniques to enhance data efficiency in NLP. Despite this, there has been no comprehensive empirical review of data augmentation specifically for NLP under limited labeled data conditions. This paper presents such an empirical review of recent NLP data augmentation studies from 2017 to 2022. We summarize the various augmented data types and evaluation metrics employed in recent work, followed by a detailed analysis of data augmentation's impact on sequence-to-sequence (S2S) models in machine translation and language modeling, as well as encoder-decoder models in named entity recognition (NER), focusing on settings with constrained labeled data. Our empirical analysis reveals that recent data augmentation efforts have yielded an average improvement of 1.17% in S2S machine translation tasks using encoded limited labeled data, and a 1.39% improvement in NER tasks using limited training data. Despite these gains, we note a scarcity of recent studies addressing data efficiency through augmentation and call for standardized benchmarking protocols to facilitate meaningful comparisons among different methods. We hope this review encourages future research directed at maximizing data efficiency in NLP.

Recent advancements in pre-trained language models have yielded impressive results across numerous natural language understanding (NLU) and generation tasks. Building upon these models, researchers have developed frameworks that perform exceptionally well across multiple domains and domains with limited data. Although many papers report performance improvements using limited labeled data with data augmentation, current methods operate in isolation, making it difficult to determine which techniques are truly effective. We report performance across 18 tasks spanning nine papers to construct a systematic overview of data augmentation in NLU and generation. Our comprehensive empirical study shows that while models do see average improvements of 1.3% across 28 datasets, performance varies significantly by task (ranging from -3.6% to +7.1%). We catalog 52 distinct augmentations across 12 categories utilized in 29 papers and discuss the limitations of existing work to offer directions for future investigation.

Yet, current assessments and policy guidance on market design and ancillary services often fail to account for the intricate interactions between markets and services. To address this gap, this paper introduces an open-source agent-based model designed to evaluate design options for electricity markets and ancillary services. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM) integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA toolbox for power system analysis. This model offers adjustable design parameters for both markets and agents, alongside detailed clearing algorithms for day-ahead markets, intra-day continuous trading, redispatch, and imbalances. Additionally, ASAM features extensive policy performance indicators, including new metrics for price mark-ups and redispatch efficiency. A stylized simulation scenario was used to validate the model and explore a specific redispatch design issue. The findings regarding multi-period all-or-none order types in redispatch markets reveal three key implications: (1) The order design minimizes risk for market participants by ensuring full order clearance. (2) Large orders can create dispatch ramps before and after delivery periods, potentially triggering ramp-risk mark-ups and necessitating extra intra-day imbalance trading. (3) In liquid market conditions, an all-or-none design leads to grid operator over-procurement of redispatch because partial order activation is impossible; furthermore, incomplete activation often forces grid operators to introduce system imbalances, as upward and downward redispatch volumes become unequal. The study concludes that a partial-or-first order design is preferable for redispatch markets. By adjusting growth conditions, we generated various surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films, which were analyzed using low energy electron diffraction (LEED) and photoemission spectroscopy. Our findings indicate that the MIT can be partially or completely suppressed near the surface, depending on the specific termination. This suppression arises from distinct electron filling levels in surface and sub-surface layers relative to the bulk, as well as alterations in the screening length. Across the transition, we observed a significant redistribution of spectral weight, transferring from high to low binding energy regimes over a broad energy scale. Notably, the total spectral weight in the low-energy regime is not conserved across the MIT, signaling a violation of spectral weight sum rules—a hallmark of strongly correlated systems. These spectral changes likely stem from variations in hybridization, lattice volume (effectively carrier density), and spin degrees of freedom during the transition. Our results confirm that the MIT in this system is driven by strong correlations, with electron-electron interactions playing a central role. Furthermore, these findings offer deeper insight into the electronic structure of strongly correlated materials and underscore the necessity of considering surface effects when interpreting physical property data obtained through surface-sensitive techniques like surface resistivity. Finally, our discovery that electronic properties can be engineered through surface termination suggests a potential strategy for creating two-dimensional correlated electron systems.

This report details the fabrication of a fiber-based surface plasmon resonance (SPR) sensor utilizing a silver core optical fiber. The process involved cleaning the fiber, applying a sulfur coating, and then adding a thin gold layer to establish the sensing surface. Characterization revealed that the final fiber structure retained the original cladding of the glass core optical fiber. Leveraging the prism coupling method, we measured the fiber's refractive index and determined that the sensor operates within a single mode. We also examined how the fiber's sensing characteristics change with water coating and proposed a model for calculating the index of refraction of other liquids using this fiber sensor. Additionally, we measured the SPR angle for an uncoated silver-core fiber by coupling light from an LED source, successfully observing an SPR dip in the transmission spectrum. This demonstration confirms the fiber's potential as a practical SPR sensor capable of detecting different chemicals based on their refractive indices. Although scattered light inherently contains both the amplitude and phase of the electromagnetic field, phase data is frequently discarded during standard intensity measurements. Data analysis in x-ray scattering experiments often faces limitations due to a lack of prior knowledge about the sample. Scattering from quantum probed targets provides a powerful avenue for hybrid quantum light-matter interactions. Connecting quantum error-correcting codes to classical disordered statistical mechanics models has created a powerful framework for assessing the inherent error correction thresholds and fundamental resilience of these codes across various noise models. While previous work has focused on encoding and syndrome measurement circuits, this paper extends that methodology to encode-and-readout circuits. We explicitly apply this method to the three-qubit repetition code, ranging from simple readout configurations to more complex ones, covering both error-resilient and non-error-resilient scenarios. , which naturally display topologically non-trivial properties within their honeycomb lattice structure (HLS), has driven significant research into achieving similar behaviors in group VI elemental monolayers. While theoretical predictions previously deemed group VI HLS impossible, recent experimental findings contradict this view. This letter demonstrates that the HLS of group VI elemental monolayers, exemplified by Tellurene, can achieve dynamic stability when functionalized with Oxygen. This functionalization induces peculiar orbital filtering effects (OFE) and breaks spatial inversion symmetry, thereby generating a non-trivial topological character. The system exhibits exotic quantum behavior characterized by a large spin-orbit coupling-induced gap of approximately 0.36 eV and an isolated edge Dirac cone, suggesting potential for room-temperature spin-transport applications. Additional analysis of spin Hall conductivity and Berry curvatures reveals higher conductivity than previously observed in Xenes. The non-trivial topology is quantified by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant of $\nu = 1$ and a Chern number of $C = 1$. Furthermore, we show that \textit{h}BN/TeO/\textit{h}BN quantum wells can be strain-engineered to produce a substantial non-trivial gap of about 0.11 eV. In conclusion, Oxygen functionalization of group VI elemental monolayers yields robust exotic quantum properties resistant to surface oxidation and degradation, offering viable electronic degrees of freedom for developing future quantum and spin-transport devices. This work represents the first report of a group VI elemental monolayer hosting an isolated edge Dirac cone. Furthermore, the ability to tune the energy gap through strain engineering positions these systems as prime candidates for spintronic applications.

Recently, T. Kimoto and H. Matsui highlighted that intrinsic oxygen impurities degrade mobility in group IV elemental silicon. Given that Oxygen functionalization of group VI elemental monolayers is essential for generating exotic quantum properties, it is crucial to confirm that such functionalization does not introduce defects that impair electronic transport. This confirmation remains an open question.

applied to a new hybrid-dimensional model for single-phase Darcy flow in fractured porous media. The model represents fractures as $(d-1)$-dimensional interfaces within a $d$-dimensional domain, where $d$ equals 2 or 3. Fractures are categorized into two types based on the permeability contrast between the fracture and the surrounding matrix: those with significantly higher permeability are termed {\it conductive}, while those with significantly lower permeability are termed {\it blocking}. Conductive fractures are modeled using a standard hybrid-dimensional interface approach assuming continuous pressure across the interface, whereas blocking fractures utilize a recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach that enforces continuity of the normal Darcy velocity component. A key advantage of this formulation is that the velocity field is precisely represented as velocity-only data within the global velocity space, which consists of independent velocity traces defined on the blocking fractures and the boundary. Consequently, the pressure field is derived a posteriori from this global velocity. Despite the heterogeneity introduced by the blocking fractures, the global velocity space remains conforming relative to the whole domain, thereby guaranteeing mass conservation at the discrete level. Numerical experiments in both two and three dimensions demonstrate the scheme's optimal convergence rates and its capacity to accurately resolve local high velocities in conductive fractures and enhanced permeability regions. Furthermore, the computed global velocities can be directly utilized to determine well production rates, even when wells intersect blocking fractures, thereby ensuring mass conservation throughout the entire simulation without requiring any modification to the well modeling component. Numerical extensions explore well intersecting blocking fractures and networks of such fractures. The paper concludes with a summary of the theoretical error analysis presented in the cited reference \cite{DDB21}. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it remains unclear whether bridge sampling yields unbiased estimates for complex analyses; we address this by employing simulation-based calibration for the first time to assess the accuracy of such estimates. Our analysis also covers the stability of Bayes factors across different MCMC samples, their dependence on data variations, and the variability of resulting decisions, proposing methods to optimize these decisions via utility functions. We outline a reproducible workflow for researchers to test the robustness of Bayes factors in their specific analyses, illustrated with a case study from cognitive science. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework for evaluating the strengths and limitations of Bayes factors as a metric for scientific evidence. This research addresses an urgent problem in both basic and applied statistics: extending standard statistical tests to scenarios where multiple hypotheses are evaluated, each incorporating data information through test statistics. Specifically, we propose a novel framework for evaluating multiple hypotheses using a single dataset. Unlike traditional methods that rely on extreme test statistic values for rejection, our framework utilizes the probability of events defined by multiple test statistics. This approach offers a fresh perspective on multiple hypothesis testing, avoiding the need for multiple comparison corrections typically associated with simultaneous inference. Repetition probability evidence ratios (RPRs), a specific type of probability, serve as the metric for evidence. Simulations and an empirical case study confirm the validity of the framework. Repetition probability evidence ratios align with the frequentist probability of event $A$ given data $x$, denoted as $P(A|x)$, enabling the comparison of model predictions against observed data. For instance, one can assess a specific parameter range $A$ using $P(\theta \in A | x)$. Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. Our analysis of this data supports the hypothesis that markers indicating textual organization (like {\it by contrast}) encompass a variety of distinct logical relations (for instance, {\it However by contrast}, {\it Yet by contrast}, and {\it Although by contrast}). Additionally, our work reveals the utility of this bottom-up characterization in aiding the training of Sentence Representation models and enhances their performance on textual entailment tasks. The code for generating DiscSense and our analyses are available online.

By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a rigid metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. The extent of this transmission relies on how virus-laden droplets evolve spatially and temporally amidst changing environmental factors. Consequently, this study examines droplet evolution considering Brownian motion, evaporation, gravity, and varying weather conditions. We track droplets until they either settle on the ground due to gravity or evaporate into aerosols measuring 2$\mu$m or smaller. Droplets with radii of 2$\mu$m or less can persist in the air for extended periods through diffusion. Our findings indicate that relative humidity and temperature significantly impact evaporation rates. Under strong airflow, droplets can travel considerable distances. Larger droplets tend to fall to the ground because gravitational forces dominate over diffusion, even as they lose mass through evaporation. Conversely, smaller evaporating droplets often remain suspended due to the supremacy of diffusive forces. The trajectory of intermediate-sized droplets is contingent upon weather conditions and plays a critical role in infection spread. These environment-dependent dynamics suggest that relying solely on physical distancing is insufficient to prevent viral transmission, thereby underscoring the necessity of wearing face masks. Finally, we suggest that the risks of infection can be more effectively modeled by integrating droplet dynamics with human movements rather than depending exclusively on average relative humidity and temperature. This dynamic drop model offers a foundational framework that may enhance COVID-19 risk assessments. In the future, tracking individual droplets within crowded spaces alongside fluid dynamic interactions could provide even more precise risk estimates. Additionally, this approach holds potential for evaluating the efficacy of various face mask designs. Finally, our findings imply that existing aerosol particle counters, commonly used to assess room sanitization, may yield misleading safety assessments because evaporating droplets can still pose infection risks.

However, quantifying errors and uncertainties within NN-based inference remains a major obstacle to their practical deployment. This paper introduces a novel approach to error minimization and uncertainty quantification in NNs by reinterpreting them as discrete change-of-variable transformations. Although deep learning has achieved remarkable success across numerous fields, including image super-resolution and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction, its ability to generalize to new data remains limited. Chained neural networks (CNNs) represent a cutting-edge learning methodology that has shown exceptional performance in various reconstruction tasks. This work investigates how hyperparameters and data statistics influence the generalization capabilities of CNNs. Specifically, we introduce a generalized Cramér-Rao bound (CRB) to evaluate the theoretical lower limit of estimation variance for any unbiased estimator. Leveraging this insight, we formulate an optimization problem to simultaneously reduce CRB and improve the invertibility of the transformation learned by the network. Experimental results confirm that simultaneously optimizing these two components yields superior outcomes compared to optimizing either in isolation. These findings offer valuable insights for enhancing the generalization of neural networks in both research and real-world applications. Keywords: Generalized Cramér-Rao Bound, Chained Neural Networks, invertibility, Generalization, simultaneous optimization.

We address safety concerns regarding modern convolutional neural networks (CNNs) used in real-time, safety-critical systems. By simulating software executions, we evaluate how clipping activations improves fault detection without significantly compromising accuracy. Our experiments cover various CNN architectures, error models, and image datasets. Our findings indicate that even minimal, coarse activation clipping substantially increases the system's ability to detect faults caused by soft errors, hardware faults, and software bugs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the defect coverage gained from activation clipping can assist in validating that the system behaves as intended under specific constraints and can aid in determining an appropriate confidence level for online fault management strategies. Our code repository is accessible at https://github.com/marionf/activ-clip-saf.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are widely adopted in safety-critical real-time applications, yet they remain vulnerable to software defects and hardware faults. This study examines the reliability of classification CNNs under such failures and introduces a method to enhance system dependability through moderate clipping of network activations. The research quantifies the improvements in defect detection and system reliability resulting from this technique. Key findings indicate that moderate activation clipping raises the distinct fault density observable on a CPU simulator by 317.50 \% and 167.50 \% when the data path is 32-bit and 64-bit, respectively. a concept with significant economic implications, shaping inter-company exchanges and interactions. Briefly, netting offers an alternative to standard payment methods by establishing an agreement where parties offset mutual debts. Instead of settling all individual transactions between two parties, only the net difference is settled; for instance, if Party A owes Party B €10 and B owes A €30, A pays B the net amount of €20. This paper introduces a dynamic netting framework designed to model and simulate debt networks over time, incorporating evolving transaction lists and credit limits. The model utilizes a set of differential equations to track debts and employs a discrete algorithm to handle transaction events. Additionally, it integrates an agent-based model of credit limits, accounting for their impact on payment behaviors and the resulting netting processes. Validated against real-world data, this framework can be extended to investigate financial crises and their dynamics within debt networks. Ultimately, this model serves as a foundational step toward understanding counterparty risks and potential default scenarios in such systems. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmed-gharib/debt-netting.

Although refined versions (MultiWOZ 2.1–2.4) have recently emerged, they still suffer from numerous noisy labels, particularly within the training sets, and manually correcting these issues is expensive. Consequently, unlike shorter-wavelength lines such as H$\alpha$, the conversion of SFR to predicted line luminosity relies minimally on specific dust models or posterior dust parameters. Our results indicate that Prospector predicts Br$\gamma$ luminosities and equivalent widths with minimal offsets ($\sim$0.03 dex) and scatter ($\sim$0.2 dex), both of which align with measurement uncertainties, although we note that the derived offset varies depending on the selected stellar isochrones. Furthermore, we show that even when Prospector-derived dust attenuation fails to accurately characterize H$\alpha$ line properties or observed reddening between H$\alpha$ and Br$\gamma$, the fundamental SFRs remain accurate, as confirmed by the dust-insensitive Br$\gamma$ comparison. Finally, we explore how Br$\gamma$ could assist in constraining model parameters when incorporated as an input and assess its viability as a precise monochromatic SFR indicator for the upcoming era of JWST multi-band imaging surveys. Introduction Understanding the connection between gas consumption and star formation remains a central theme in galactic evolution research. While it has long been established that observed star formation varies with wavelength due to stellar evolution, interpreting this behavior requires reliable diagnostics such as hydrogen recombination lines. These lines allow us to disentangle evolutionary effects from genuine physical variations in galactic consumption. Specifically, comparing line properties across a sample can reveal whether gas consumption is consistent or if it depends on other variables. Although multi-wavelength observations suggest that, on average, galaxies consume gas at a rate consistent with simple conversion efficiencies, previous studies have identified substantial scatter, particularly when including starbursts. While some of this scatter may stem from measurement uncertainties, much of it may reflect true variations in consumption rates. To advance this field, we must utilize more spectral-line diagnostics in future investigations. We re-examine our current understanding of individual LMM elements without relying on the unitarity assumption. By establishing two minimal categories of experimental constraints—direct and inherent bounds versus indirect bounds—we analyze their respective implications for leptonic non-unitarity. Furthermore, we clarify the handling of flux and cross-section predictions, specifically addressing new physics contamination within hadronic inputs. Using the ongoing FASER$\nu$ experiment as a case study, we illustrate the sensitivity of collider neutrino searches to deviations from unitarity. Our results indicate that indirect bounds restrict LMM non-unitarity to below the $10^{-3}$ level, surpassing existing constraints on CKM non-unitarity. In contrast, relying solely on direct and inherent bounds allows for ${\cal O}(1)$ unitarity violations at $2\sigma$, a scenario that the FASER$\nu$ experiment should probe during the current LHC run. Additionally, we examine three distinct classes of constraints arising from existing long-baseline neutrino oscillillation data, which limit indirect bounds on unitarity for the $\Umu$ subblock to below the $10^{-4}$ level. Finally, we outline strategies to further tighten these indirect limits using upcoming long-baseline measurements.

Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. . Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days and water-covered terrain—scenarios where traditional VIO algorithms fail to extract visual features. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional and existing learning-based VIO baselines across various scenes. The source code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/zeyadghahueh/External-Attention-VIO.

Even though the Pauli exclusion principle dictates that no two fermions can occupy the same quantum state, quantum entanglement allows two noncommuting operators to share the same eigenstate. By adapting concepts from quantum information theory, we define a "Pauli-violating quasicrystalline insulator" where the single-particle wavefunction exhibits quasicrystalline long-range order, yet certain quasi-periodic eigenstates of local Hamiltonian projects are shared by pairs of Pauli-noncommuting translation operators. We prepared this state experimentally in a optical-lattice optical cavity setup and verified its Pauli-violating quasicrystalline nature through tomographic reconstruction. Specifically, we observed long-range quasi-periodic order and confirmed that the underlying eigenstates of local projective operators violate the Pauli principle. This provides additional evidence that quantum entanglement enables the coexistence of apparently conflicting quantum phenomena. Finally, we argue that such Pauli-violating quasicrystalline insulators represent robust phases of matter.

FedSA), a novel knowledge-amalgamation problem aimed at training a student model for a specific new task using multiple decentralized teacher models. These teachers possess pre-training tasks and datasets that are distinct and mutually unknown. Our motivation arises from a current challenge in model sharing: despite significant investments in training large, capable networks, researchers and institutions often cannot share their pre-trained models due to privacy, security, or intellectual property concerns, even when they wish to contribute. FedSA addresses this dilemma by enabling the creation of a specialized student model for a task different from any of the teachers' original domains. To achieve this, we propose a dedicated strategy where the student training process employs a new saliency-based method to adaptively select participating teachers and integrate their key capabilities. We evaluate FedSA's effectiveness across both single-task and multi-task scenarios. The experimental results confirm that FedSA successfully amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models, achieving performance competitive with centralized baselines. Furthermore, in a multi-task setting, FedSA demonstrates a significant ability to prioritize and optimize for a specific target task. Experimental analysis also reveals that, compared to existing methods, FedSA effectively enhances task specificity and reduces hallucination errors. Finally, we assess the robustness of FedSA in accurately predicting participating teachers in a resource-constrained environment. These findings validate the success of our approach in prioritizing and optimizing for specific tasks while minimizing hallucination risks. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/AhmedShah2000/FedSA.

In many practical applications, it is often necessary and beneficial to combine the knowledge embedded within multiple pretrained neural networks. However, the rising cost and privacy concerns surrounding data have led to an increase in decentralized machine learning frameworks. Our work investigates the challenges of knowledge combination when each decentralized dataset has already been trained, yet the resulting models can neither be shared nor reveal information about their respective training distributions. To address this, we propose a new approach that integrates knowledge from these decentralized models to teach the student a specific task. This method is adaptable for both multi-task and single-task scenarios. Our experimental results show that FedSA can effectively learn a specific task by combining knowledge from decentralized models, even when the students' training tasks are completely unknown to the teachers.

 Approximately ten years ago, grid cells were discovered in the medial entorhinal cortex of rats, exhibiting distinct periodic firing patterns as animals moved through open spaces. While these findings were once thought to indicate a simple spatial metric, subsequent research has revealed a vast array of related properties and an even greater number of open questions. This paper provides a fundamental introduction to grid cells, describes their key characteristics, and discusses a range of theoretical perspectives on these exciting findings. It also explores related work from the last decade, covering experiments conducted both dark and light, across various environments. This survey reflects the present state of grid cell research and highlights current open questions and promising future directions. In the appendix, references published in the five years preceding this work are listed, acknowledging the rapid evolution of this field. Throughout the paper, materials have been drawn from youtube.com and wikimedia.org.

Today, grid cells are recognized not only for their role in spatial representation but also for their involvement in other spatial and non-spatial functions. Recent findings demonstrate that these cells contribute to non-spatial sequence learning, a capability that significantly complicates the creation of a unified theoretical framework for their operation. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in grid cell research, examining both their spatial and non-spatial characteristics. Following this overview, we investigate the potential of using place cell data to infer grid cell properties and discuss the implications of these insights for future studies.

After reaching the zero-age main sequence, their global rotation slows during the main sequence phase until at least the age of the Sun, a trend that aligns with Skumanich's empirical law and facilitates gyrochronology. Recent asteroseismology studies suggest that older solar-type stars may eventually reach a transition point where rotational braking ceases. Furthermore, modern 3D numerical simulations indicate that differential rotation regimes in these stars can be classified by the Rossby number. Specifically, a "anti-solar" differential rotation pattern (characterized by fast poles and a slow equator) may occur in slow rotators with high Rossby numbers. If this regime manifests during the main sequence, it raises questions about its impact on magnetic generation via differential rotation. Therefore, it is crucial to examine whether slowly rotating solar-type stars can still produce strong global magnetic fields. In this letter, we analyze over 100 main-sequence solar-type stars with measurable gyrochronous ages. We find that while most stars follow the $\\Omega-\\mathrm{B}_\\mathrm{phot}$ relation (where $\\Omega$ is global rotation rate and $\\B_\\mathrm{phot}$ is surface magnetic field strength), at least three exceptions exist: slow rotators exhibiting strong global fields (where $\\Omega$ drops by a factor of 2–3 while $\\B_\\mathrm{phot}$ remains similar to solar levels). These observations suggest that magnetic generation in solar-type stars may not strictly follow the same pattern seen in global dynamos of other species. Additionally, we explore how stellar convection zones evolve during the main sequence and how this relates to magnetic field generation. Finally, if our tentative conclusion holds, we discuss its implications for gyrochronology. We conclude by suggesting directions for future directional-gyrochronology research. To better understand the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems, we investigate whether the QNEC constrains irreversible entropy production during quenches driven by energy-momentum inflow from an infinite memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories. Our findings indicate that while the increase in both entropy and temperature—mandated by the Clausius inequality of classical thermodynamics—is necessary to avoid violating the QNEC in quenches involving transitions between thermal states with momentum (dual to BTZ geometries), it is not sufficient. For any arbitrary initial state, we establish lower and upper bounds on the increase of entropy (or temperature) given a fixed increase in temperature (or entropy). These results provide concrete examples of quantum states that satisfy, or violate, the QNEC and align with previously reported findings regarding the lower bounds of the QNEC for future null rays in collapse scenarios. Additionally, we derive upper bounds on the violation of the QNEC for future null rays following quenches in 2D holographic CFTs. Our analysis covers classical quenches, sudden quenches, and those driven by logarithmic baths. Notably, we demonstrate that for classical and sudden quenches in CFTs dual to BTZ geometries, the QNEC is never violated. However, when driven by logarithmic baths, even small amounts of perturbation lead to significant violations of the QNEC. We also determine that there exists a critical time beyond which the QNEC is inevitably violated for any non-zero perturbation strength. Furthermore, we show that the entanglement entropy of an interval of length $l$ receives contributions from modes with frequencies up to $\frac{c\pi}{l}$ for classical and sudden quenches, but for logarithmic quenches, all modes up to an infinitely large frequency participate. This unique behavior stems from the lack of unitarity in logarithmic quenches, a consequence of the absence of a complete set of scaling operators in all 2D CFTs. Our work highlights that the QNEC is not merely a consequence of unitarity but also characterizes the near-equilibrium dynamics of quantum thermodynamics. Consequently, the growth law of entanglement entropy for entangling intervals under logarithmic quenches in 2D CFTs exhibits behavior similar to the QNEC. For a smooth variety $X$ defined over a field of characteristic zero and an Azumaya algebra $\mathcal{A}$ on $X$, we develop the $\mathcal{A}$-twisted motivic spectral sequence. This is achieved by calculating the slices of the motivic twisted algebraic $K$-theory spectrum, treating them as twisted forms of motivic cohomology. Our approach extends earlier findings by Kahn and Levine, which were limited to cases where $\mathcal{A}$ is pulled back from the base field. Our methodology leverages the interplay between the slice filtration and birational geometry. Furthermore, we establish a representability theorem that characterizes the motivic space of twisted $K$-theory as an extension of the twisted Grassmannian by the sheaf of "twisted integers." These developments facilitate a proof of both cdh descent and Milnor excision for twisted homotopy $K$-theory. As a application, we provide a concise and unified proof of the Karu-Mathew-Talbot theorem, which addresses when a map of ring spectra induces isomorphisms on homotopy groups. Additionally, we derive a spectral sequence analogous to the classical Milnor excision sequence, rooted in the homotopy groups of algebraic spectra. Our work covers instances including the map between the algebraic and homotopy truncations of the motivic suspension spectrum of an Azumaya algebra, a map induced by a proper generically étale morphism, and the connection between algebraic and homotopy $K$-theory for rational function fields. Please note that this research was conducted prior to the implementation of the motivic Nullstellensatz. That breakthrough significantly streamlines the arguments presented here, although our techniques remain applicable in contexts where the Nullstellensatz is unavailable, such as over $\mathbb{Z}$.

However, these significant gains in computing power are counterbalanced by severe limitations in programming models and tools. Despite engineers having access to machines capable of performing $10^{18}$ to $10^{19}$ operations per second, it remains difficult to ensure that hundreds of billions of instructions are executing optimally. Consequently, even with potent hardware, software overhead can consume more time than the CPU's computational capacity, particularly in applications heavy on branching and looping, such as fluid dynamics, weather forecasting, and ocean modeling. This paper introduces an iterative framework designed to guarantee optimal software performance in C++ code targeting modern multicore and manycore architectures, delivering results that align closely with hardware potentials. The proposed solution comprises three key components: (1) defining software performance blocks (PBs), which represent portions of code critical to overall efficiency; (2) formulating a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) problem that leverages GPU parallelism to transform PBs into efficiently parallelizable super-PBs; and (3) deploying an adaptive strategy to generate the requisite instance of the MILP problem tailored to the specific hardware in use. By applying this multi-tiered optimization method to problems in computational fluid dynamics (CFD), we demonstrate substantial improvements in performance across various flow scenarios, including incompressible flow with and without separation, aeroelasticity, and explicit large eddy simulation (LES). Our findings indicate up to a 3.0-fold improvement in CPU execution time for CFD problems at Reynolds numbers up to $10^6$, and a 1.6-fold improvement for Reynolds numbers up to $10^7$ on a single NVIDIA P100 GPU. Furthermore, the developed techniques are applicable to other computational domains, offering significant potential for enhancing software performance in scientific computing. This work reports the initial stages of that optimization journey.

is renowned for its ideal conservation properties, guaranteeing exact preservation of total mass, energy, and both linear and angular momentum up to machine precision when correctly implemented. This feature is crucial for computational astrophysics applications involving binary dynamics, mergers, and the accretion of compact objects like neutron stars, black holes, and white dwarfs. However, in scenarios requiring gravity, the computational cost of calculating pairwise particle interactions becomes prohibitive. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) addresses this by substituting these interactions with symmetric forces between distant particle clusters organized in tree nodes. While standard FMM conserves linear momentum, it generates spurious torques that compromise angular momentum conservation. This paper introduces a modified FMM that eliminates these spurious torques and ensures explicit angular momentum conservation, all with negligible computational overhead compared to the conventional approach. This work utilizes the accessible Wess–Zumino model to investigate how the BRS operator functions across different orders of the 1/c expansion. The findings indicate that the 1.5 order formalism, despite claiming to yield a closed algebra, actually results in an incorrect and deficient algebraic structure. This conclusion applies universally to all supergravity theories. The paper further explores why the 1.5 order formalism creates these problems and proposes how to rectify them. The analysis begins with the simplest possible model, the free massive Wess–Zumino theory. Since the 1.5 order formalism should be understood as a mathematical tool rather than a physical reality, its inherent flaws are both surprising and significant. We conclude that future efforts should incorporate delensed maps when training and testing NNs, ensuring they remain robust against variations in $N_{\rm{cs}}$. In this MuLE setup, a single LE mirror is partitioned into multiple segments, directing X-rays reflected from each segment onto one image sensor within a multiplexed arrangement. When each LE segment is oriented at a distinct rotation angle, the azimuthal rotation of the reconstructed cross-like image from a point source allows for the identification of the specific segment responsible for focusing the X-rays onto the imager. Furthermore, the simulations demonstrated that the direction of transients with fluxes ranging from 14 to 17 mCrab at 0.6 keV could be determined with 99.7% accuracy using only a two-imager MuLE configuration. Finally, we propose that the MuLE concept could facilitate a wide-field X-ray monitor capable of detecting all transient events with a redshift limit of z < 0.5, complementing the all-sky surveys conducted by Swift and Fermi. We recommend that MuLE designs be incorporated into future LE simulations to optimize their configuration for maximum efficiency. In summary, MuLE offers a cost-effective solution for creating a wide-field X-ray transient monitor with LE capabilities.

### 1 Introduction

Music Information Retrieval (MIR) encompasses various tasks related to musical performance, including tempo tracking, note transcription, and instrument identification. Among these, Music Transcription—deriving time-domain representations (like MIDI) from audio signals—plays a crucial role. These derivations are essential for low-rank matrix factorization system evaluation at the SIAM competition and facilitate the creation of musical publications. Despite significant advancements in Audio Source Separation over the last decade, progress in Music Transcription has been more limited. While machine learning has enabled the reliable separation of mixed audio from diverse instruments, automatically determining the exact time instances when notes are played (i.e., onsets and offsets) remains difficult. Although several state-of-the-art source separation methods have been established, there is still a lack of specialized automatic music transcription systems tailored to compete in the SIAM competition.

Designed with quasi-static evolutionary applications in mind, our method utilizes a custom-developed Lagrangian formulation. Unlike the standard Eulerian approach, this formulation solves force balance equations to determine the positions of fluid elements mapped to grid points. Distinct from prior literature, we do not rely on the first integral of the Euler equation, which typically lacks a general analytic solution. Instead of prescribing the spatial distribution of angular velocity or angular momentum as previous methods do, we assign specific mass, angular momentum, and entropy to each fluid element; the angular velocity and momentum distributions are subsequently derived once the positions of all elements are established. These sequences are intended to be integrated into the full version of our code, the Constructalstar, which will eventually apply to realistic equation of state and to solve for magnetic fields. We conclude by comparing our results with those obtained from the constructstar code. We find that our formulation accurately recovers analytical solutions for known analytic solutions for barotropic solutions, correctly distributes angular momentum on the surface for both barotropic and baroclinic cases, and properly transports angular momentum and entropy during evolutionary processes. Our approach offers distinct advantages over existing methods for both computational efficiency and numerical stability. This work represents the second paper in a series; the first part is referenced for additional technical details. In upcoming work, we will present results for more realistic stellar models, including magnetic fields, and apply this formalism to explore the evolution of compact binary precursors. Document information extraction (DIE) employs natural language processing to automatically pull data from unstructured documents into structured formats. While recent deep learning methods have shown promising results, two key challenges persist: (1) a lack of generalization when transferring between different document types, and (2) the difficulty of obtaining large volumes of high-quality labeled data. To address the latter, we propose Selective Labeling, which reduces the cost of acquiring labeled data by approximately 10x with minimal impact on extraction accuracy. We validate this method on document types in the financial sector, specifically invoices. Our system, developed for French invoices and trained on partially labeled datasets using selective labeling, achieves a mean F1 score of 77%. The system is available online at https://inv-extraction.fr/.

By applying a 1D code to resolve dynamics down to the stellar surface, we post-processed prior 3D simulation results. Our findings reveal that the burst-like deposition of material into the inner disc observed in 3D models does not invariably produce powerful accretion bursts; instead, only high-density clumps that have undergone collapse and crossed the inner computational boundary generate observable bursts. The complex physics of the inner disc significantly influences these bursts in four key ways: (1) While objects in standard turbulent viscosity discs may stall at migration traps a few astronomical units from the star, those in magnetised wind-driven discs can cross these traps to create bursts matching current observations. (2) Migrating objects can interact with and alter the thermal (hydrogen ionisation) instability of the inner disc, potentially causing longer-lasting, lower-luminosity bursts in HMYSOs. (3) If the central star is bloated by prior high-accretion episodes or if the migrating object is sufficiently dense, the outcome is a merger rather than a disc-mediated burst. (4) Disruption bursts from these objects may exceed the Eddington limit, driving episodic feedback on the HMYSO environment through powerful outflows. Additionally, we note that migrating objects can serve as probes for the density structure of discs by causing burst durations to scale with local sound speed as Luminosity-Efficiency relations are approached. These observations may help constrain migration traps and the onset of magnetic wind-driven angular momentum transport in future studies. Colliding with stationary obstacles such as walls, furniture, and debris is a frequent cause of failures for autonomous mobile robots navigating unstructured indoor spaces. The suitability of sonar sensors for navigating corridors and navigating around static obstacles is examined in this paper. A mobile platform equipped with sonar sensors (or a multi-sensor system offering similar performance) can detect and track nearby stationary barriers. Leveraging the range data from these sensors, appropriate sonar-based control layers can be implemented to prevent collisions with static obstacles. Furthermore, an upper control layer can enable the robot to navigate down corridors using sonar data fusion, wall-follower logic, and heuristic guidance.

By applying Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we simulate the evolution of these fields to determine the Gaussian curvature of the parametric space, examining its behavior across phase transitions. The simulations reveal an unexpected phenomenon termed the \emph{curvature effect}, signifying a pronounced asymmetric geometric deformation within the parametric space triggered by substantial fluctuations in the system's entropy. This asymmetric pattern is linked to the onset of hysteresis, thereby establishing an intrinsic arrow of time within the system's dynamics. Furthermore, we introduce a \emph{complexity effect}, which underscores the asymmetric informational structure inherent in such systems. Collectively, these findings indicate that both an intrinsic complex geometry and a directional arrow of time emerge from random field systems possessing Gaussian probability density functions. These observations may provide critical geometric and dynamical insights into cosmological phenomena, cosmic structure formation, and related stochastic processes. In conclusion, we propose that these effects could offer novel perspectives on interpreting data from large-scale cosmological surveys.
This work advances upon the foundational findings presented in references \cite{HongHong2020, HongHong2021}.

These systems are defined by a white dwarf spin period that deviates slightly (typically by a few percent) from the binary orbital period, being either faster or slower. Their disproportionate detection in soft gamma-ray surveys has prompted speculation that they possess intrinsically harder X-ray spectra. By comparing asynchronous and standard polars to investigate the link between synchronization status and spectral morphology, our analysis of the full asynchronous polar sample suggests they may indeed exhibit harder spectra, though this finding lacks statistical significance. Furthermore, we investigated whether the asymmetry in their spin-orbit desynchronization directions influences spectral shape. Surprisingly, the results indicate no such correlation. Finally, by determining the minimal and maximal synchronization times based on evolutionary constraints, we attempted to establish if these boundaries correspond to distinct evolutionary phases. However, such a correlation was not detected, and the calculated estimation ranges were found to be non-physical. Additionally, a detailed examination of elemental compositions was conducted to search for evolutionary stage correlations; again, no significant correlation was found. Nevertheless, the determined estimated ranges were this time physical, though they spanned several gigayears. These novel insights will aid in refining evolutionary models for this class of CVs. To support this study, we constructed a new catalog for asynchronous polars, which is more comprehensive than any previously available resource.

We detail the implementation of two reduction procedures and apply them to a shared test case. First, we develop a reduction technique rooted in a monolithic framework, solving both fluid and solid domains simultaneously. Subsequently, we present a second technique based on a partitioned (or segregated) method, where the fluid and solid problems are solved independently and coupled via a fixed-point iteration. To ensure that constructive type systems like the Calculus of Constructions (Coq) remain consistent, they must avoid deriving contradictions from valid expressions. On SIMD accelerators like GPUs, this limitation stems primarily from memory allocation and access issues. Although a few libraries offer parallel memory allocation for accelerator devices, they all suffer from uncoalesced memory accesses.

We have identified a broad category of object-oriented programs, including many significant real-world applications, that can be efficiently executed on massively parallel SIMD accelerators. We term this category Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), as it expresses parallelism by executing a specific method across all instances of a given type.

To enable average programmers to utilize fast GPU programming for SMMO applications, we developed DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework. DynaSOAr comprises three core components: (1) a fully parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator; (2) a data layout Domain-Specific Language (DSL); and (3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. By controlling both memory allocation and access, DynaSOAr outperforms state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators.

DynaSOAr enhances memory utilization by adopting a Structure of Arrays (SoA) data layout and reduces memory fragmentation through the efficient management of free and allocated blocks using lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps. Unlike other allocators, our design relies heavily on atomic operations, prioritizing overall application performance over individual thread efficiency.

The data layout DSL translates object methods into efficient, parallel do-all operations on data arrays. This layout separates data memory from code memory, allowing all instances of a specific type to share a single contiguous memory block containing only data arrays.

Our extensive evaluations on GPUs demonstrate that DynaSOAr achieves comparable execution times for standard OOP applications on parallel architectures while offering up to 5.79x improvement for our test applications. Additionally, DynaSOAr delivered significant speedups (ranging from 2.11x to 46.9x) for applications with inherently parallel workloads, such as Monte Carlo simulations. DynaSOAr was also evaluated on multi-GPU systems; our two-node, eight-GPU results show up to a 4.6x improvement over its single-GPU performance. To our knowledge, DynaSOAr represents the first dynamic framework designed for executing SMMO applications on parallel accelerators.

### 1 Introduction

Instance segmentation is a core task in computer vision that involves delineating individual object instances within an image. While significant research has focused on this area, most existing methods rely on heavy neural networks. Although these approaches have delivered impressive outcomes, they suffer from low inference speed and poor memory efficiency due to the vast number of parameters required.

To address these limitations, we turn to implicit neural representations. Recent advancements have enabled these representations to model high-resolution images with significantly reduced memory footprints. Building on this foundation, we propose a method to segment instance masks using implicit functions.

In practice, we observe that when multiple objects of the same class appear in an image, their boundaries can be described by similar boundary patterns. For example, two chairs will have similar front views but distinct back views because of their unique instance coordinates. This leads to the hypothesis that an implicit function can capture the general appearance pattern of a class while also encoding the specific instance details through its input coordinates.

To test this, we employ a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) trained to map image coordinates to discrete mask values. We enhance the MLP's training efficiency and its ability to generalize instance-specific details by applying a Fourier series to the image coordinates before feeding them to the network. To our surprise, this simple strategy yields strong results.

To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to utilize implicit functions for instance segmentation.

In chirped pulses, the temporal variation of frequency relative to the fundamental frequency induces a corresponding time-dependent critical density ($n_c$). We employed a chirp model that extends beyond linear approximations. Specifically, negatively (positively) chirped pulses initially interact with the target via their high (low) frequency components, followed by low (high) frequencies. Our findings indicate that the threshold plasma density required for pulse transmission is elevated for negatively chirped pulses compared to unchirped or positively chirped ones. At higher densities ($6n_c$), the improved transmission of negatively chirped pulses facilitates efficient electron heating, generating a stable, persistent longitudinal electrostatic field behind the target. This creates an electron void that drives ions to expand in both directions, yielding a broad energy spectrum. Furthermore, we introduced a thin, low-density ($< n_c$) secondary layer behind the primary target. Ions from this secondary layer are accelerated as a mono-energetic bunch by the electrostatic field established by the primary layer upon interaction with the negatively chirped pulse. Under optimal conditions, proton energies reach approximately 100 MeV using a 10 fs (intensity fwhm), circularly polarized, Gaussian, negatively chirped laser pulse with a peak intensity of $\sim 8.5\times 10^{20}$ W/cm$^2$. Our results suggest that adjusting the chirp rate enables precise control over ion energies without requiring multi-layer targets. We hope these insights regarding chirped pulse-driven ion acceleration contribute to circularly polarized laser pulse propagation in low-density plasmas and enable mono-energetic ion acceleration using simple, single-layer targets. Additionally, the designed chirp rate offers a pathway for scalable ion therapy applications. Importantly, this laser-plasma interaction scheme utilizes naturally generated electron voids from a single plasma density, removing the need for complex multi-layer target constructions. Target transparency to chirped pulses may also enhance ion acceleration efficiency through quasi-relativistic electron heating. Finally, the proposed target configuration holds significant potential for producing clinically relevant proton beams for cancer treatment using petawatt-class peta-amperes laser systems. This paper addresses the question of determining the maximum value of $\lambda$ such that any 2-edge-coloring of the complete graph on $\mathbb{N}$ guarantees a monochromatic infinite $F$-factor with a vertex set possessing an upper density of at least $\lambda$, for a given finite graph $F$. We establish a novel lower bound for this problem; for specific graphs $F$, including cliques and odd cycles, this bound is optimal as it aligns with a previously known upper bound. Furthermore, in the specific instance where $F$ is a triangle, we provide an explicit lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \approx 0.62203$, which surpasses the earlier best result of $2/3$. We also prove multiple lower bounds for the general case, utilizing two key components: a new threshold of $\frac{3}{4}$ (improving the prior best of $2/3$) and a link-coloring tool developed by Axarodi and Schacht in 2021. Scalar Quantum Electrodynamics (SQED) in $(1+1)$ dimensions serves as a simplified model for $(3+1)$-dimensional Quantum Electrodynamics. While prior attempts to simulate SQED on superconducting quantum computers using the Tolerant Measurement Approximation have successfully distinguished between massive and massless cases, these simulations were limited to very low masses or short evolution times due to hardware constraints. To advance SQED simulation beyond current hardware limits, we must improve both qubit and qudit approaches by developing more efficient circuit designs and leveraging the inherent advantages of qudits. Our findings demonstrate that for the same level of accuracy in the mass gap, qudit simulations are roughly $10^2$ times more resilient to noise. We also demonstrate methods to further enhance measurement precision. This research paves the way for more effective simulations of relativistic quantum field theories on quantum computers. Sources code can be found at https://github.com/aharukaw/Qudits-SQED.

While it has been analytically shown that purely toroidal or purely poloidal fields inevitably develop instabilities, numerical simulations confirm that roughly axisymmetric configurations within stably stratified stars can remain stable. Its utility depends on deriving flow equations that track the evolution of the quantum effective action as a coarse-graining parameter varies. This study details a new strategy for solving these equations by leveraging the fact that renormalization group (RG) equations can be reformulated to mirror fluid dynamics conservation laws. This analogy enables two main advancements: first, it permits the use of robust numerical methods from fluid dynamics to solve RG equations, ensuring reliable handling of nonanalytic behaviors in the effective action's flow, such as those arising from spontaneous symmetry breaking. Second, the fluid dynamics parallel offers fresh perspectives on interpreting RG flows and their inherent irreversibility. We demonstrate this connection using zero-dimensional quantum field theory models, with a discussion of extending it to higher dimensions. These results are anticipated to enhance future FRG investigations of quantum field theories in higher dimensions, improving both qualitative understanding and quantitative accuracy. The specific formalism presented here will be applied to zero-dimensional quantum gravity in this work.

Zero-dimensional quantum field theories offer a distinct environment for examining renormalization group flows. Their simplicity allows all quantities to be computed exactly, enabling a direct comparison between these calculations and other methods like lattice Monte Carlo simulations. In this paper, we explore field theory quantities in zero dimensions using FRG equations for both real and complex theories. Our findings indicate excellent agreement between the FRG results and exact solutions, while also highlighting the significance of maintaining the stochastic structure of the FRG equations.

We present an overview of the duality between renormalization group equations and fluid dynamics. This connection allows us to utilize sophisticated numerical techniques typically employed in fluid simulations to solve renormalization group equations. A primary benefit of this approach is its ability to accurately treat theories exhibiting phase transitions and non-Gaussian fixed points. Furthermore, this framework clarifies key features of renormalization group equations, such as the absence of time reversibility and the presence of a regulator-dependent "pressure" term. Finally, we outline how this formalism can be extended to higher dimensions.

It allows users to query lyrics, song metadata, audio files, or any combination thereof, efficiently delivering relevant results. Statistical tests reveal that protostellar cores possess greater mass than starless cores, even when accounting for biases related to temperature and opacity. We propose that this mass disparity signifies core growth occurring after formation. Consequently, massive star formation may not necessarily originate from massive prestellar cores, contingent upon the rate of this collapse-after-formation process. The implications of this potential mass acquisition mechanism for the overall formation of massive stars remain an area for future research. Furthermore, the presence of these protostellar cores, which are linked to molecular outflows at the earliest observable stages, challenges the hypothesis that outflows are triggered by the dynamical interaction of infalling gas with a disk. This paper investigates the algebraic and relational semantics of G\"odel modal logics by utilizing the duality between finite G\"odel algebras and finite forests, defined as finite posets where principal downsets are totally ordered. We examine various subvarieties of the basic variety of G\"odel algebras with two modal operators (GAOs) and their associated classes of forest frames, featuring either single or dual accessibility relations. These relational structures function as prelinear adaptations of standard relational semantics for intuitionistic modal logic. Specifically, we analyze two primary extensions of finite G\"odel algebras with operators: one derived from adding Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intuitionistic logic fragments, and another based on Fischer Servi axioms. Furthermore, we establish J\'onsson-Tarski-style representation theorems for the distinct types of finite GAOs addressed in this study. Finally, we derive sound and complete characterizations for the syntactically distinct but semantically equivalent formulations of the relevant G\"odel modal logics. This work serves as a sequel to [L.~H\'{e}nat and S.~Tabchourli, Algebraic and relational semantics of G\"odel modal logics with a single modal operator, 2020]. H\'{e}nat's initial research [I.~H\'{e}nat, Notes on Godel modal logics, Thesis, University of Lille 3, 2016] preceded our collaborative investigations. Within our research program, we developed complete finite G\"odel algebras with operators (GAOs) possessing two dual accessibility relations, which we presented to the model theory community at the second European Conference on Mathematical Logic (ECML-15) in Athens, Greece, and the Fifth International Conference on Algebraic Logic and Its Applications (ICLQA-8) in Qu\'{e}bec City, Canada. A promising strategy to address this mystery involves correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, as neutrinos directly trace hadronic interactions and remain unaffected by magnetic deflection. This paper outlines three distinct methods for correlating the arrival directions of these particles. Data on neutrinos come from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES, while UHECR data (with energies exceeding ~50 EeV) are sourced from the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array. Both datasets offer enhanced statistics and refined reconstructions compared to our 2015 findings. To account for potential energy-dependent effects in UHECRs and ensure fair comparisons across datasets, we divide UHECRs into two energy intervals. Correlations were assessed using the standard transverse test and additional statistics tailored to the specific characteristics of UHECR propagation. We examined various hypotheses, including point sources, extended sources, and random sky distributions. As in our previous study, no significant individual source—neither point nor extended—was identified. However, an excess of correlated events between IceCube's high-energy neutrinos (above 270 TeV) and Auger-data-derived UHECRs suggests a potential common origin, though this excess does not correspond to any known point or extended source. Furthermore, an extended excess of neutrinos relative to the UHECR sky is visible when restricting the analysis to the highest UHECR energies. No similar excesses were detected between IceCube's lower-energy neutrinos and UHECRs. Overall, no significant excesses or deficits were found against the isotropic background for any of the proposed hypotheses. Finally, we confirmed that measurement uncertainties and flux knees can explain the observed excesses between IceCube's highest-energy neutrinos and Auger-data-derived UHECRs, while a key finding from our prior study explains the excess between IceCube's 270 TeV neutrinos and the UHECR cutoff. Despite this prevalence, there is a scarcity of research dedicated to interpreting the opaque nature of these deep-learning algorithms. Existing studies suggest that such scoring models are easily manipulable. This paper investigates the causes of their surprising adversarial brittleness. Leveraging recent interpretability advancements, we examine the relative importance of features like coherence, content, vocabulary, and relevance in automated scoring. We analyze the phenomena of oversensitivity (where minor input changes cause significant score fluctuations) and overstability (where major input changes yield minimal score shifts). Our findings reveal that, despite being trained as "end-to-end" models with rich contextual embeddings like BERT, AES models function similarly to bag-of-words models. A few isolated words often dictate the final score without necessitating context, rendering the models largely overstable. This contrasts sharply with recent probing studies on pre-trained language models, which demonstrate their ability to encode complex linguistic features such as morphology and parts of speech. Furthermore, we observe that these models have internalized dataset biases, leading to oversensitivity. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose detection-based protection models capable of identifying samples exhibiting oversensitivity and overstability while maintaining high accuracy. Our results show that these models can successfully detect anomalous attribution patterns and flag adversarial inputs. Additionally, we demonstrate that AES models can be inverted to scrape nearly the entire training dataset. Finally, we test the hypothesis that syntactically stripped datasets enhance model robustness. We hope these insights into the interpretability and adversarial weaknesses of AES models will motivate developers, deployers, and regulators to implement protection measures against vulnerabilities in automated essay scoring.

Additional outcomes include extending the analysis to the scenario where increments possess a strictly positive mean, as well as investigating two-scenario mixes: (a) concatenating a sequence of asymmetric zero-mean steps with another of symmetric steps, and (b) linking sequences featuring a positive bias. Nucleus segmentation technology is commonly employed to automate these tasks; however, training robust segmentation models remains challenging due to issues like nucleus adhesion, stacking, and excessive background fusion. Although recent approaches based on point annotation have significantly enhanced model performance, they still require experienced pathologists to provide the necessary annotations. To leverage the benefits of point-annotation-based methods while reducing manual workload and improving the efficiency and accuracy of cancer diagnosis, an automatic nucleus detection algorithm is needed to efficiently locate nuclei and extract valuable information from pathological images. This paper introduces a W-shaped network for automatic nucleus detection. Unlike traditional U-Net-based methods that directly map pathology images to target masks, our approach decomposes the detection task into two sub-tasks: first mapping the original image to a binary mask, and then mapping that binary mask to a dense mask containing 300 evenly distributed positive sample points. Experimental results indicate that this W-shaped network not only achieves superior performance but also reduces manual annotation time, enhancing both the quantity and quality of cancer-related dataset annotations. The proposed method opens up prospects for further research in automatically extracting precise and high-value information from pathological images. In the broader context of artificial intelligence-assisted cancer diagnosis, our approach paves the way for developing comprehensive automatic cancer diagnosis systems utilizing only point annotations.

Pathology images are crucial for identifying, classifying, and monitoring cancer. Automatic cancer diagnosis relies on locating and counting cells within these images. Recent methods using sparse point annotations have achieved remarkable results by mapping image points to a dense mask. However, these techniques often fail to accurately segment adhering nuclei and struggle to generalize when cell density changes. This paper introduces a novel W-shaped network that maps sparse cell annotations to a dense mask for cancer diagnosis. The network employs an auxiliary task of mapping the original image directly to a binary mask, which significantly enhances performance on cells with overlapping boundaries and improves accuracy across cells of varying densities. Evaluations across three public datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques. Specifically, our approach achieves a mean intersection over union (mIOU) of 88.16% on the CTR dataset, 86.78% on the PanNuke dataset, and 88.71% on the DREAM CH dataset.

We introduce "SelfPlay with Value Expansion," a straightforward algorithm designed to accelerate policy optimization in multi-agent games. Our theoretical analysis proves the algorithm's sample efficiency, and empirical results show substantial improvements in training speed for agents learning cooperative policies in multi-agent Atari games. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/danijar/rew_breakdown_mdp.

Despite the success of policy optimization in learning policies for multi-agent settings, the field lacks robust statistical guarantees regarding both end-to-end reward optimization and policy performance. We analyze the statistical efficiency of generic policy optimization algorithms, focusing on two information sources that provide insights into the reward function: additional queries of the function and auxiliary tasks. We characterize the minimax optimal sample complexity for a specific class of Markov Decision Processes, and our proposed algorithm with hyperparameter tuning achieves this bound. Our results offer new understanding of the tradeoffs in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning information structure and inspire future work on designing RL algorithms that maximize these information sources. This research advances the understanding of policy optimization in multi-agent reinforcement learning, and the experimental code can be found at https://github.com/danijar/rew_breakdown_mdp.
